The company claims more than 30 years of field experience in over 30 countries, supporting hundreds of programs.

Caseloads span GPS tracking, radio frequency monitoring and alcohol testing, all watched from a single platform. One home curfew unit connects over an LTE network, Wi-Fi or a landline and includes a handset for voice communication. The command center for a monitoring program is EM Manager, and a mobile version lets staff perform essential monitoring functions in the field. The monitoring centers operate around the clock, every day of the week. Customizable services on offer include alert triage, outbound alert resolution calls and officer notifications.

Corrections agencies and probation services worldwide are named as the customers, whether they are starting new programs or expanding existing ones. The pitch to those agencies is an alternative to incarceration that lowers recidivism, improves reintegration and reduces prison overcrowding. paragraphs: Recidiviz is a non-profit that partners with criminal justice agencies on technology and data. Its customers are state departments of corrections and the staff who run prisons and community supervision.

The Corrections Platform is modular, so an agency can replace its legacy software entirely or plug in modules as it wants them. Underneath, the organization joins disconnected agency databases into one standardized data layer that feeds the tools above it. Those tools surface people who are eligible for programs, reclassification, or release.

Day-to-day users are administrators, case managers, and officers, whom the team says it goes into the field to talk with before designing anything. The organization says it works with 19 state departments of corrections responsible for almost 1 in 2 people in U.S. prisons and on community supervision. It began as a volunteer project at Google. In 2019 it became a standalone non-profit.

paragraphs: Corrisoft is a supervision technology company that sells electronic monitoring tools to the agencies responsible for people serving sentences in the community. The company builds its offering around the AIR suite, which it says started with AIR Mobile, the first smartphone-based supervision solution.

Staff work from a web-based platform that ties the field tools together and carries case management, GPS tracking and calendar functions. Supervising administrators can also run monitoring and reporting from a Supervisor app on their own phones. On the participant side, a check-in app provides passive GPS monitoring and facial detection for scheduled or randomized check-ins. Hardware in the same suite includes a one-piece ankle monitoring device. A portable alcohol monitoring device pairs with the phone apps so tests can be taken away from an office.

Supervisors can also assign coursework, appointing participants to virtual courses from the Corrections Rehabilitation Institute through MaxxLMS and tracking their progress. An in-house call center answers participant questions and handles technical troubleshooting. The company frames the need around program violations, citing a figure of 25% of state jail populations facing incarceration for them.

paragraphs: 4Sight Labs sells a biometric monitoring system for correctional facilities, meant to help staff watch over the health of people held in custody. Its main product, OverWatch, is presented as the core of a unified correctional biometric platform built for settings where ordinary monitoring falls short.

People in custody wear sensors that track heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature and motion, along with other indicators of physiological distress. Readings are processed as they arrive, so that anomalies produce structured notifications instead of an after-the-fact review. Thresholds can be set by the facility so staff hear about a pattern that points toward a crisis.

The company says the platform is built for county detention centers, state systems, private facilities and complex housing units. It also states that the technology is designed and manufactured in the United States, with a controlled hardware and firmware supply chain. The site reports that the Harford County Sheriff's Office publicly announced putting OverWatch into its custody and safety strategy.

Behind the hardware sits Command Cloud, a platform of integrated applications and services for corrections staff. Long-range readers create customizable zones over housing units, out of cell areas and corridors. Officers carry a rugged Android handheld for data collection and evidence gathering. Check frequencies can be configured by location and inmate classification. Electronic medication orders carry administration times, allergies, dosage, frequencies and routes.

The company says over 75,000 corrections staff across the United States rely on it. Facilities need no servers of their own, since the system is cloud based. It integrates with a wide range of jail management systems as well as offender and case management systems. An ongoing System Renewal Fee covers software upgrades for Command Cloud and Mobile Command. That fee is invoiced 12 months after go-live.

The jail management platform is browser-based and built for county and local jails, handling inmate records, biometrics and analytical reporting. paragraphs: DigitalOptometrics is a technology company whose software lets a patient sitting in an optical exam location receive a comprehensive eye examination from a licensed optometrist working somewhere else. The exam and the prescription are meant to be done in under 30 minutes.

The visit starts with preliminary testing carried out on site in the clinical area. A video slit lamp records high-definition footage of the outside structures of the eye for the remote doctor to evaluate. That doctor can control the phoropter remotely and reviews the findings in real time. A comprehensive exam is described as covering ten subject areas, including a vision analysis. At the end the optometrist finalizes and delivers the glasses or contact lens prescription within minutes.

Buyers are optical providers, and the company describes itself as optometrist founded and optometrist driven. Dr. Fried formed the company in 2016 and assembled a team of optical software development specialists. The technology was shown publicly at the Vision Expo in New York City. The company states that its system is used in more than 30 states in the United States and in Canada.

after.name: Guard1
after.description: The PIPE guard-tour hardware and software documenting inmate well-being checks (TimeKeeping Systems)

paragraphs: Guard1 sells hardware and software that prove where staff have been and when, working with correctional agencies, behavioral healthcare facilities and security teams. The central device is The PIPE, a wand that staff touch to a metal memory button on the wall to document that rounds were completed.

In practice an officer touches the button with the wand, and a red light flash or a beep confirms the check was recorded. A mobile option swaps the wand for a handheld digital logbook that shows a real-time task list of the checks and activities still to be completed. A separate duress system puts a device on staff and visitors that sends a signal once per second. When the button is pressed, the location is shown on a control room monitor.

The company says hundreds of agencies have used The PIPE to document officer rounds and hold defensible logs for inspections and incidents. It puts its corrections figure at over 1400 customers served, including 20+ DOCs, hundreds of county jails, ICE facilities and juvenile facilities. For guard tour work more broadly it dates the product to 1990 and claims over 100,000 customers.

before.name: CourtCall
before.description: Remote appearance and virtual hearing services for courts

after.name: CourtCall
after.description: Remote appearance and virtual hearing services for courts

paragraphs: CourtCall sells a remote appearance service that lets attorneys and other participants take part in court proceedings without traveling to the courthouse. The company says its platform can meet the remote collaboration needs of a court, law firm, administrative agency or corrections facility.

Appearances run over video, audio or telephone. Attorneys use it to appear for routine matters in civil, family, criminal, probate and bankruptcy cases. Participants schedule, continue or cancel an appearance before the hearing. Before doing so, the site asks users to check its list of participating courts.

CourtCall states that it was established in 1995 to make remote court appearances simple, accessible and affordable for all parties. It describes providing supported remote legal collaboration services throughout the United States, Canada and worldwide. A home page announcement says the company was the successful bidder on the Colorado Judicial Department solicitation RFP #25005 and entered into an agreement with the department.

quote.text: Remote Justice. Simplified.

before.name: For The Record (FTR)
before.description: Digital court recording and record management technology for judiciaries

after.name: For The Record (FTR)
after.description: Digital court recording and record management technology for judiciaries

paragraphs: For The Record makes recording technology for courts, capturing what is said in a proceeding and turning it into text that can be searched. One audience is court administrators trying to keep operations running at lower cost. Judges are a second audience, able to pull up audio, video, and speech-to-text without leaving the bench.

Recording runs on multiple audio channels, so individual speakers stay distinct even when they talk over one another. Courts that need local infrastructure can run the FTR Gold software in the courthouse rather than in the cloud. The cloud option is described as centralized storage built to NIST 800-53 Rev. 5 with more than a thousand security and privacy controls. Access is governed by role-based permissions, audit trails, and encryption of both transmission and storage.

The company says it supports courts in more than 80 countries. Its software is API-ready and meant to sit alongside the case management and evidence systems a court already runs. The work extends past software into specifying equipment and installing courtroom hardware.

quote.text: A court record is the official, permanent account of a legal case.

provenance.quote: advanced audio capture, real-time speech-to-text, secure cloud-based storage, and instant access to records
help court administrators run more efficient, economical, and resilient operations
Instantly access audio, video, and speech-to-text transcripts without leaving the bench.
Multi-channel audio capture isolates speakers for clarity, even with overtalk in noisy environments.
Reliable, on-premises recording for courts with local infrastructure needs
Centralized, secure storage meeting NIST 800-53 Rev. 5 standards with 1,200+ security and privacy controls
role-based access, audit trails, and encrypted transmission and storage
Supporting courts in more than 80 countries around the world
API-ready and designed to work with your existing Case Management Systems, evidence management, or other infrastructure
from equipment specification to hardware installation

paragraphs: May Mobility develops autonomous driving technology and brings it to ride-hail platforms, cities, campuses and businesses. Its operations run from rural Minnesota to Atlanta and the dense streets of Japan.

The cornerstone of the technology is a system the company calls Multi-Policy Decision Making. It is described as a real-time, reinforcement-learning AI algorithm. Vehicles generate training examples relevant to their current environment and learn while driving. The sensor stack and the decision-making platform work together to monitor the road and run simulations of possible situations and hazards.

An autonomous ride-hail preview is live on Lyft. The site notes a first autonomous vehicle fleet deployed with Lyft in Atlanta. It also lists a strategic partnership with Uber to scale autonomous vehicles. An investment from Grab is tied to expansion into Southeast Asia. The chief executive is Edwin Olson.

paragraphs: Blaise Transit sells software for running transit without a fixed route or a fixed schedule. It was built to equip municipalities, cities, transit agencies, and transit operators. One platform covers demand-responsive service, paratransit, fixed-route integrations, and private shuttles.

The system comes in three parts. Blaise Engine lets operators set the vehicles, drivers, stops, and payment options that make up a transit system. A passenger app is available on Android, iOS, and as a website, where riders book, pay, and follow live vehicle locations. A driver app supplies turn-by-turn navigation on optimized routes and a passenger manifest at each stop. A separate simulations service recommends which transit models to implement and the parameters for each service.

Blaise was started in 2018 by a small group of transit-loving engineers. The site says more than 70 communities have chosen it to optimize their transit services. It reports working with agencies serving a few hundred rides a month up to a few million. Its optimization models are described as patent pending and customizable.

paragraphs: Beep plans, deploys and manages autonomous shuttles for private and public communities. The services answer demand for alternative modes of transportation within communities, campuses and municipalities. Routes run inside geo-fenced areas at a controlled speed.

Deployments are built around first and last-mile trips, linking retail to residential areas, remote parking to campus amenities, and underserved communities to transit stops and stations. The service portfolio runs from upfront analysis, planning and design through turnkey operation of an autonomous mobility network. Underneath sits AutonomOS, a vehicle-agnostic platform for multi-passenger autonomous mobility services. It plans service modes from fixed route to demand-responsive variants. In-cabin monitoring built on machine learning lets remote supervisors react to a passenger safety or roadway issue.

The platform is built for public transit operators and authorities. The company reports deployments in six states and two dozen deployments overall. The purpose-built shuttles carry ADA-compliant wheelchair ramps and restraints. One announced project, ATL Spoke, is a pilot with Atlanta Beltline that the company says is in service and open to the public.

The stated aim is to extend public transport with a weatherproof first and last mile link running from a bus, tram or train stop to the doorstep.

The current shuttle, MiCa, is electronically limited to 25 km/h. The specification lists operating time of up to twenty hours a day. One case study describes a scheduled last mile service in Takamatsu, Japan, with the shuttle operated by Boldly. That route ran 2.6 kilometres between a car park and a viewpoint.

paragraphs: Ecolane sells scheduling and dispatch software designed for public transit agencies that operate paratransit, non-emergency medical transportation, and microtransit services. Whichever way a trip is booked, the optimization that follows is autonomous and does not require manual intervention from a human.

The software optimizes service at the individual trip level and updates schedules as conditions change during the service day. That lets agencies account for no-shows, cancellations, delays, and staffing changes without rebuilding schedules manually. Eligibility rules, reporting, and compliance are integrated into daily operations. Managers can capture data for every vehicle, including rides per hour, run utilization, on-time performance, and deadhead. For medical trips, the platform helps agencies locate providers, verify rider eligibility, and schedule trips with vehicles equipped to accommodate rider needs.

Agencies supported by city, county, state, or federal funds are the intended buyers. The company says it is a U.S.-based company with U.S.-based product, engineering, and support teams. It states that its self-service applications are compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 Level AA. It also says it holds three clean Voluntary Product Accessibility Templates. The hosted service is described as providing significant cost savings for transit agencies.

paragraphs: 3AM Innovations sells FLORIAN, safety software that shows a command center where every responder and resource is while an incident is under way. The company says it was started by firefighters, and it now aims the same idea at any team that has to keep track of people in the field.

FLORIAN runs on the phone or tablet a responder already carries, sending location and movement back to the command center in real time. It reports position in three dimensions, including elevation, so command can tell where someone sits inside a structure. Licensing splits in two, with the Advanced plan positioned for teams that regularly face complicated calls. That tier adds geofencing and Mayday alerts. Groups that need to stand something up quickly can order deployable kits, which ship with devices already carrying Advanced licenses.

Beyond the fire service, the company points to campus security teams and the organizers of large events such as marathons. 3AM says it belongs to purchasing vehicles including GSA and SAVVIK, which can let a buyer skip the RFP process. It also offers support services covering setup, training and deployment.

paragraphs: Prepared builds assistive artificial intelligence for 911 centers, aimed at the people who answer emergency calls and send help. The company states that it is now the intelligence layer of Axon 911, an emergency communications platform it describes as covering the full lifecycle of a call.

During a call the software transcribes speech as it happens, captures details automatically, and translates, so staff can watch the caller rather than the keyboard. Incoming audio is translated automatically in more than 40 languages, according to the homepage. The call-taking page claims support for over 200 languages for callers who do not speak English. Call-takers can also request a livestream from the caller to see the scene. A separate voice assistant answers non-emergency lines and converses with callers in English or Spanish.

Buyers are public safety answering points, the centers that take 911 calls. Prepared describes the product as a cloud based platform laid over existing systems, with no rip and replace required. Supervisors get automated quality assurance and keyword triggers for visibility into the operation. Its chief executive, Michael Chime, appears in a recorded discussion with three 911 leaders about non-emergency calls.

paragraphs: Corti sells AI infrastructure to developers building healthcare and life science software. The pitch is that a team can ship clinical features without standing up the model infrastructure underneath.

paragraphs: Comtech works on mission-critical communications systems that underpin public safety, global security, supply chains and public infrastructure. Its Satellite and Space Communications segment supplies secure, all-domain communications solutions for military missions. Allerium, formerly the Terrestrial and Wireless Networks segment, sells what the company calls dependable, life-saving solutions to public safety professionals.

On the public safety side, its equipment connects originating service providers and public safety answering points, the centers known as PSAPs. The company has announced Allerium Mira, a cloud-native call handling platform for NG9-1-1. It also offers Global Navigation Satellite Systems reference data feeds for location-based products and services. Its wireless portfolio includes end-to-end SMSC and Wireless Emergency Alerts solutions.

The business began as Comtech Laboratories, Inc., founded in 1967 in Smithtown, New York. It is now headquartered in Chandler, Arizona. Ken Traub is listed as chairman, president and chief executive officer. The company has announced a definitive agreement to sell most of its satellite and space communications business to Gilat.

paragraphs: Aurelian builds software for the 911 centers known as public safety answering points. One of its two products answers non-emergency calls instantly, so callers are not left on hold. The other sits with call-takers during emergencies and gives real-time, context-aware guidance without taking control.

The automated line resolves routine calls on its own. It detects and escalates emergencies to a person. During live calls, the guidance tool surfaces the relevant SOP checklist for the incident. It also flags missing information before the call ends. The company says the system learns a center's workflows, SOPs, and systems in order to support the full call flow. Aurelian states that humans remain in control of emergencies and decision-making.

The customers page says PSAPs around the country use Aurelian to cut non-emergency workload and return time to their teams. Published stories include Hamilton County 911 automating more than 300 non-emergency calls a day. The about page says the founders, Max and James, were building call automation technology for hair salons before starting the company. That insight led them to pivot to public safety and build for PSAPs.

quote.text: Automate the calls that don't need a telecommunicator.

paragraphs: IamResponding sells an end-to-end emergency response system for first responders. The system is described as covering dispatch communication, incident coordination and department management.

Responders get time-saving alerts and critical incident data. An integration from RapidSOS is advertised on the home page. paragraphs: Intrado sells call handling and management systems for emergency response. It describes itself as the connective tissue that gets the right help to the right location as quickly as possible.

Alongside the call center products, one line keeps employees safe wherever they work while meeting state and federal regulations. Another covers incident management for schools from prevention through response and recovery. For carriers, call routing, location and data products connect subscribers to emergency services and keep providers compliant. Network services are offered to improve call routing and data sharing and to deliver on i3 compliance. ECaTS, the Emergency Call Tracking System, generates descriptive reports from 9-1-1 call data.

The company puts its history in the emergency services industry at 45 years. That history includes acquisitions of Lucent Public Safety, Positron Public Safety Systems, ECaTS, 911 ETC and 911 Enable. Headquarters are in Longmont, Colorado, with a manufacturing site in Montreal, Quebec. The company reports approximately 950 employees worldwide, most of them in the Longmont and Montreal regions.

after.name: Handtevy
after.description: Pediatric emergency dosing system and app for EMS agencies

paragraphs: Handtevy sells clinical workflow software for emergency medicine, pairing precision dosing and protocol access for clinicians with control and reporting for the administrators who oversee them. The buyers are agencies and hospitals looking to raise their standard of emergency care.

Handtevy Mobile puts precision dosing, real-time protocols, and clinical decision support directly in clinicians' hands. Weight-based calculations are cross-checked against clinical thresholds and customized to local protocols. An admin portal lets administrators manage pharmacology, protocols, order sets, and checklists across an organization and control exactly what clinicians see at the point of care. The software connects directly with ePCR and EHR platforms, which the company says involves no PHI exposure and no IT infrastructure.

The company says it is used by more than 200,000 clinicians in all 50 states. Pediatric Emergency Standards, Inc. has operated under the name Handtevy since 2010, offering evidence-based software to healthcare providers domestically and internationally. Its founder, Dr. Peter Antevy, is a practicing pediatric emergency medicine physician and EMS Medical Director. The company started in pediatrics and now describes its goal as improving emergency care for adults as well.

paragraphs: Carbyne builds and supports Axon 911 Core, a cloud-native infrastructure layer deployed in agencies across the United States and internationally. Its call-handling product, APEX, pulls call management capabilities into a single user interface for telecommunicators.

Patented live video lets responders see through the eyes of a caller. Location tools pinpoint a caller and track movement as permitted. AI-powered translation arrives directly on the call taker's screen. During call surges, an AI triage tool sorts through calls to identify redundant bystander and onlooker reports, freeing call takers for other emergencies. A continuity option has the AT&T Resolution Center redirect 911 calls and texts to devices running APEX Continuity. That reroute is triggered manually by the center rather than automatically.

The company states 99.999% call-handling uptime in the cloud. It describes the platform as providing the security of AWS GovCloud. Carbyne counts more than 100 partners and over 40 integrations on its open platform. The site names Orleans Parish Communication District as a center using its Emergency Call Triage.

before.name: Tablet Command

after.name: Tablet Command
after.description: Mobile incident command and response for fire/EMS departments

paragraphs: Tablet Command makes mobile incident command and response software for fire and EMS agencies. Commanders run an incident on a digital command board, dragging and dropping unit assignments.

The software is built on the iPad platform. A commander can tap and drag responding apparatus onto a scene, track progress against critical checklists, and time-stamp every maneuver and benchmark. Maps carry pre-plans and custom layers for hydrants, hospitals, landing zones, flood hazards and fire trails. The app is native and designed to run entirely independent of internet connectivity. It connects to CAD systems and integrates Esri GIS map layers, pre-plans, FireMapper and AVL.

The site reports over 250,000 incidents managed, covering everyday calls and multi-agency coordination. The product is also positioned as a complete replacement for mobile data terminals in the fire service. San Bernardino County Fire is named as using it in every front line response unit. A case study describes Stockton Fire Department turning to it as an MDT replacement and fire ground accountability tool.

paragraphs: EasyVote Solutions sells software that modernizes election administration, designed specifically for election offices. The buyers are city, county and state election offices. One module handles poll worker scheduling, training, communication and performance tracking in one system.

An asset tracking module combines tracking, chain of custody, GPS tracking of equipment, and reporting and audit history. Support staff are described as experts in both technical support and election knowledge. Pricing and licensing agreements are simple and do not require a long-term commitment.

paragraphs: Clear Ballot Group builds voting technology for the officials who run elections. The company started out doing post-election auditing. Its stated position is paper ballots that voters can review and verify.

paragraphs: Hart InterCivic sells voting systems and election services to the officials who run elections. In one configuration, voters mark a paper ballot with a pen and the ballot is scanned to capture the vote digitally. A hybrid option combines touchscreen voting with a voter-verifiable paper trail. Absentee and mail ballots are handled through central scanning.

On the paper-based products, voter choices are never encoded in a digital seal for tabulation. Products carry role-based controls meant to keep an election transparent end to end. The company announced certification of a newer product line, Vanguard, to the VVSG 2.0 standard by the Election Assistance Commission. Within that line, Flex is a universal ballot marking device. Vault handles the scanning of ballots, whether marked by hand or by machine. Workspace covers end-to-end election management.

Hart says it has worked side by side with election professionals for more than 100 years. Its regional offices span coast to coast. The company also states that Vanguard is the only voting system available in the United States that delivers on both the latest EAC standard and the conditions of the executive order it cites.

paragraphs: Aristotle sells software, data, and consulting to political campaigns, political action committees, and advocacy groups. Its campaign management product, Campaign Manager, is cloud-based and covers compliance, fundraising, and accounting reporting. The firm also sells voter and consumer data to campaigns, PACs, corporations, and advocacy organizations in the United States and abroad.

The compliance practice files campaign finance, lobbying, pay-to-play, and Foreign Agent Registration Act reports federally, in 49 of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico. That team of attorneys and paralegals is described as assisting over 230 clients with campaign finance, lobbying, and government ethics compliance. A division called Integrity sells identity and age verification products to commercial and government buyers. Overseas, the company says it has worked with candidates and political parties from Afghanistan to Ukraine and Kenya to Georgia.

Two brothers started the firm in 1983 to build what they described as the first campaign finance and reporting database. It is headquartered on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC. Compliance services are led by a former two-term Federal Election Commission chairman. The company claims that over more than 40 years almost every U.S. president has used its solutions, along with senatorial and congressional campaigns and state party initiatives from both major parties. It presents itself as a non-partisan provider open to members of all parties.

paragraphs: Fort Orange Press is a printing and mailing company, family-owned and operated since 1905. It handles the production, printing, and mailing of essential documents for federal, state, county, and local governments. Election ballot printing and mailing services are a central part of that work.

Services run from planning, design, printing, and variable data-processing through inserting, finishing, fulfillment, mailing, shipping, tracking, and reporting. For elections, the company has developed tools that can better format and prepare voter databases. Printing and inserting pass through a security crosscheck system that uses barcodes and multiple cameras to match all components of the ballot package. A proprietary reporting platform gives clients real-time production and USPS tracking data. That platform also lets voters look up and track their ballot through the mail stream.

Beyond ballots, government agencies order property tax statements, appraisal notices, utility bills, and business licenses. Work is produced from a manufacturing facility in Albany, NY. The company calls itself a proud union shop. It also describes itself as a second-generation business. It states that it is SOC 2 Type II compliant, tested annually. Since 2012 it has held a G7 Master Qualified status for proofing and press equipment.

quote.text: Partner with states to uphold Democracy by ensuring that every ballot is printed and mailed according to the highest standards of accuracy, security and transparency.

paragraphs: Enhanced Voting sells an electronic ballot delivery solution for states and localities. paragraphs: BallotTrax tracks the status of every mail-in ballot and sends voters proactive alerts telling them where their ballot is, from printed to accepted. The company calls it a mail ballot locator and notification system. It is available in select counties, and voters can check whether their own county is eligible.

By integrating with state and county election offices, print vendors and USPS, the system knows when a ballot has been printed and mailed, returned, received and accepted for counting. Voters can choose notifications by text, email or voice alert. Election officials get tracking, reports and branding customization. Those reports are meant to help run a better election and reduce administrative costs through better forecasting and planning.

BallotTrax is a division of i3logix, Inc., based in Denver, Colorado. The site announces a second U.S. patent for its mail ballot tracking and voter notification system. It also posted that BallotTrax achieved SOC 2 compliance. Among the testimonials on the page is one attributed to the director of Multnomah County Elections in Portland.

paragraphs: Democracy Works is a nonpartisan nonprofit that builds tools meant to make it easier for voters to take part in every election. It works with election officials, major platforms, civic organizations and companies so that voters can reach accurate information.

TurboVote, the voter engagement platform, offers personalized support across the whole voting journey. Underneath it sits official election information collected, verified and published straight from state and local election offices. An Elections API delivers that enterprise-grade data across thousands of elections at every level of government. The Voting Information Project gathers voting location data directly from election officials and distributes it to voters through the Google Civic Information API. Participating jurisdictions are not charged for that program. In 2025 the organization published data for 3,462 elections across all 50 states, covering municipal, school board, county and other local contests.

The organization was founded in 2010 with the goal of making voting easier for Americans. It is a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It has also partnered with platforms such as Perplexity AI and Anthropic to place reliable election information in the AI space. On the employer side, the Civic Alliance it co-founded with the CAA Foundation supports more than 1,300 member businesses.

after.name: VotingWorks

paragraphs: VotingWorks is a nonpartisan nonprofit that builds election technology for the officials who run American elections. There are two products. VxSuite is a complete voting system designed to the latest federal standard. The organization calls it the only open-source voting system used in United States elections. Arlo is an open-source application for auditing vote tabulation after an election.

Voters mark a paper ballot by hand or with a ballot-marking device, then scan it in under three seconds. A full precinct sets up in under three minutes and the equipment folds down for transport. Arlo audits tabulation whether the ballots were counted on VxSuite or on another vendor's system, using peer-reviewed statistics. Source code and documentation are published for anyone to verify. Software integrity can be checked in the field in 30 seconds.

Jurisdictions in New Hampshire and Mississippi run real elections on the voting system. Nine states are listed as using Arlo for statewide risk-limiting audits, among them Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Texas. The work dates to 2018. It is organized as a 501c3, funded by equipment sales and support, government contracts and grants, and donations. The equipment complies with the Help America Vote Act, and HAVA grants can be used to buy it.

after.name: Disaster Tech

paragraphs: Disaster Tech builds PRATUS, a platform for AI-driven emergency management aimed at organizations and communities. The product provides AI-powered real-time data insights. The company frames the work as protecting lives and property, from extreme weather to critical infrastructure failures.

PRATUS integrates live weather data, critical infrastructure impact models and analytics for near-instant situational awareness. One view brings together objectives, assets and operational tasks. Its AI lets users generate SITREPs, access real-time updates and produce after-action reports in seconds. The platform also supports training and exercises, from tabletop drills to full-scale deployments. It is available for purchase through the Microsoft Teams App Store.

The company describes itself as a certified Veteran-Owned Business committed to advancing public safety and resilience. It is headquartered in Alexandria, VA. Contract vehicles are offered so government, defense, energy and public safety organizations can reach the platform. Sean Griffin is CEO and co-founder, and previously served as Director for Incident Management Integration Policy on the U.S. National Security Council at the White House.

paragraphs: Juvare sells critical operations software for organizations that need to anticipate disruption and protect communities and assets. Its best-known line, WebEOC Nexus, was built for real-time coordination, routine efficiency, and incident-level accountability from a cloud-based command center.

WebEOC consolidates internal and external data sources into built-in boards so teams work from current information. During an incident, teams track incident progress, assign tasks, deploy resources, and communicate across jurisdictions. Afterward, they document lessons learned, analyze performance metrics, and facilitate After-Action Reviews. A federal product called UCP runs on FedRAMP High and IL5-authorized infrastructure. Juvare HealthSuite covers routine disruptions through major disasters, letting healthcare teams track resources, share data, and maintain operations.

The company says UCP is used by more than 60 federal programs and all 50 US states for presidential inaugurations, disaster response, and operational continuity. Healthcare systems use HealthSuite for multi-site incident management, patient tracking, and regulatory compliance during emergencies. Its patient tracking tools are described as compliant with CMS, TJC, NEMSIS and HHS standards.

before.description: Digital asset management and media libraries for DMOs and tourism boards

after.name: Brandkit
after.description: Digital asset management and media libraries for DMOs and tourism boards

paragraphs: Brandkit gives an organization one searchable, shareable home for its logos, guidelines, images, video, presentations, stories and press releases. It bundles a brand portal, media center, brand guidelines, digital asset management, a CMS, a knowledge library and file transfer into one system. The buyers it names include national and local government agencies, tourism boards, place brands, economic development agencies, universities and franchises.

Uploaded assets are organized with automatic tagging and metadata generated by AI. Search combines multi-faceted keywords with AI-powered semantic search. Brand guidelines, rights management and licensing information surface alongside the assets themselves. The platform also generates llms.txt and llms.html plain text files so chatbots and language models can read the content. Pricing is based on usage rather than per seat, which the company ties to public sector bodies sharing resources with many end users.

The founder writes that Brandkit began in 1994 to fix the same problem it addresses now. The company says it is still privately held, has never taken outside money, and is profitable. It says it runs brand hubs, media centres, image libraries and partner toolkits for tourism boards, place brands, universities and government departments. One published case study covers how VisitScotland built a media library across several organisations.

paragraphs: Bandwango sells mobile passes that let a destination showcase its local restaurants, breweries and attractions while tracking visitor interactions. The pitch to tourism organizations is an easier way to measure economic impact.

Staff start from one of the pass templates and customize it to their needs and brand. They then add local places to go, discounts and admissions, with Bandwango helping onboard each business added. after.name: Key Data Dashboard
after.description: Lodging occupancy and vacation-rental benchmarking data for DMOs

paragraphs: Key Data sells lodging market data and analytics used by vacation rental property managers, destination organizations, investors and enterprise analytics teams. The argument it makes is that its figures come from actual bookings rather than estimates read off public listing calendars.

The dataset joins direct-source short-term rental reservation data with Airbnb and Vrbo listing coverage and hotel performance benchmarks. The company states integrations with more than 80 property management systems and direct-source data from more than 17,000 property managers, covering over 1.15 million vacation rental properties. Reporting covers occupancy, ADR, RevPAR, guest nights, booking pace and length of stay.

Destination organizations use it to understand event performance, find high-value feeder markets, time campaigns and report results to boards, elected officials and stakeholders. The company says more than 300 destination organizations choose it. after.name: Ridango

paragraphs: Ridango is a mobility technology group built around automated fare collection, payments and real-time information systems for public transport. It sells to transport authorities and operators, working with them on the efficiency, accessibility and sustainability of their transit services.

The account-based ticketing platform is modular, pulling customer management, fare models, products, media, sales channels, device control and reporting into one configurable environment. Authorities and operators are meant to define their own products and fare matrixes and push updates without waiting on the vendor. Ridango also makes the hardware, including a self-service validator that reads contactless bank cards, EMV smart cards and QR mobile tickets. A compact handheld device covers both ticket inspection and on-board ticket sales.

The group is headquartered in Stockholm, Sweden and was established in 2009 in Tallinn, Estonia. It reports that more than 150 public transport authorities and operators use its systems, across more than 25 countries. Among the customers named on the solutions page is a mobility authority in Vilnius. Under recognitions and memberships the site describes the International Association of Public Transport, a non-profit advocacy organization for public transport authorities and operators.

after.name: Emovis
after.description: Tolling operations and back-office payment services for toll agencies

paragraphs: Emovis sells tolling and mobility technology and operating services to road operators and transport agencies around the world. Its remit covers the tolling chain from roadside systems and revenue collection through enforcement and customer service.

The products bring together vehicle identification and classification, data analytics and back-office software to process large volumes of tolling transactions. An operational back office takes the data captured at the roadside and makes it accurate, enriched and ready for billing. A manual image review service pairs automated processing with human checking to validate vehicle passage records. The gantry-based Identify system reads passing vehicles using video tolling or pay by plate, so no physical barrier is needed.

Buyers are public entities and private companies that need a partner to run tolling operations. The company reports more than 850 experts worldwide and over four decades of experience. It is backed by Abertis Group, which it describes as managing 5000+ miles of motorways with over 17,000 employees. Emovis says it has helped clients in the mobility and transportation industry in more than 10 countries.

after.description: Contactless open-loop transit payment infrastructure for 400+ providers in 30+ countries

paragraphs: Littlepay sells payments infrastructure for transit, and public transit providers and vendors of all sizes use it to accept payments in person or online and simplify ticketing for passengers.

Open APIs allow flexible configuration of its capabilities alongside existing AFC and ABT fare collection systems. A single data platform gives operators visibility of passenger behaviour across vehicles, gates, kiosks, mobile apps and web. Risk models optimised across global volumes are meant to minimise losses from fraud and uncollected payments. Advanced PAN and PAR deny lists target card flipping fraud. Multi-operator brokerage services connect operators and agencies in a region under unified customer ticketing.

The company set out in 2016 with a vision to make contactless bank card acceptance faster, cheaper, and less complex for the public transit sector. It now describes working with over 400 transport and mobility providers in over 30 countries, powering payments on local buses, city networks and national public transport systems. One published case study describes Monterey-Salinas Transit deploying a contactless transit fare payment system in May 2021, the first of its kind in California.

paragraphs: Genfare sells fare collection systems to public transit agencies, and describes itself as a partner to transit agencies of every size across the United States and Canada for more than forty years. Its systems cover fixed route service, microtransit, paratransit, ferries, and light rail.

The company is moving its Genfare Link platform to a fully cloud-based software-as-a-service model. Transaction, ridership, and device monitoring data from fareboxes, mobile apps, e-Fare portals, and retail channels are consolidated in one central location. For riders paying with a contactless bank card or phone, existing Fast Fare fareboxes can be upgraded for open payment, or an Open Link validator can be mounted next to the farebox. The Mobile Link application and the e-Fare online ticketing system use open APIs to work with microtransit and shared ride providers.

Genfare Link is built on Amazon Web Services, with APIs linking agency platforms to each other and to riders. Alongside the hardware and software, the company sells packages for training, maintenance and repair, and technical support.

paragraphs: three+one sells liquidity analysis to public finance offices, showing them when and for how long their cash can be put to work. The firm presents itself as an operation created by public officials for public officials.

Its cashVest program produces weekly cash balance projections as a complement to traditional cash-flow forecasting. It gives a consolidated view of how much cash is available and how long each dollar can work before it is needed. Banking services and fees are analyzed to keep the relationship equitable. Marketplace and peer-interest benchmarks are offered so an office can gauge the value of its cash. A dedicated team works on liquidity-management strategy as an objective, third-party data provider.

Published case studies describe county and city finance offices, among them Suffolk County, New York, which the site says began using cashVest to complement its cash-management, finance and audit departments. Another says Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania, partnered with the company in 2017. A separate product, the rfpPrep digital portal, is described as a way to issue an investment services RFP. The company also states that it is a national partner of NACo Financial Services Corporation.

paragraphs: Caselle makes government accounting, ERP, and payments software. It is right-sized, in the company's words, for small to medium local governments, cities, and districts.

Accounting, utility billing, and reporting run in one system whose modules pass data to each other. Built-in tools produce audit-ready statements and track budgets in real time. Payroll and human resources are covered as well. So are permits and code enforcement. Business licensing and tax collection sit in the same system. A further set of tools is meant for sharing information with residents and collecting feedback.

Caselle dates its commitment to community to 1978. The company says its story began with Duane Hutchings, a CPA in Spanish Fork, Utah. Working with his sons and Spanish Fork City, he developed software to improve the workflows of people in local government. In 2024 Caselle joined Govineer Solutions. A published case study describes a city choosing Caselle after an extensive RFP process. That study says McPherson, Kansas explored six different government accounting software solutions before choosing Caselle. It reports the city saved four full workdays each month after the transition.

paragraphs: FUNDVIEW sells an ERP platform to local governments, covering finance, workforce, utilities, community development, and court and citizen services. The pitch is aimed at cities running several disconnected systems and entering the same figures by hand in each one.

Every module posts into the same real-time general ledger, which is what removes the second entry. The finance side covers budgets, purchasing, payables, reconciliation, assets, cash receipting and reporting. Workforce management joins payroll, human resources and employee time onto one record. A jurisdiction can buy the whole thing at once or add one module at a time. Because every department works in the same system, the company says there is a single version of the truth to rely on. paragraphs: PSTrax sells digital inventory and asset management software built for first responders. The system tracks inspections of vehicles, stations, equipment, supplies, controlled substances and blood products.

Rather than handing over a toolkit, the company builds and implements each system for the department and to that department's specs. Systems are meant to be ready to roll out in a matter of weeks. Ongoing support for changes is unlimited and comes at no extra cost. A one-year money back guarantee is offered to customers.

PSTrax, short for Public Safety Tracking Systems, was founded by Scott Bergeron and Cliff Long in 2009. It is headquartered in Littleton, Colorado, with 22 full-time employees. The company says it serves more than 1,000 organizations worldwide. That count includes more than 850 Fire-EMS agencies across the United States, Canada and Australia. It is privately held and says it answers to customers rather than to VC firms or shareholders. It reports a 98.5% customer retention rate.

paragraphs: First Due sells cloud software that fire and EMS agencies use to run records and daily operations in one place. The suite pulls incident reporting, prevention, pre-incident planning, scheduling, assets, hydrants, training and mobile response behind a single login.

Government customers are described as federal, state, tribal and local land managers. On the community side, the site names WUI neighborhoods, fire safe councils and cooperatives. The company says it is a qualified contractor for both personnel and equipment, supporting state and federal agencies. It says it was built by fire practitioners, scientists and foresters. Its headquarters is in South San Francisco, California.

paragraphs: Dryad provides ultra-early wildfire detection and autonomous drone systems for public and private forests. The sensors are meant to detect fires within minutes from ignition so firefighters can put them out before they spread out of control.

The fourth generation sensor combines VOC, CO and PM2.5 sensing to catch a fire as early as the smoldering phase. The units form a wireless environmental sensor network based on LoRaWAN. A patented distributed architecture is meant to allow large-scale deployments in areas without existing network coverage. A cloud platform handles deployment planning, operation, analytics and alerting for those networks. An observation drone is dispatched when a sensor detects a fire, and a second drone applies fire suppressant liquids to extinguish fires autonomously.

Beyond forest owners, the company pitches utility and grid operators on protection against liabilities. Published case studies include a fire in Lebanon stopped by early detection. The founders say they came to this work after several startups and exits in IT, electronics and telecommunications.

paragraphs: Frontline Wildfire Defense sells exterior sprinkler systems and companion software that defend homes and businesses against wildfire. The company describes its mission as providing faster, safer and more precise ways to protect homes, families, businesses and communities from wildfire.

The second-generation defense system is tied to fire tracking software and turns on automatically when fire comes within seven miles of a home. Once running, it saturates the property with water and biodegradable firefighting foam to create conditions the company calls too wet to burn. A commercial version is aimed at businesses, campuses and critical infrastructure, meant to cut risk before a fire reaches the property. A companion app carries wildfire alerts, maps, fire danger indexes, emergency contact groups and evacuation checklists.

Homeowners, businesses and new housing developments are the audience, and the company says its system will safeguard 151 homes at a Woodside Homes community. Installation is handled by licensed contractors in each state rather than by the company itself. Financing options, including zero-down wildfire protection, are offered to buyers. The company points to embers as the central danger, saying they cause up to 90% of structure loss during a wildfire.

paragraphs: Forward Thinking Systems sells fleet management technology that puts vehicle tracking, cameras, compliance, routing, driver coaching and asset management on one platform. The product itself is a browser-based console for an entire fleet.

Vehicle and driver data arrives in real time, including location, speed, ignition status and hours-of-service duty status. More than sixty built-in reports break that data down by fleet, vehicle and driver. The camera product saves footage automatically when it detects behavior such as distracted driving, hard braking or texting. A driver-facing app lets drivers watch their own scorecard, review those events, and dispute the ones they consider inaccurate. Routing is handled by a separate optimization tool for building efficient multi-stop routes.

Government and public sector fleets are one of the segments the company addresses. For those buyers it points to real-time GPS built for emergency operations. Asset tracking extends past vehicles to trailers, heavy equipment and containers. The software also integrates with fuel card providers named on the site.

after.description: Atom asset/maintenance management and Coordinate ROW/project coordination (ex-SADA, ex-dotMaps)

paragraphs: AtomAI Solutions sells a suite of software that agencies use to manage assets, work orders, project and utility coordination, permitting, and safety. Its two flagship products are Atom, an asset and maintenance management platform, and Coordinate, formerly dotMaps, a right-of-way and project coordination tool used by state and local agencies across the country.

Work templates can be defined by each agency so that task structures, fields, and workflows match its own operational processes. Forms built inside the platform can include required fields, dropdowns, conditional logic, and photo or video uploads. Every work order records labor hours, equipment usage, and materials consumed, either automatically or through entry in the field. Templated reports are meant to meet compliance and reporting requirements from agencies such as the FHWA, FRA, and EPA.

The company began as an internal startup within SADA Systems Inc. The full team and product suite divested in early 2023 to form AtomAI Solutions, Inc. as an independent company. Since then it has expanded its offerings to include a permitting solution built specifically for state and local governments.

The company frames the work as a four-part improvement process folded into daily fleet operations. Driver scoring is meant to show managers and drivers alike how safely they are driving. Azuga says customers have relied on it since 2013 for GPS fleet tracking and asset tracking. Insurance companies use its telematics data to measure and price risk in commercial vehicle portfolios. The company also says it works with government agencies on how transportation taxes, emissions data and tolls are collected. States and municipalities, it states, use the data to understand traffic patterns and road surface conditions.

paragraphs: IVU develops integrated IT systems for public transport, and says it has done so for more than fifty years. paragraphs: Citiri sells CitiriOS, a system owners use to define readiness, assign accountability, collect accepted evidence, and govern gate decisions. The company aims it at organizations launching complex infrastructure and services.

The premise is that finishing construction is not the same as being ready to operate. The discipline the company calls Owner Scope Management runs as a chain in which the owner defines what must be true to operate, evidence proves it, and gates authorize it. The output is a Ready Score along with accepted evidence and gate decisions. An agent named Opti surfaces false greens, aging blockers, and the decisions that still need an owner. People, not the software, approve every evidence and gate decision.

The company is direct about the boundary, saying CitiriOS is not a PMIS, commissioning tool, EAM/CMMS, document repository, or BI replacement. Citiri says it is helping the ATL team manage a $13B capital program that includes more than 114 distinct projects. It also describes the SFO team using CitiriOS to keep the Harvey Milk Terminal One project on track. A companion layer, OpsCenter, is listed as generally available, while an ecosystem orchestrator called Struxis is listed as limited access.

paragraphs: Clever Devices builds technology for public transportation providers, meant to help them run more efficiently, spend less and deliver the service riders expect. The company says agencies with anywhere from 50 to 5,000 vehicles have chosen it over more than thirty years.

At the center is CAD/AVL software that gives dispatchers real-time information to monitor and manage the fleet. A vehicle health monitoring product is aimed at cutting repair costs and stretching the mean distance between failures. Onboard, automated passenger announcements are synced with LED signage so riders know where they are. Service planning is handled by the MAIOR scheduling suite, a modular set of planning and optimization tools. For agencies that would rather not run servers, CleverCloud takes on the on-premises hosting burden.

The company tells an unusual origin story, beginning in the early 1980s in the basement of a bar on Long Island. It turned to transit in 1990 when the Americans with Disabilities Act passed. The first product automated the stop announcements bus drivers were required to make. Today the company reports over 600 employees across 12 locations in the United States, Canada, Brazil and Italy. It puts more than 30,000 vehicles on its transportation systems technology. The homepage announces that Hitachi Rail has completed its acquisition of the company.

paragraphs: CalAmp sells telematics devices and cloud software that organizations use to monitor, track, and protect vehicles, equipment, and cargo. Devices on the vehicle collect location, speed, engine health, driver behavior, and outside sensor readings in real time. The cloud then turns protocols such as CAN bus, J1939, OBD-II, and Modbus into clean, structured output. Customers pull that data through APIs, a cloud connector, or event-driven alerts. A device management layer lets administrators assign roles governing who can view, change, or execute particular management functions. Software can be prototyped, tested, and deployed to devices over the air.

CalAmp says the platform is built for commercial fleets and software providers in construction, trucking, utilities, the public sector, and equipment manufacturing. The company states it has been in business for 40 years, with thousands of customers and more than 275 approved or pending patents. For data handling it cites SOC 2 Type II certification along with GDPR and SB327 compliance.

paragraphs: Cylus makes cybersecurity software for railways, built to continuously monitor, detect, and protect every layer of rail operational technology. Its product, CylusOne, covers mainline, urban, and freight rail operations.

The system integrates passively into an operator's network and existing monitoring tools. It automatically discovers and classifies all assets in the operational networks. Vulnerabilities are prioritized and scored by analyzing their severity in the rail environment. Detection runs continuously using deep packet inspection and machine learning to identify and classify threats across railway and IT protocols. Coverage reaches trackside and wayside networks, train-to-ground communications, operational control and maintenance centers, and station networks.

The company says the product lets operators prove compliance with frameworks including IEC 62443-3-2, NIST 800-82, and EN TS 50701. It describes CylusOne as the first rail cybersecurity solution certified to IEC 62443-4-2 at Security Level 3. Cylus says it works with technology providers, integrators, and rail experts worldwide. For passenger rail, detection is tuned to separate expected supervision and control traffic in ERTMS environments from anomalous behavior.

before.name: TransTrack Solutions Group
before.why: The homepage describes both products and the reporting workflow in plain prose, and the who-we-are page gives the founding year and the service list.

paragraphs.text: TransTrack Systems writes software for public transit agencies that pulls scattered operating data into one place so performance can be watched and reported.
paragraphs.quote: TransTrack Systems provides software designed specifically for transit agencies to centralize operational data, monitor performance, and simplify reporting.

paragraphs.text: The main application collects data from across an agency so teams can follow trends and produce the reports decisions rest on.
paragraphs.quote: TransTrack Manager™ brings together data from across your organization so teams can track performance, monitor trends, and generate the reports needed for informed decision-making.

paragraphs.text: Much of the appeal is federal reporting: agency data is applied automatically to the required National Transit Database forms, which the company says turns most of the annual filing from weeks of work into days.
paragraphs.quote: automatically applying agency data to required forms so transit leaders can complete most annual reporting in days instead of weeks

paragraphs.text: A companion analytics product presents the same operating data as dashboards, reports and metrics an agency can adjust.
paragraphs.quote: ViewPoint BI helps transit agencies turn operational data into clear, actionable insights through interactive dashboards, reports, and customizable metrics.

paragraphs.text: The point of it, in the company's framing, is to replace manual spreadsheets and disconnected systems and keep the numbers behind federal funding accurate.
paragraphs.quote: By replacing manual spreadsheets and disconnected systems, TransTrack helps agencies improve efficiency, strengthen accountability, and ensure accurate reporting for federal funding.

paragraphs.text: The firm was formed in 2002 by transit management professionals.
paragraphs.quote: TransTrack Systems® was formed in 2002 by transit management professionals who understand the need for streamlined processes and improved management reporting.

paragraphs.text: More than twenty years on, it describes its business as helping agencies turn operating data into better decisions.
paragraphs.quote: For more than 20 years, TransTrack Systems has helped transit agencies turn operational data into better decisions.

paragraphs.text: Alongside the software it lists consulting work such as transit financial planning and cost analyses.
paragraphs.quote: Transit financial planning and cost analyses.

paragraphs.text: The platform itself was built with transit professionals involved.
paragraphs.quote: Developed in collaboration with transit professionals, the platform reflects real-world agency needs and workflows.

quote.text: TransTrack Systems provides software designed specifically for transit agencies to centralize operational data, monitor performance, and simplify reporting.

before.name: Citiri
before.why: The home, platform, solutions, and case study pages state what CitiriOS governs, the criteria-evidence-gate model behind it, what the product deliberately does not replace, and the airport programs the company cites.

paragraphs.text: Citiri sells CitiriOS, a system owners use to define readiness, assign accountability, collect accepted evidence, and govern gate decisions.
paragraphs.quote: CitiriOS gives owners one system to define readiness, assign accountability, collect accepted evidence, govern gate decisions

paragraphs.text: The company aims it at organizations launching complex infrastructure and services.
paragraphs.quote: BUILT FOR LAUNCHING COMPLEX INFRASTRUCTURE AND SERVICES

paragraphs.text: The premise is that finishing construction is not the same as being ready to operate.
paragraphs.quote: Construction complete ≠ ready to operate

paragraphs.text: The discipline the company calls Owner Scope Management runs as a chain in which the owner defines what must be true to operate, evidence proves it, and gates authorize it.
paragraphs.quote: You define what must be true to operate. Evidence proves it. Gates authorize it.

paragraphs.text: The output is a Ready Score along with accepted evidence and gate decisions.
paragraphs.quote: Output: Ready Score, accepted evidence, gate decisions

paragraphs.text: An agent named Opti surfaces false greens, aging blockers, and the decisions that still need an owner.
paragraphs.quote: surfacing false greens, aging blockers, and the decisions that need someone to own them

paragraphs.text: Swiftly sells a cloud platform to public transit agencies for sharing real-time passenger information, running daily operations, and improving service performance.
paragraphs.quote: Agencies rely on Swiftly’s cloud-native platform to share real-time passenger information, manage day-to-day operations, and improve service performance.

paragraphs.text: The company puts its customer count above 200 agencies.
paragraphs.quote: Trusted by 200+ agencies

paragraphs.text: Those agencies are described as large and small, around the globe.
paragraphs.quote: Swiftly is improving public transit at agencies large and small around the globe.

paragraphs.text: The platform combines GTFS schedule data with whatever real-time vehicle location feed an agency already has.
paragraphs.quote: Swiftly combines GTFS and any other available real-time vehicle location data in our data engine

paragraphs.text: It then analyzes billions of data points to say where a vehicle was, where it is, and where it will be next.
paragraphs.quote: Swiftly analyzes billions of data points to create the industry’s most accurate information about where a vehicle was, is, and where it will be next.

paragraphs.text: Operations staff use it to make real-time adjustments for on-time performance and headway adherence.
paragraphs.quote: Boost on-time performance and headway adherence with real-time adjustments for your operators and historical insights for operations staff.

paragraphs.text: Schedulers work from actual run times, vehicle speeds, and dwell times.
paragraphs.quote: Optimize your schedule using actual run-times, vehicle speeds, and dwell times.

paragraphs.text: APIs push the same data out to rider-facing apps, vehicle hardware, and internal tools.
paragraphs.quote: Swiftly's APIs make it simple to integrate with the entire transit ecosystem, including rider-facing apps, vehicle hardware, and internal tools.

paragraphs.text: Customer service teams are another audience, answering rider questions from the same information.
paragraphs.quote: your customer service team can instantly answer any question a rider has about your system

paragraphs.text: The site carries comments from transit staff, including an operations technology lead at the MBTA in Boston.
paragraphs.quote: Dave Barker, Operations Technology | MBTA, Boston, MA

paragraphs.text: Another comes from a transportation planner at MDOT MTA in Baltimore.
paragraphs.quote: Krae Stieffenhofer, Transportation Planner | MDOT MTA, Baltimore, MD

paragraphs.text: Jonny Simkin co-founded the company and is its chief executive.
paragraphs.quote: Jonny Simkin is the Co-founder and CEO of Swiftly.

paragraphs.text: Swiftly describes itself as a transit reliability platform meant to keep public transportation a fast and attractive alternative to the private vehicle.
paragraphs.quote: Swiftly is a transit reliability platform to keep public transportation a fast, frequent, and attractive alternative to the private vehicle.

before.name: Netradyne
before.why: Three solution pages spell out the hardware, the coaching model, the scoring system, the fleet management and compliance features, plus named fleets and a mileage figure.

paragraphs.text: Netradyne sells AI-powered video safety and fleet management technology to organizations that operate vehicle fleets.
paragraphs.quote: Only Netradyne’s AI-powered video safety and fleet management solution provides full context by analyzing 100% of drive time.

paragraphs.text: Its Driver·i platform combines 360-degree AI cameras, real-time in-cab coaching, and positive driver recognition.
paragraphs.quote: Netradyne Driver•i is the only platform that combines 360° AI-powered cameras, real-time in-cab coaching, and positive driver recognition

paragraphs.text: The company says it analyzes 100% of driving time, provides real-time alerts, and delivers safety insights meant to improve fleet performance.
paragraphs.quote: Netradyne analyzes 100% of driving time, provides real-time alerts, and delivers actionable safety insights to help fleets improve safety performance.

paragraphs.text: Instant in-cab alerts let drivers self-correct before incidents occur.
paragraphs.quote: Netradyne provides instant in-cab alerts, helping drivers self-correct before incidents occur and reducing preventable collisions.

paragraphs.text: Driver performance is summarized in a GreenZone Score the company ties to proving safety impact and retaining drivers.
paragraphs.quote: Prove safety impact and retain drivers through the GreenZone Score®.

paragraphs.text: The same platform covers fleet tracking, fuel efficiency, preventative maintenance, and compliance.
paragraphs.quote: Track your fleet, maximize fuel efficiency, reduce downtime with preventative maintenance, and streamline compliance

paragraphs.text: Fleets named on the site include Rumpke Waste & Recycling, where severe distracted driving alerts dropped more than 30% over twelve months.
paragraphs.quote: Severe distracted driving alerts dropped more than 30% over 12 months at Rumpke Waste & Recycling.

paragraphs.text: The site also reports that Knight-Swift adopted the fleet safety product, bringing in-cab coaching and full drive-time analysis to its trucking fleet.

paragraphs.text: More than 25 billion miles have been analyzed, according to the company.
paragraphs.quote: With more than 25B miles analyzed, Driver•i enables results.

paragraphs.text: It describes its mission as building intelligence for the physical world.
paragraphs.quote: We're on a mission to build intelligence for the physical world.

quote.text: We're on a mission to build intelligence for the physical world.

paragraphs: Neara sells physics-based digital twin software to electric utilities, which use it to model their networks. The pitch is to unify assets, surroundings and workflows in a single physics-accurate view.

The model is built from a utility's existing LiDAR, imagery, GIS and asset records. Teams then simulate wind, ice, thermal, flood, vegetation, reconductoring and new builds on the real network geometry. Outputs include prioritized hardening plans, regulator-ready reports and field-ready work orders. Solution areas cover resiliency and reliability, wildfire mitigation, asset management, risk and value optimization, and design and construction.

On the asset side, replacement candidates are ranked by measured load rather than by install date. Wildfire work pulls pole loading, asset condition, vegetation, GIS accuracy, weather and consequence into one physics-backed model. Resiliency work prioritizes mitigation by how asset condition, vegetation proximity and environmental conditions interact across the network. Case study quotes on the site are attributed to the chief executive of Essential Energy. Another comes from a general manager of network management at SA Power Networks.

quote.text: Utilities on four continents run their networks on Neara, from ambitious regional co-ops to national grid operators.

paragraphs: Survalent sells control room software to utilities, bringing SCADA, outage management and distribution management into one system. Operators work from real-time equipment status, metering data, alarming and control, with the aim of catching problems before outages start. A metering interface pulls readings from the AMI system using the MultiSpeak protocol, and a lightning interface fetches strike data and filters it by the utility's area of interest.

MultiSpeak itself is described as an initiative for rural electric co-ops and municipal utilities. The site says more than 700 utilities worldwide use its SCADA product. paragraphs: Copperleaf sells decision analytics software that helps large organizations decide how to spend limited money on the infrastructure they own. The buyers are agencies and companies running critical infrastructure, where choices about maintenance, sustainment, or growth projects always involve a trade-off. The site groups the work by industry, among them electric utilities, government, rail and transit, roads and highways, and water and wastewater.

The method puts every proposed investment on a common footing so dissimilar options can be compared objectively. A single collaborative repository stores all asset and investment data, with proposals entered in one format and common financial metrics. Analytics then weigh hundreds of thousands of possible investments and return an optimal plan, with what-if scenarios for different budgets, timing, and constraints. A companion product, Copperleaf Asset, forecasts the long-term risk exposure of an entire asset population and bundles planned interventions to reduce service outages.

The company says its decision analytics is used to manage over $2.9 trillion of assets globally. Copperleaf is now paired with IFS, aimed at asset-intensive organizations allocating capital and operating expenditure. Its planning approach is described as embodying the key principles of ISO 55000. The enterprise software also connects to existing EAM, APM, ERP, and GIS systems.

paragraphs: Heimdall Power sells sensors and software to electric utilities, with capacity tools meant to help them safely adjust transmission limits, improve operational planning and stay compliant with industry standards. The company was founded in Norway in 2016.

Its dynamic line rating offering combines physical and virtual Neurons to take real-time, on-line measurements. The sensors report temperature, current and inclination on the conductor. Deployment is handled by an autonomous drone installation system that the company says places Neurons in remote or hard-to-reach areas. A facility ratings module consolidates all ratings into one unified system and is aimed at simplifying NERC FAC-008 compliance. Further tools give grid operators real-time visibility into threats like icing, line movement, electrical faults and wildfire risks.

The about page states that the company has grown 10x in two years, raised a $25M Series B and expanded with a North American headquarters in Charlotte, NC. A news item on the site reports that Heimdall Power was selected by Statnett for a new Dynamic Line Rating project.

paragraphs: Camus Energy sells software that electric utilities use to interconnect data centers and local generation. What it sells is the flexible grid connection, in which the utility guarantees firm capacity for most of a site's demand and applies conditional limits to the rest.

Camus uses real utility data to map how much additional load each conductor and substation can safely serve in every hour of the year. Utilities then decide what portion of the load is served firmly and set operating limits for the conditional portion. Day-ahead operating forecasts show when those conditional limits will apply, alongside closed loop controls. The platform pulls SCADA data, GIS assets, network models, AMI, and DER telemetry into one consistent system model. Two applications sit on it: FlexConnect for interconnections and ODMS, which gives utilities a unified view of the distribution grid.

The company says it supports investor-owned and public power utilities. It counts 12 or more utility partners across the United States. It states that joint studies with Google, AES, and Princeton's ZERO Lab set the benchmark for how utilities and developers evaluate flexibility and grid capacity. On security, it says OAuth authentication, MFA, role-based access, audit logging, and continuous monitoring protect the platform.

paragraphs: Anterix provides private 900 MHz spectrum to utilities so they can run their own wireless networks instead of leaning on commercial carriers. The company frames that as operational control, with the utility owning the communications infrastructure behind essential services. Licensed spectrum is sold together with deployment solutions and ecosystem partners so utilities can get networks running faster.

The deployment accelerators are described as simplifying site access, device onboarding, and connectivity management. Two of them, TowerX and CatalyX, are named on the solutions page. A partner program helps utilities integrate devices, applications, and network components so deployments move faster. That program spans over 150 technology providers, from rugged device manufacturers to software companies, with solutions validated for 900 MHz networks.

Eleven utility customers are deploying its 900 MHz solutions, the company states. It describes itself as the largest holder of licensed 900 MHz spectrum in the United States, counting the contiguous states plus Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico. The about page also claims over 93% of Texas counties served. The same page traces the founders back to Nextel.
