before.name: Virtual Peaker
before.description: Cloud DERMS and demand flexibility software for municipal utilities and co-ops

after.name: Virtual Peaker
after.description: Cloud DERMS and demand flexibility software for municipal utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Virtual Peaker sells cloud software that lets an electric utility reach the smart devices already sitting in homes and businesses and use them to shave peak load and cost. The buyers are utilities standing up demand response programs.

Three suites make up the product, and the company presents them together as a virtual power plant platform that aggregates distributed energy resources at the edge of the grid. The Shift suite is the dispatch side, aggregating resources at homes and at commercial and industrial sites to hold down peak market costs and defer new construction. The Relay suite handles the customer side, signing people up and paying out the incentives. A utility can run several program types at once across electric vehicles, thermostats, water heaters and batteries.

The company describes partnerships with more than thirty device types, from thermostats to electric vehicle chargers. It states that the platform is SOC 2 Type 2 certified. Municipal energy providers are named as one audience, using demand response to meet grid goals and engage customers. One published case study covers Sacramento Municipal Utility District optimizing hot water heater efficiency on the platform.

after.description: AI platform that turns field crew video and voice into risk, safety, and productivity intelligence for utilities and infrastructure operators - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: FYLD sells a platform that turns the realities of frontline work into structured, real-time data. It is built for critical infrastructure operators who need jobs done right the first time. The pitch starts from lost time, with the company saying a fifth of a field worker's day goes to paper processes and unseen admin.

A phone app converts video, photo, audio and text into work assessments. Crews use it to record progress through the day, evidence issues and flag problems to managers. On the office side, the cloud product alerts managers only to events that need action. Centralised records leave an audit trail the company positions as protection against fines.

The company reports injuries and incidents falling 20 percent for one client over a twelve-month period. It also claims at least six times return on investment across sectors. FYLD announced a $41 million Series B round aimed at infrastructure field work. Amey has deployed the platform for highways operations, according to a company announcement.

after.name: CUSI
after.description: Utility billing and customer information software for small and mid-size municipal water, sewer, and multi-service utilities - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, GFOA 2026

paragraphs: Continental Utility Solutions, Inc., known as CUSI, has spent decades building utility management software. The line runs from customer information systems and utility billing applications to mobile meter reading and customer web portals.

Billing comes in two forms: UMS, installed on premise, and UB4, a hosted application. The customer web portal gives residents tools to view usage history and financial activity rather than only a place to pay a bill. Mobile meter reading runs on any phone, tablet, or device with a modern internet browser, reading meters and uploading usage data wirelessly back to the billing software. Service orders can be handled from any modern internet-enabled device.

The company states that its products are PCI and FIPS compliant. Support is available by telephone, email, and online chat from 7:00 AM to 6:00 PM Central, Monday through Friday. CUSI says it implements around 70 clients each year. A free web-based learning platform called CUSI Academy provides access to over 100 learning modules.

before.description: Smart grid AMI and grid analytics for public power utilities and co-ops

after.name: Tantalus Systems
after.description: Smart grid AMI and grid analytics for public power utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Tantalus is a technology company selling grid modernization systems to public power and electric cooperative utilities. It has been delivering data-centric products to that market for more than 35 years.

The products sit on the Tantalus Grid Modernization Platform, a modular architecture meant to move data across devices, systems and vendors. One piece is edge-computing metering infrastructure aimed at resiliency, reliability and lower total cost of ownership. Another handles load management and distributed energy resources sitting behind the meter. A gateway device fits any ANSI meter socket and adds visibility and control behind the meter without replacing the meter itself.

Utilities across North America partner with the company on distribution grid work, with published case studies including one in Bolivar, Tennessee. Tantalus Systems trades on the TSX under the symbol GRID and on OTCQX. It is based in Burnaby, British Columbia. Recent announcements include a debt restructuring and an annual survey of how utilities view grid modernization.

before.name: AiDash
before.description: Satellite + AI vegetation management (IVMS) and climate/asset risk SaaS for utilities

after.name: AiDash
after.description: Satellite + AI vegetation management (IVMS) and climate/asset risk SaaS for utilities

paragraphs: AiDASH sells software that electric utilities use to find vegetation, asset, wildfire and storm risk before it takes the grid down. The method starts with continuous satellite monitoring, then adds targeted aerial, vehicle-mounted and on-demand inspection.

Very high resolution satellite passes refresh vegetation health data up to twelve times a year. Higher-cadence imagery tracks fuel load, moisture and burnability up to seven times a week. One system covers asset inspection and monitoring. Another handles wildfire situational awareness and risk mitigation. A storm system predicts outages 120 hours ahead so crews can be pre-positioned. The platform exposes REST APIs for automation or for integrating with systems a utility already runs.

The company says it was founded by serial entrepreneurs in 2019. Its about page claims more than 150 customers of every size around the world. The platform page states SOC 2 Type 2 certification. A news item on the site announces that Schneider Electric agreed to acquire AiDASH for $350 million.

paragraphs: Oracle Utilities sells software to energy and water providers for serving customers and for managing networks and assets. Billing is presented as one place holding the data, processes and insights a utility needs.

Billing workflows use AI anomaly detection intended to cut errors on complex accounts. The outage management system is deployed for electric, gas, water or wastewater networks and coordinates restoration with field, mutual aid and asset management teams. Field crews record network updates straight into the network management system rather than relaying them verbally to control room staff. Analytics tools look for trends among customers and pick out electric vehicle owners for targeted recommendations and service. A commercial account product pulls billing history, consumption, appointment scheduling and service interruptions into a single dashboard.

The outage page states more than 60 million meters in production worldwide. The industry page counts 3.8 trillion AMI data reads managed annually. Those figures carry a footnote saying they are calculated from client deployments from 2009 through 2024. Oracle also cites recognition as a leader in the 2025 IDC MarketScape for utility meter data management.

paragraphs: Hansen builds software for energy and communications service providers, aimed at getting new products to market and delivering them to customers. The company says it has served the utilities, energy and communications industries for more than fifty years.

Community solar is another described use, served with the customer information system plus managed services. The company has announced a partnership with ERTH Holdings to widen the reach of those systems.

paragraphs.quote: Over 30,000 users and 72 million customers served worldwide.

paragraphs.quote: Esri Gold Partner with Utility Network Management Specialty.

before.name: Copperleaf Technologies (IFS)
before.why: The solutions and asset pages explain the product and the method in detail, and the home page carries the scale claim and the IFS pairing.

paragraphs.text: Copperleaf sells decision analytics software that helps large organizations decide how to spend limited money on the infrastructure they own.
paragraphs.quote: Decision analytics that drive business results

paragraphs.text: The buyers are agencies and companies running critical infrastructure, where choices about maintenance, sustainment, or growth projects always involve a trade-off.
paragraphs.quote: Major decisions about maintenance, sustainment, or growth projects always come with a trade-off

paragraphs.text: The site groups the work by industry, among them electric utilities, government, rail and transit, roads and highways, and water and wastewater.
paragraphs.quote: Airports Chemicals Electric Utilities Government Mining Natural Gas Utilities Oil & Gas Other Rail & Transit Roads & Highways Telecommunications Water & Wastewater Wind Offshore

paragraphs.text: The method puts every proposed investment on a common footing so dissimilar options can be compared objectively.
paragraphs.quote: so that you can objectively compare dissimilar investments

paragraphs.text: A single collaborative repository stores all asset and investment data, with proposals entered in one format and common financial metrics.
paragraphs.quote: Copperleaf provides a single collaborative repository to store all asset and investment data.

paragraphs.text: Analytics then weigh hundreds of thousands of possible investments and return an optimal plan, with what-if scenarios for different budgets, timing, and constraints.
paragraphs.quote: assess hundreds of thousands of possible investments and identify the optimal plan within minutes

paragraphs.text: A companion product, Copperleaf Asset, forecasts the long-term risk exposure of an entire asset population and bundles planned interventions to reduce service outages.
paragraphs.quote: automatically bundles asset interventions together to plan service outages in the most efficient and cost-effective way

paragraphs.text: The company says its decision analytics is used to manage over $2.9 trillion of assets globally.
paragraphs.quote: solution is being used to manage over $2.9 trillion of assets globally

paragraphs.text: Copperleaf is now paired with IFS, aimed at asset-intensive organizations allocating capital and operating expenditure.
paragraphs.quote: The combination of Copperleaf and IFS allows asset-intensive organizations to strategically allocate and execute

paragraphs.text: Its planning approach is described as embodying the key principles of ISO 55000.
paragraphs.quote: embodies the key principles of ISO 55000

paragraphs.text: The enterprise software also connects to existing EAM, APM, ERP, and GIS systems.
paragraphs.quote: integrates seamlessly with existing EAM, APM, ERP, GIS, and other systems

quote.text: Decision-making needs to be rigorous, agile, and defensible.

before.name: Tantalus Systems
before.why: The homepage lays out the market, the platform and the individual products, and the newsroom and case study pages supply the listing details, location and recent corporate announcements.

paragraphs.quote: Tantalus is a technology company that helps public power and electric cooperative utilities

paragraphs.text: It has been delivering data-centric products to that market for more than 35 years.
paragraphs.quote: For more than 35 years, the company has delivered data-centric solutions

paragraphs.text: The products sit on the Tantalus Grid Modernization Platform, a modular architecture meant to move data across devices, systems and vendors.
paragraphs.quote: a flexible and modular technology architecture that delivers true data interoperability across devices, systems and vendors

paragraphs.quote: can be installed in any ANSI meter socket to deliver secure, edge-level visibility and control of devices located behind the meter

paragraphs.quote: BURNABY, BRITISH COLUMBIA

before.name: Bentek
before.description: Benefits administration and enrollment built exclusively for public-sector employers - exhibited at SALGBA 2026

after.name: Bentek
after.description: Benefits administration and enrollment built exclusively for public-sector employers - exhibited at SALGBA 2026

paragraphs: Bentek sells benefits administration software purpose-built for the public sector. The company describes it as designed exclusively for states, local governments and educational institutions. It says its focus is the benefits administration needs of schools, counties and city governments.

The platform is put to work through configurable workflows, automated processes and adaptable reporting tools. It integrates with HRIS and payroll systems so data moves between platforms with less manual entry. Bentek says the platform carries more than 5,000 business rules. A library of more than 60 ready-made reports covers enrollment, engagement and compliance. Self-service enrollment handles active employees, retirees and COBRA participants.

Bentek says it was founded to serve public sector organizations. The company says its story began in 2006. It started when a local school district struggled to manage its benefits. The company puts its experience in the public sector environment at more than 20 years. It says it serves more than 300 employers in the public sector. One story on the site describes helping the Government of the U.S. Virgin Islands transform its benefits administration in four months.

quote.text: We Make the Complex Simple for State and Local Government and Education

provenance.quote: Benefits Administration Purpose-Built for Public Sector
The ONLY benefits administration platform designed exclusively for states, local governments, and educational institutions.
Bentek is the only platform with a singular focus on serving the benefits administration needs of schools, counties, and city governments.
Put Bentek to work for you with configurable workflows, automated processes, and adaptable reporting tools.

paragraphs: Holly sells an AI-powered classification and compensation platform for government human resources departments. It is built for HR teams that manage hundreds of classifications, compete for talent and negotiate pay.

The platform scores an existing job spec for clarity, completeness and equity, calling out outdated duties, dense sentences or qualifications that screen out strong candidates. Its similarity scoring compares actual job duties across more than 45,000 public sector roles rather than titles alone. Drafts move through subject matter expert, HR, management and final approval steps, with reviewers commenting the way they would in a shared document. Market data is turned into recommendations for council meetings and union negotiations.

The users are local government HR staff, and one published case study follows Long Beach, California, a port city of about 450,000 residents. Its workforce numbers roughly 6,000 employees across close to 350 civil service classifications. Holly was started by Brendan Hellweg and Cherie Chung, who met as graduate students at Harvard Business School and Harvard Kennedy School. The company says it is supported by J2 Ventures, Roble Ventures, Gaingels and angel investors.

paragraphs: Neighborly Software sells a cloud platform for administering and disbursing government funds. It connects administrators, participants, contractors and homeowners in one system for local, state and nonprofit organizations.

The programs covered include housing, economic and community development, disaster recovery and mitigation, home energy rebates, and housing choice vouchers. Community development activity runs from application to closeout on a single platform. Integration with the IDIS reporting system is meant to end duplicate data entry. For disaster recovery grants, the company says it implements in weeks rather than months.

The company says more than a third of HUD entitlement jurisdictions choose it. Published case studies include Prince William County, Virginia. It dates to 2016 and says it has delivered software to more than 700 public and private sector entities across the country. Co-founder and president Jason Rusnak previously held management positions at Accenture and ADP.

paragraphs: Tanium sells software that gives IT and security teams continuous visibility across an entire endpoint estate. A single agent covers real-time threat hunting, autonomous detection and response, and deep forensics. Vulnerability monitoring runs continuously with risk scoring based on actual exploitability rather than CVSS alone.

A layer called Atlas sits on top, unifying investigation and remediation with agentic AI over real-time endpoint intelligence. Operators type questions in plain English and Atlas translates them into live endpoint queries. Actions then execute within autonomy limits the operator defines. Native connectors link the platform to ServiceNow, Microsoft and Splunk.

Customer pages describe Best Buy consolidating data into a single pane of glass. Another describes Leeds and York Partnership NHS Foundation Trust keeping thousands of endpoints patched and up to date. That page says the platform gives full visibility into all 3,000 PCs and servers. The homepage says the company was named a Leader and positioned furthest in Completeness of Vision in a 2026 Gartner report.

paragraphs: Nutanix sells infrastructure software that lets organizations build, manage and optimize IT across on-premises, edge and public cloud environments. At the core is a platform with hyperconverged compute, storage, virtualization and networking.

The storage layer consolidates file, object and block storage into one platform with integrated cyber security and ransomware protection. A database service automates provisioning, patching, cloning, backup and recovery, and supports Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Day-to-day work happens in Prism, which monitors and manages VMs, storage and networks across on-premises clusters and public clouds from a single console. Prism is included with Nutanix Cloud Infrastructure at no additional cost. For larger estates, Nutanix Central is a cloud console for viewing and managing Nutanix services deployed on-premises or on Nutanix Cloud Clusters.

The home page counts more than 30,000 companies as customers. Public sector examples include the Indonesia Election Committee, which the company says improved legal response times by 90% across 210 million voter records. Another describes London Gatwick Airport scaling support to fifty million passengers. The company also reports being named a Leader in the 2025 Gartner Magic Quadrant.

paragraphs: Harmonize sells collaboration tools that higher education instructors run inside the learning management system they already use. The suite covers discussion, peer review, document annotation, and more. It works with any major LMS and, the company says, feels familiar enough that there is virtually no learning curve.

Discussion boards are multimedia enabled and come with Turnitin integration, multiple due dates, and auto grading. Social annotation moves the conversation into the document itself, by highlighting text and dropping pins. AI features generate captions, audio descriptions, and alt text on both instructor and student content. Instructors can also run polls, set up small groups, or enable anonymous posting. Engagement Insights is offered for reporting on student performance and for compliance with RSI guidelines.

The team says it has worked closely with educators since 2008. It started as 42 Lines, a custom development shop for higher education. The press page says the product reaches institutions from the University of Michigan to Piedmont Community College. Listed announcements include a partnership with the Oklahoma State Regents for Higher Education.

paragraphs: Honorlock proctors online exams, pairing software monitoring with review by people. For schools and colleges it sits inside the learning system students already use. The same service is sold to employers for hiring and workforce compliance.

The software monitors each exam session and alerts a live proctor when it detects a potential problem. That proctor can enter the session and help the student get back on track rather than simply recording a flag. A separate service looks for exam questions posted online and gets them removed.

Honorlock says it began with two students at Florida Atlantic University who set out to level the playing field for online assessments. paragraphs: Cirrus Identity sells hosted sign-on services to colleges and universities of all sizes, university systems, research institutions, and medical centers. The problem it addresses is that campus identity systems were never designed to work together. Instead of replacing what a school already runs, Cirrus proxies authentication across identity providers, federations, and legacy systems.

The Bridge solution provides multilateral SAML and CAS for Entra ID, Okta, Duo SSO, and others. That lets a school meet the multilateral federation requirements of eduGAIN federations such as InCommon, CAF, and GakuNin without running Shibboleth, ADFS, or SSP. The Proxy solution handles people outside the enterprise directory, so guests, collaborators, alumni, and lifelong learners sign in without being given enterprise identities. Those users can bring credentials from Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn, Amazon, Apple, an ORCID iD, or a Cirrus Identity OrgBrandedID. Applicants can sign in to selected applications with their existing Slate credentials.

The buyers named on the site are identity and access management, security and privacy, systems architect, and enterprise application teams. Administrators get a console for reaching log events and configuring the products. The service is fully cloud hosted with 24x365 production support. Pricing is an annual subscription plus a one-time implementation fee, quoted for each use case. The company calls itself an InCommon Catalyst community partner.

Underneath sits what the company calls an ontology, a model of how the institution actually operates, with agents, applications and machine learning models built on top of it. Existing records are ingested as they are and projected into that model. In admissions, an agent answers prospective students by email, text and phone in more than 50 languages. The same office can push transcripts through at a stated rate of 10,000 a day. In advancement, an agent reads each gift agreement and matches restricted funds to students who qualify for them. In the business office, an agent fields staff questions about expense reports, purchase requisitions and policy approvals. It also produces standing board reports, IPEDS filings and dashboards on schedule.

The company claims hundreds of institutional partners. It describes them as public and private, R1 and community college, liberal arts and HBCU, with operating budgets from $50M to $5B. after.name: CampusIQ
after.description: Wi-Fi-based space occupancy analytics and planning software for colleges and universities - exhibited at NACUBO 2026

paragraphs: CampusIQ sells colleges and universities real-time space analytics meant to improve utilization, right-size facilities, and optimize occupancy. Its customers are institutions using the product for space utilization and campus planning.

Occupancy is read from the campus wireless network, so coverage scales as far as WiFi is available, with additional hardware sensors placed where it is not. Monitored spaces include classrooms, libraries, dining halls, recreation centers, residence halls, research facilities, and outdoor areas. The company says the system captures occupancy data without identifying individuals. It claims compliance with FERPA and other educational privacy regulations. Full implementation typically ranges from two to eight weeks. Field tests are reported at 95%+ accuracy in occupancy detection.

A published case study describes the University of Kentucky launching a pilot with CampusIQ in the fall of 2024. In that account, a 5% reduction in planned space translated to approximately $8M in avoided construction costs. Core pricing is based on gross square footage. Subscription models include software licensing, installation, and ongoing support.

paragraphs: AWE Learning sells self-contained childrens learning workstations to public libraries and community organizations across the United States and Canada, aimed at learners ages 2 to 12. The stations arrive turnkey, meant to support school readiness and early literacy and to extend programming without adding staff time.

The current release, Platinum Version 4 of the Early Literacy Station and AfterSchool Edge, carries more than 250 titles and runs without an internet connection or ads. Modules span literacy, math, STEM, and creativity. Rather than tap-and-swipe alone, each station combines touchscreen, mouse, and keyboard so children practice navigation, coordination, and early typing. The environment is closed and child-safe, built around structured, play-based learning children can work through on their own.

The company was founded in the mid-1990s as a remote network technology company. Work with the Free Library of Philadelphia exposed how hard it was for libraries to manage educational software for young patrons, and the Early Literacy Station grew out of that. It says its products are used by over 49% of U.S. public libraries. More than 40,000 workstations have been sold, according to the same page. AWE Learning is headquartered in Chester, Pennsylvania, with account executives across North America.

paragraphs: Gimlet is hosted software for keeping track of what happens at a service desk. It is sold to libraries and other organizations that want to see the trends and patterns behind the questions their desks field.

Staff log each interaction on a form the organization configures with its own category values. Entries can be tagged, and the full text of a question and its answer is kept so it can be searched later. A search can cover every entry or narrow to a single building or desk. Reports can show which desks are busiest at which hours of the week and which staff field the hardest questions. Data can be moved out to spreadsheet or reporting tools such as Excel, Google Sheets or Tableau. A web browser is all a desk needs to use it, and there is no cap on the number of staff or computers on an account.

Gimlet was founded by Eric Larson, a librarian, and Nate Vack, a library web application developer. The site puts the running total at more than 106,929,217 questions answered. The service is monitored around the clock for uptime, performance and security, with data mirrored, encrypted and backed up. Customers keep ownership of the data they enter. A 30-day free trial is offered.

The school version is pitched as getting students speaking from day one while giving a district the reporting it needs. paragraphs: Book Systems sells library automation and asset tracking software. Its main product, Atriuum, is cloud-based automation designed for public, academic, school and special libraries. It gathers circulation, cataloging, reporting and a modern patron catalog in one system.

The system runs in a browser with no per-seat licensing or installs. Libraries get Z39.50 copy cataloging, batch processing for bulk records, and offline circulation that keeps working without an internet connection. RFID support and barcode scanning handle checkouts. It connects to digital content providers including OverDrive, hoopla, CloudLibrary and MackinVIA. Patrons can sign in once through Google, ClassLink or Clever. A staff interface called Stax organizes the work into role-based workspaces. The patron catalog draws on linked data from the Library of Congress.

The company says it has been delivering this software for over 35 years. Its buyers range from public communities and academic institutions to K-12 schools, churches and special collections. Hosting is offered as a subscription, and the company performs daily database backups. Staff exhibit at library conferences, among them the Association for Rural & Small Libraries.

paragraphs: BiblioCommons builds the online side of a public library, covering the catalog, mobile app, website, events calendar and email marketing. The pieces are sold as a suite intended to work as one.

Staff are described as coming from both technical and library backgrounds.

paragraphs: COLBI Technologies develops software tools that help public agencies manage their capital building programs. It also provides in-person, hands-on training and support through a team of fiscal, construction, and facility experts.

Account-Ability, its program management application, rests on what the company calls three critical components. COLBIDocs puts agencies in control of their documents and processes without paying for expensive IT and storage systems. QualityBidders is a web-based tool that simplifies the prequalification process for contractors and agencies. It gives contractors an efficient way to comply with prequalification and CUPCCAA requirements. SecureBids provides an online, secure place to receive bids electronically.

The company maintains a national presence serving school districts and public agencies. It says it serves more than 250 clients managing more than 45 billion in capital building program dollars. It points to large capital building programs over the past 20 years in both California and Texas. The company came together after Lettie Boggs reached out to Chuck Olsen, an entrepreneur in computer programming, and it started in his garage.

paragraphs: Genesis Educational Services makes administrative software for New Jersey school districts, sold as an integrated, paperless set of tools for daily operations and compliance. Its Student Information System is web-based and built to meet state requirements, including state reporting. A companion product, SchoolFi, handles business office work such as payroll, budgeting, HR and evaluations.

SchoolFi was created with input from business administrators, HR directors and payroll administrators who work in districts. Both products are backed by a help desk, an implementation team and a systems support department. The company says its software connects with Google Classroom and OneRoster.

The business began when Rick Smith and Rich Dilts set out to create a web-based student record system for K-12 school districts in New Jersey. paragraphs: BECS Technology builds electronic controllers, starting with water chemistry and filtration controls used on swimming pools, water parks, spas and splash pads. A second line goes into pork and poultry barns, where the company says its products help assure livestock health. A third covers refrigeration, with controls that supermarkets, convenience stores and liquor stores use to hold groceries at temperature.

A water chemistry controller watches the pool continuously and decides when the water needs attention. Operators reach those controllers through an online service the company describes as simple and secure. On the livestock side, the systems track feed inventory across a farm and send real-time data back to feed mills.

The company was incorporated in 1991. Its original ownership group has remained unchanged and has been together for over 30 years. More than 50,000 controllers have been designed and manufactured over that period. All manufacturing is performed onsite at a facility in Saint Louis, Missouri. The BECSys line of water treatment controllers was introduced in 2005. Before that, many products were marketed and distributed under the names of partner organizations.

before.description: Weather data, alerting and decision tools for government agencies

after.name: Baron Weather
after.description: Weather data, alerting and decision tools for government agencies

paragraphs: Baron Weather sells weather data, forecasting and alerting tools to businesses, government agencies and communities. Its catalog holds hundreds of datasets, with information down to the street level. The company argues that free or incomplete sources leave organizations either over-prepared and wasteful or under-prepared and at risk.

Baron blends data from many sources into insights using analytical processes, machine learning, and AI. Many of its products carry built-in alerting and recommended actions to guide a decision. The company also builds weather radar hardware it describes as engineered for durability and sustainability. Its forecast modeling covers atmospheric, hydrological, marine, air quality, and road surface coupled models. Content is prepackaged so it can be shared quickly and understood without expertise.

The company traces its mission to 1989, when an F4 tornado devastated parts of Huntsville, Alabama. Its customer base spans government agencies, emergency managers, small startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Baron lists ISO 9001 quality management among the credentials behind its processes. ISO 14001 environmental management is listed as well.

paragraphs: Greenzie makes self-driving software meant to improve the safety, productivity and profitability of a landscaping fleet. It partners with OEMs to manufacture Greenzie-equipped, Robotic Ready mowers sold at outdoor power equipment dealers throughout the United States. Buyers shop for those mowers at dealer locations nationwide.

Each Greenzie-equipped mower carries sensors the company says are field tested for obstacle avoidance, smooth driving and clean stripes. Operators can switch between manual and autonomous modes. A crew mows the perimeter once and lets the software finish the job while they move on to other tasks. The software is designed in accordance with ANSI/RIA R15.08-1-2020 safety requirements for industrial robots.

The customers are commercial landscaping crews, and the company frames its work as making jobs easier, faster and safer for large landscapers across the country. Greenzie began in 2018, when co-founder Charles Brian Quinn started calling every landscaper he could reach. The team describes itself as roboticists, software engineers and landscaping professionals. It says it is backed by venture capital firms and investors.

after.name: Perry Weather
after.description: Weather safety platform: WBGT heat monitoring, lightning alerts, stations and sirens for parks and athletics

paragraphs: Perry Weather sells a weather safety platform that pairs monitoring hardware at a customer site with automated alerting, so an entire staff works from the same reading of conditions. The buyers it names are schools, cities, golf clubs, and industrial firms.

Stations at the customer location measure heat stress, lightning, precipitation, wind, and air quality, refreshing every five minutes in the mobile app and dashboard. Each organization writes its own thresholds and decides who gets notified when one is crossed. Alerts can go to phones or to an outdoor siren system. Countdown timers mark the moment it is safe to resume play or work. All-clears go out automatically once the threat has passed.

Colin Perry founded the company in 2013. It reports more than 5,000 organizations nationwide as customers. It also counts over 200 million alerts sent, covering hazards from heat stress to lightning. Arthur Ventures led a $15M Series B. The stated markets run across athletics, golf, parks and recreation, energy, and airports.

after.name: CurbIQ

paragraphs: CurbIQ sells curb management software to cities, universities and airports, giving them one place to keep curb regulations and usage data. The problem it addresses is balancing curb access among pedestrians, parking, deliveries, rideshares and vendors.

The platform pulls curb regulation and usage data from multiple sources into a single database. Records are held in curb data standards including CDS, D-TRO and CurbLR. Map overlays show when and where regulations are in effect, and the tool models what a proposed policy change would do. Data sharing runs through APIs so couriers, ride-hailing companies and navigation platforms can see the current rules.

CurbIQ was founded by Peter Richards, formerly chair of the Institute of Transportation Engineers Parking Standing Committee. The team managed the Southern California Association of Governments Curb Space Management Study. The company belongs to the Open Mobility Foundation, a nonprofit that builds open-source tools for cities. CurbIQ itself is a product of the design firm Arcadis.

paragraphs: AIMS is parking management software from EDC Corporation, built to handle citations, permits and field enforcement for whoever runs the parking operation. The company writes that the system is meant to scale whether the buyer runs a city, a university, a hospital campus or an airport.

Citations are entered in real time from the field, with photos, GPS coordinates and notes attached to each one. Permits can be virtual or physical, and the software carries waitlists, renewals and permit prioritization. Fixed and mobile plate recognition cameras push reads, hits and occupancy data back into the system as they happen. A self-service portal gives the public round-the-clock access to payments, permits and appeals.

The site states that more than 300 clients in the United States and Canada use the software. A move onto the platform is described as taking twelve to sixteen weeks. The company describes the system as PCI and SOC 2 compliant. It also says the developers who write the software are the ones who support it.

after.name: Fybr

paragraphs: Fybr sells parking technology and an operations platform built on privacy by design. It turns anonymous, real-time parking activity into the tools that run an operation and the insights to improve it. The range covers every space, facility, and curb.

The foundation is the FybrPuck, the company's own fourth-generation occupancy sensor, a compact, self-powered, wireless edge device. It covers on-street and off-street spaces, loading zones, no parking zones, ADA spaces, and EV charging stations. Occupancy status feeds real-time guidance through a mobile application, web browsers, and dynamic wayfinding signage. For enforcement, officers can be directed to potential violations rather than running continuous sweeps. Where an ordinance requires vehicle identification, license plate recognition scans vehicles for compliance. Payment is pay-per-use inside the mobile application. A dashboard tracks turnover, session duration, dwell times, rule compliance, peak demand, and utilization trends.

The homepage carries testimonials from municipal staff, one crediting the real-time enforcement app with helping officers identify issues and respond to violations. Another says the sensor technology improved parking enforcement operations in Marysville. A third says that after the parking system was implemented, spots could be found easily through the app.

paragraphs: Autura sells software to the people who handle towing on public roads, from the officers and dispatchers who order a tow to the impound teams who store and release the vehicle. The company says it supplies towing management and unclaimed vehicle auction software to public safety agency leaders and towing and recovery business owners.

On the agency side, the product handles tow requests and rotation, and Autura says it gives agencies complete control over their towing program. Impound work is pulled into a single compliant system covering storage lookup, regulated fees, and lien and notification workflows. Lien handling uses state-approved lien search and notification capabilities. A separate marketplace covers how impound facilities sell unclaimed vehicles. Agencies can also see private tows logged in their jurisdiction.

The company took its current shape after a 2024 merger with TRAXERO and other acquisitions. It says many of its team members are former tow operators, impound managers, law enforcement officers, and telecommunicators. Its stated reason for the work is roadside safety.

paragraphs: Arrive sells urban mobility technology to city governments, parking operators and businesses. On the parking side that means demand insight and digital payments for parking and EV charging.

Drivers start, stop, extend and pay for a session from an app. Operators run payment stations and in-car integrations from the same platform. License plate recognition can start and end sessions automatically as cars enter and leave. The company says its EV solutions connect with more than 400 charge point operators. For city planners, dashboards report parking use, traffic trends and mobility patterns to guide planning.

That timeline opens with Cale installing its first parking meters. Within the group, Flowbird is described as delivering mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries. after.name: AirGarage
after.description: Full-service automated parking operations for cities and airports

paragraphs: AirGarage runs the parking lots and garages that sit on other people's real estate, managing them for the owner. Instead of selling equipment or a booking app on its own, the company takes on the hardware, the software and the daily operations together.

Cameras on site gather data in real time, and dashboards turn that into a picture of how the property is performing. Rates then move automatically with the market rather than sitting at a fixed posted price. Enforcement is handled by staff on the ground, backed by LPR and aerial camera technology. The company also markets each lot to drivers on the parking aggregator sites they already use. Owners are billed through a revenue share rather than a flat management fee. Agreements run month to month rather than on a long term contract.

AirGarage started in 2017. It says it now partners with hundreds of properties nationwide, from independent owners to institutional investors. Its published case studies include 75 Saint, a 185-space lot and garage in Boston owned by Jefferson Apartment Group. The about page also lists news coverage of a $12.5M round led by a16z.

paragraphs: Cleverciti sells outdoor and on-street parking detection, monitoring and guidance systems. Deployments span retail, smart city, entertainment, education and transportation settings. Airports are one target, where the pitch is winning back customers from off-airport parking.

Digital signage placed at each intersection and parking aisle entrance keeps drivers from circling or driving into fully occupied areas. The displays are meant to blend into the existing streetscape, wrapping around lampposts. Occupancy data can be published to any other system through a REST API. Rather than launching another app, availability, search and guidance components can be built into an app visitors already use. Fully digital 360 degree displays can push updated messaging visible from all directions.

Cleverciti was founded in 2012 by Thomas Hohenacker and Konrad Prinz-Dreher. It reports deployments at over 200 locations in over 20 countries. Offices include European headquarters in Munich, Germany, and North American headquarters in Atlanta. paragraphs: Computronix sells off-the-shelf software solutions for permitting, licensing, alcoholic beverage control, and gaming control. Those products run on POSSE, a web-based platform for automating permitting, licensing, enforcement and compliance workflows.

The permitting product automates workflows for building, planning, engineering, permitting, inspections and code enforcement. The alcoholic beverage control product manages the business and data behind liquor licensing, compliance and enforcement. The gaming product is aimed at agencies seeking a risk-based regulatory model for the gaming industry. The company says the software is engineered to comply with high security and regulatory compliance standards, including NIST, FedRAMP and ISO. Newer offerings include AI-powered portal assistance that helps applicants find answers and navigate permitting processes.

Computronix was founded in 1979 by Herman Leusink. It describes growing from a single employee to nearly two hundred employees and dozens of clients in major population centers across North America. One case study covers the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission, which regulates and controls that state's alcoholic beverage industry. The same alcohol system is used in nine other states and two provinces for alcohol industry regulation. Another case study describes the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario using POSSE ABC for liquor control, gaming, horse racing and recreational cannabis.

paragraphs: City Detect sells a camera and software service that helps municipalities and counties find and address urban blight before complaints pile up. Cameras ride on a city's existing fleet vehicles and collect images of properties as those vehicles drive their normal routes. The company's PASS AI then detects and maps signs of urban blight and decay from the public right of way.

Roof-mounted data collection units capture street-level imagery during routine city operations. Once the images are processed, each detection is assigned a severity score from 1 to 4 and placed on an interactive map. The conditions it picks up run to illegal dumping, tire accumulations, snipe signs, and graffiti. Staff can export timestamped, image-backed reports in a few clicks.

The company says it was founded in 2021. One published case study describes Cathedral City partnering with City Detect in June 2025. For each municipality the company performs local calibration meant to cut false-positive detections and match local rules.

paragraphs: Clariti sells community development software to local governments, pitched at any size and budget. One edition is permitting software for large local governments. It also tracks code violations from report to resolution, with automatic case assignment and links to local zoning and codes. Staff can build a report, adjust a page layout, or create a new permit type themselves. The large-jurisdiction edition runs on the Salesforce Platform, whose APIs let a government connect its other tools. Launch customers can copy a peer's permitting workflows using a cloning tool. The company says the large-jurisdiction product was built with input from government customers over 16 years. Its home page names Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Orange County among the cities and counties using Clariti. Launch pricing is stated as based on population rather than user count.

paragraphs: Deckard Technologies sells software that local governments use to deal with residential property problems in their jurisdictions. The products cover short-term rentals, long-term rentals, and foreclosed and vacant properties.

The short-term rental product monitors a jurisdiction by analyzing more than 15 million listings from over 10,000 rental websites in real time. The vacancy and foreclosure side watches court records and mortgage reassignments instead. Other tools handle transient occupancy tax filings and payments. A published case study describes a city adopting the Rentalscape platform in 2024 with a structured letter outreach campaign, in which the vendor develops the mailing list and generates, prints and mails the letters to identified hosts.

The company was founded in May 2018 by Greg Rose, Jess Flanagan and Tony Moriarty, starting in both Australia and the United States. It now keeps offices in the United States, Colombia and Australia. Its own count of customers is more than 500 jurisdictions worldwide. The company timeline records several seed rounds, among them a Seed-4 raise.

paragraphs: Accela sells software that government agencies use to run permitting, licensing, and asset management from a single system. Its applications are built for individual government service workflows and can operate together or be deployed only where an agency needs them.

For building departments, intake, plan review, inspections, and permit issuance sit in one workflow rather than in separate disconnected steps. Reviewers from different departments work the same record at once, with annotations and approvals tracked as they happen. Planning teams get the same shared review model, plus automated public notice generation, hearing schedules, and agency notifications. Applicants can see where a case stands and receive consolidated feedback from every reviewing department.

The company says it has thirty years of government expertise built into the product. Testimonials on the site are attributed to municipal staff, including a chief building official in McAllen, Texas. Residents and businesses who encounter Accela through a local agency are directed to that agency rather than to the company.

paragraphs: Can/Am Technologies sells Teller, a cashiering and point-of-sale package made for local and state government agencies across North America. More than 80 state and local governments use it for cashiering, payment technology, and credit processing. The idea is a single hub that centralizes revenue collection, credit processing, and reconciliation.

Residents pay through web and mobile portals, which clear through a processor cloud. Departments that collect revenue submit structured batches directly instead of handing paper to a cashier to re-key. Lockbox files, third-party systems, and online application payments import automatically on a schedule the agency sets. At the close of business Teller posts a single organized general ledger entry while accounts receivable stays in sync. paragraphs: Autoagent sells payment software to local government offices, built around the work of collecting public revenue. The company says its payment products work together or independently, to fit how a government office operates.

EscrowCloud handles bulk property tax payments by holding current tax data that mass payers must pay against, so they cannot submit a different amount or pay on an invalid property ID. A tax office adds its start and due dates to the system, and payers are notified of the collection cycle in real time. On the payer side, each parcel is validated and the amounts and exceptions are displayed before payment. The company states that it works with data files from all major tax administration systems. A second product, MuniciPay, brings online, in-person, IVR, eCheck, bankcard and mobile wallet payments into one platform. A third lets residents split an annual property tax bill into monthly payments.

The company describes county and municipal tax offices across 48 states as its users. It states that the platform integrates directly with more than 900 tax offices nationwide. EscrowCloud is free for property tax offices, with mortgage lenders, tax servicers and property managers paying a per-property fee. The company says the product is PCI DSS Level 1 certified and SOC 2 Type 2 compliant.

A vendor dashboard saves keyword searches and agency watchlists. Vendors can search open RFPs, ITBs and other contracting opportunities. Those searches can specify keyword tags and commodity codes. On the agency side, setting up a new solicitation for vendor bid submission takes moments. Submitted bids are then reviewed through a bid review dashboard.

Agencies from coast to coast use it to publish contracting opportunities. The agencies browsable by region include the Kentucky Community and Technical College System. Seattle Public Schools also appears on that list.

paragraphs: Avila sells an AI grant platform aimed at local government. The site says it finds the opportunities an agency qualifies for and writes its proposals. It also says it helps governments, schools and nonprofits discover and apply for funding.

Discovery matches state, local, regional and foundation opportunities to a customer's own projects. For applications, the platform simplifies dense notices of funding opportunity into clearer requirements. It fills in federal forms including SF-424, SF-424A, SF-LLL and program-specific attachments. Once an award lands, it ingests invoices and auto-categorizes expenses against the approved budget. It also flags compliance issues against 2 CFR 200 and the awarding agency's rules.

Users named on the site include the Houston-Galveston Area Council. One case study describes a mid-sized county government in the western U.S. Another describes a statewide public university system in the northeast. The company states that it is SOC 2 compliant. It says all data is encrypted in transit and at rest. The about page says NVIDIA Inception, Microsoft for Startups and MongoDB have welcomed the company into their programs.

after.name: Emburse
after.description: Expense management and payment software - exhibited at NIGP 2026, NACUBO 2026

paragraphs: Emburse sells travel and expense management software to finance teams. The platform covers expense, travel, accounts payable, cards, invoices and ACH payments, with localization for more than 100 countries.

Receipts are read by optical character recognition, whether the paper original or a digital copy. Spend is sorted automatically across dozens of categories, with VAT reconciliation and multiple currencies handled along the way. Policies are written once and enforced across the organization rather than checked afterward. A compliance layer examines receipts before and after submission, applying policy consistently and flagging risk early. For travel, the company sits alongside a customer's existing travel management company rather than replacing it, rebooking air and hotel when prices fall under rules the customer sets. It also connects to ERP, finance and accounting systems.

The company states that it serves over 20,000 organizations in 200 countries and territories. Those customers are described as large enterprises, smaller businesses, public sector agencies and nonprofits. Marne Martin is the chief executive. In July 2026 the company announced that it had been named to CNBC's list of the world's top fintech companies for that year.

after.name: Casepoint
after.description: Cloud eDiscovery and legal hold platform for government agencies and courts

paragraphs: Casepoint sells a cloud platform for eDiscovery, FOIA, investigations, and compliance work. Inside it, teams collect, process, analyze, review, and produce data in one place. The pitch is that all the data for a matter is managed in one place rather than moved between tools.

Connectors pull data straight from platforms such as Slack, Microsoft 365, and Teams. The processing engine supports over 600 file types. A separate FOIA product is built around how agencies respond to public records requests. Requesters use a portal to file requests and pay for them through pay.gov. For Canada, ATIPXpress carries access and privacy requests from submission through search, review, redaction, exemption analysis, and delivery.

The company describes the platform as purpose-built for corporations and government entities. It states that Casepoint holds FedRAMP Moderate and High authorizations, ISO 27001 certification, and Department of Defense Impact Level 5 and Impact Level 6 authorizations. It also claims to be one of only six SaaS companies globally with DOD IL6 authorization. Its AI is described as built for legal and regulatory work.

paragraphs: WebIZ is an immunization information system sold to state and local government public health agencies. The registry is now offered inside InductiveHealth's public health platform. It is built to meet CDC standards for tracking and administering immunizations in any jurisdiction.

The system follows vaccine inventory from ordering through delivery and administration. Clinic record systems send administered doses straight into the registry, which cuts duplicate entry. Embedded dashboards report coverage rates by ZIP code, vaccine type, age group and provider. School entry rules are configured once for a state and then applied to every student and grade. Residents pull their own immunization records from a secure portal with multi-factor authentication.

The company says the product has served more than 20 jurisdictions across two decades. Under a shared development model, one jurisdiction's funded enhancement reaches the rest in the next monthly release. InductiveHealth dates its founding to 2013. It works with federal, state, tribal, local and territorial jurisdictions on disease surveillance. Staff include epidemiologists and public health experts alongside engineers and technologists.

Screen puts real time transportation information and managed communications on displays. Journey is a trip planner a customer can brand and customize. Insight, an add on to those subscriptions, reports how deployments are used, from a scanned QR code through to a trip that gets started. Matt Caywood incorporated it and was soon joined by co-founder Ryan Croft. The company says it now works with over 1,000 customers in more than 50 cities across ten countries. Its own AI is said to drive trip recommendations and insights for transportation and real estate.

before.name: Axon Vibe

after.name: Axon Vibe
after.description: Mobility behavior platform powering operator apps: journey detection, BIBO ticketing (built the MTA app)

paragraphs: Axon Vibe sells a smartphone-based, multi-modal mobility platform to public transport operators and authorities. The idea is to match a rider's predicted travel patterns against real-time traffic on roads and rail, then offer more efficient and less polluting travel options.

Patented location tracking predicts what people are going to do next, and psychological communication interventions are used to shift their behaviour. Riders who respond are rewarded with travel fare incentives financed by green governmental funds, plus rewards provided by local merchants. The platform is also sold to enable automatic ticketing, incentivise behaviour change and optimise customer flow management. For cities, understanding why and how people travel in real time is presented as the basis for more accurate planning.

Door-to-door journey detection powers Deutsche Bahn check-in and be-out ticketing, for example in Greater Nuremberg. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority launched its official MTA app in March 2024. Founded in 2014, the company describes a team of more than 100 software engineers, data scientists, location analytics experts, psychologists and communication specialists. Its predecessor Endoxon delivered core technology for Google Maps and was acquired by Google in 2006.

paragraphs: Deledao sells web filtering to K-12 schools, built on patented technology the company says analyzes each webpage as a human would. The product line later grew to cover student safety and classroom management.

The filter blurs, mutes, and screens inappropriate images and video frame by frame. It detects gaming behavior from keyboard and mouse activity without logging keystrokes. Proxy sites students use to bypass filtering are caught automatically. Teachers get visibility into student tabs or screens. Websites can be allowed or blocked by group or by individual student. The wellness product looks for cyberbullying, self-harm, and toxic language across platforms. High-risk alerts receive human review and escalation to the district.

The company names Shuang Ji as its chief executive. Its first product, a web filter using real-time AI, launched in 2019. It says it now supports schools in the United States, Canada, Europe, New Zealand, and Australia. Case studies on the site describe schools adopting the filter for CIPA compliance and student safety.

paragraphs: Xtract One makes AI-powered concealed weapons detection systems for building entrances. The company sells them for schools, hospitals, and other public venues.

The premise is that the systems flag actual threats while ignoring laptops, phones, keys, and everyday items. SmartGateway uses AI-powered passive magnetic field sensor arrays to identify firearms and bladed weapons. It is rated to screen up to 4,000 individuals per hour per lane. A second system, Xtract One Gateway, is built for places where people carry a medium volume of personal belongings, with no conveyor belts or divestment bins. Multiple units are managed centrally through Xtract One View.

On privacy, the company states that SmartGateway collects no personally identifiable information and does not use facial recognition. It also says the magnetic field sits well below safety limits set by the IEEE, FCC, and international health organizations. Among the deployments it publicizes is Manor ISD, which it says put Gateway across its high school campuses as one of the first Texas districts to do so at scale. Another cites Community Health Network preventing 6,007 weapons across 9 entry points in 6 months.

after.name: Centegix
after.description: CrisisAlert wearable panic buttons for school staff; 18M+ people covered

paragraphs: CENTEGIX sells emergency alerting for schools, built around a solution called CrisisAlert that lets any staff member call for help. The alert carries the exact floor, room or hallway rather than just a building name.

When a full alert fires, strobes and intercoms activate across the campus. Arriving responders are shown the precise location of the person who pressed the button. The company is careful to say that most of what it handles is not an active shooter but a medical emergency, a behavioral crisis or a student leaving campus. Around the alerting sit other modules, including visitor management for authenticating and locating people on campus. Reunification is handled the same way, with a guardian verified before any student is handed over. Rollout starts with a short discovery call that maps buildings and looks for gaps in response.

School districts are the core audience, with the product framed as giving staff the confidence to act quickly. The same technology is offered to healthcare organizations facing workplace violence. A third line is aimed at public servants and the staff who work alongside them. The company says the product was built by former educators, law enforcement officers and caregivers. It also convenes an invitation-only customer advisory board drawn from senior safety leaders.

quote.text: CENTEGIX was founded on the idea that technology can create safer, more secure environments.

after.name: Lightspeed Systems
after.description: Web filtering and student safety monitoring for school districts - exhibited at CoSN 2026

paragraphs: Lightspeed Systems sells a connected platform of K-12 edtech products that give schools visibility and control across safety, security, compliance, device management, and analytics. Its filter covers every digital interaction on and off the network, protecting students from cyber risks and distractions while keeping access and compliance in place.

Filtering is enforced on the device itself, with an on-device SmartAgent and SmartShield DNS filtering covering school-managed, BYOD, and IoT devices. Lightspeed Alert monitors online activity, flags concerning behaviors, and enables intervention before a tragedy occurs. Those alerts are backed by round-the-clock monitoring from the company's own safety specialists. Lightspeed Classroom gives teachers visibility into and control over student activity to minimize distractions and maximize instructional time. Lightspeed StopIt is an anonymous reporting system for safety, misconduct, or compliance concerns. An analytics product shows granular app and device usage down to the grade and student level.

The company states that 28 of the 50 largest US school districts use its software, naming Los Angeles Unified, Houston ISD, Miami-Dade County Public Schools, and Fairfax County Public Schools. It puts the wider count at 31,000 schools around the world. The filter is described as designed for CIPA, FERPA, and NIST-aligned environments, with exportable audit trails and long-term retention.

before.description: Passive airspace monitoring sensors for airports and government agencies

after.name: Hidden Level
after.description: Passive airspace monitoring sensors for airports and government agencies

paragraphs: Hidden Level sells radio-frequency sensing hardware and data services to government, defense and commercial security teams. The sensing is passive, which the company says leaves the equipment undetected and hard to jam.

The Breaker sensor is built for fixed sites and is meant to coexist with infrastructure and telecom equipment already there. The Surge mounts to land and water vehicles and is made to withstand harsh conditions. Customers who would rather not run hardware can buy data from a global sensor network the company owns, operates and maintains. That service pinpoints drone operator location and lets users define zones so alerts arrive only for activity in chosen areas. Data reaches other systems through an open API secured with FIPS 140-2 compliant cryptography, or through a web interface.

Stated uses include protecting airspace around stadiums, airports and buildings, and preventing contraband drone deliveries to correctional facilities. The hardware page cites FCC compliance along with TRL9 and MIL-STD-810 testing. The company says its sensors analyze the physical characteristics of signals without decoding private information. Researchers can reach the collected captures through APIs for training and benchmarking work.

paragraphs: Alcatraz makes facial authentication products that work with the badge readers and access control systems an organization already runs. The device, called Rock X, sits in line between the badge reader and the access control panel over Wiegand or OSDP.

Employees enroll at a station, remotely from a browser or phone, or automatically after repeated badge swipes at a door fitted with the device. Authentication happens on the device itself, and the company states that no sensitive data is stored or transmitted. Profiles are anonymized and tied to the badge ID already held in the customer's access control system. The same unit can act as a passive second factor, so a person badges in as usual and the face confirms the match. In lobbies it can be built directly into certain turnstiles. The management platform runs on premise or in the cloud.

Airports are one setting the company writes about, pairing face recognition with badges or PINs to add a second factor at restricted doors. One unnamed case summary on the site describes a global enterprise that put the device on turnstiles for more than 150,000 employees. The company says its approach helps customers conform with privacy regulations such as BIPA, CCPA and GDPR.

paragraphs: Liberty Defense makes AI-based detection equipment for finding concealed weapons and other threats in urban security and aviation settings. Its main product, HEXWAVE, is a walkthrough portal that screens for nonmetallic and metallic threats without asking people to remove shoes, jewelry, belts or jackets.

It uses active millimeter wave, video-rate 3D imaging and AI to detect concealed metallic and non-metallic weapons and other prohibited items. The company says the imaging captures over 400,000 voxels. No images are stored, and none are accessible by the security operator. The operator sees only a go or no-go screen with a clear alert. For aviation, Liberty holds exclusive licenses to two solutions developed by PNNL and funded by the Department of Homeland Security.

The home page states that Liberty delivers HEXWAVE to the TSA. It also says the company is developing screening for aviation workers. before.description: Access control and perimeter security for airports and critical government sites

after.name: Gallagher Security
after.description: Access control and perimeter security for airports and critical government sites

paragraphs: Gallagher Security designs and manufactures integrated security products across access control, perimeter security, intruder alarms, and cybersecurity. Its customers range from small businesses to enterprise organizations and critical infrastructure sites. Systems are sized from a single door to thousands across multiple sites.

Access control runs on card readers, mobile credentials, and biometric devices that verify permissions. Controllers act as the central hub, processing access requests and communicating with connected systems. Roles, schedules, and activity are managed in Command Centre, the company's centralized platform, with customizable dashboards and reporting. On the perimeter, high-tensile pulse fences form a visual barrier and deliver safe, short pulses that deter intruders. Sensors alert a team the moment a fence is touched. Perimeter protection is a native part of Command Centre, the same software that runs access control and intruder detection. It works with most existing fence types, so a site can add detection without replacing its fencing.

paragraphs: UVeye builds automated inspection systems that scan the full exterior, undercarriage, and tires of a vehicle in seconds. Dealerships use the scans to document pre-existing damage and avoid unnecessary claims. Seaports and logistics hubs use touchless inspections to speed vehicle handoffs and settle disputes. Bus and truck operators run standardized inspections to improve compliance.

A scan combines high-resolution imaging, sensors, and patented AI to surface problems the eye cannot catch. Findings run from tire wear and misalignment to leaks, rust, and underbody damage. Output arrives as images and measurements of dents, scratches, and undercarriage issues. Automatic notifications flag critical issues that need immediate attention.

Brothers Amir and Ohad Hever founded UVeye in 2016. The first application was undercarriage security screening, which grew into a platform that scans whole vehicles. Systems are now deployed across hundreds of dealerships, fleets, rental agencies, and manufacturing lines worldwide. The company names Amazon, General Motors, Volvo, and CarMax among the companies using it. It reports over $380 million raised.

after.name: Dedrone by Axon

paragraphs: Dedrone by Axon sells counter-drone systems that secure fixed locations such as airports, correctional facilities and critical infrastructure from unauthorized drones. Law enforcement, military and public safety organizations are named as the buyers for its mobile unit.

A fixed installation combines radio-frequency sensors, radar and pan-tilt-zoom cameras over the airspace at a site. The radio-frequency sensors analyse signals to detect and locate both the drone and its pilot. Cameras add visual verification of a drone incursion. Command and control software called DedroneTracker.AI fuses those tracks and reports drone and pilot location. A towable trailer packages the same mix for temporary sites and is described as set up in less than twenty minutes. A city-wide option skips installed equipment altogether, letting users mark alert zones and get notified when drones enter them.

The company states that its fixed-site product is deployed at over 829 sites globally. It says its customers include military organizations, airports, correctional facilities, stadiums and critical infrastructure sites. The city-wide app is described as available in over 50 cities.

before.name: EarthDaily
before.description: Satellite earth-observation imagery and change-detection analytics for agencies, insurance, and ag - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026

after.name: EarthDaily
after.description: Satellite earth-observation imagery and change-detection analytics for agencies, insurance, and ag - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: EarthDaily is a geospatial company selling satellite imagery and analytics to governments and enterprises whose work depends on the physical world. Its stated purpose is daily monitoring of the earth's surface for broad area change detection.

Raw satellite data is captured through a purpose-built constellation and ground system. That data is then processed, calibrated and quality-controlled into scientifically accurate image products. One product, AiRD, is analysis-ready observation data engineered from the start for machine learning. Its spectral bands are calibrated to match Sentinel-2 and Landsat specifications. A second product, Maritime, is tuned for fast processing and detection of anomalies at sea.

The company focuses its products on agriculture, financial services, infrastructure, forestry and governments. Security organizations, analytics providers and coastal agencies are the named audience for the maritime data. A company timeline states that it was created in partnership with Antarctica Capital. The same timeline lists an acquisition of Descartes Labs and funding from Trinity Capital. It also records more than 500 agreements signed. A news item states the company achieved CEOS Analysis Ready Data compliance.

quote.text: A new era of change detection through earth observation has begun.

before.name: Balancing Act
before.description: Interactive budget simulation and priority-setting tools for public agencies

after.name: Balancing Act
after.description: Interactive budget simulation and priority-setting tools for public agencies

paragraphs: Balancing Act sells simulation-based public engagement tools to government. The company describes an online simulation that draws stakeholders in so that leaders can make hard choices with public input behind them. The suite is aimed at budget, housing, climate and planning work.

In a budget simulation, residents see a model of the budget and their input is collected. A companion tool asks a few questions, estimates the taxes a household pays and shows where those dollars go. A mode for meetings turns the simulation into a facilitation tool for in-person and online sessions. There is also a research version for use with representative samples. The Prioritize product goes past a survey by having users pick items and then rank their picks. Its consensus analysis reports how many stakeholders end up with at least one of their choices included.

The housing product addresses cities and counties that struggle with public participation as they try to meet demand for new housing. Those simulations put residents in the shoes of decisionmakers and ask them to help solve the problem, with an interactive map showing where housing would be placed. Prioritize has been offered for input on stimulus funds such as ARPA and ESSER. A testimonial on the site is attributed to a village administrator in Germantown, Wisconsin.

quote.text: Balancing Act is an easy-to-use online simulation that engages stakeholders to help leaders make tough choices.

paragraphs: AchieveIt sells software for moving a written plan into measurable progress. It pitches itself to public agencies and other organizations that find performance hard to measure. The idea behind it is connecting people, plans and data in one place.

A plan is structured to match whatever methodology a customer already uses, from pillars and objectives down to initiatives, KPIs and milestones. Update requests then go out on a chosen cadence, asking owners for status, percent complete, commentary and metric values that flow into dashboards and roll-up reports. A tree view shows how each item in a plan lines up with the rest. Custom dashboards can display information drawn from any plan in the organization. A multi-plan view lets a customer filter, segment and drill into progress across everything at once.

AchieveIt says strategy consultants and customer success managers work alongside each customer. Onboarding, training and hands-on help come with the move away from manual tracking. The site sorts prospects by sector so a buyer can see how the software fits their way of working. One page groups its public sector claims under a heading about proven results.

before.name: Corporater

after.name: Corporater
after.description: Governance, performance and risk management platform for public sector organizations

paragraphs: Corporater sells enterprise software that brings governance, performance, risk and compliance together in one system. The company aims the platform at medium and large organizations, including multinational groups working across several regions and regulatory environments.

At the center is a digital model of the organization that connects strategy, processes, risks, controls, KPIs and policies instead of leaving them spread across separate tools. Customers assemble solutions from configurable business objects rather than commissioning custom development. Processes handled on the platform include strategic planning, enterprise risk management, internal audit, policy and incident management, ESG reporting and business continuity. A conversational assistant named TIVA lets users register risks, complete compliance tasks and trigger workflows by asking in plain language.

Buyers can run the platform as SaaS, on their own premises, or in a private cloud. The company describes customers in regulated industries across more than fifty countries. It states that the platform is VL5 Veracode Verified. Its work on digital twins of an organization has been named in Gartner market guides, according to the site.

after.name: Dimonoff
after.description: Streetlight control nodes and SCMS smart-city management platform for municipalities and utilities

paragraphs: Dimonoff sells smart street lighting control, connecting street and commercial lighting to a single platform so teams can monitor every fixture in real time. The site dates its work in smart street lighting control back to 2006.

A controller fits a NEMA or Zhaga socket on any LED fixture, from any manufacturer, and dims over 0-10V or DALI. The nodes network over Wi-SUN, RF mesh or LTE-M, and keep running their schedule if the link drops. In the office, one interface holds groups, schedules, dimming profiles, faults and reports, and pushes work orders into the asset system a city already runs. The platform also manages nodes from third-party manufacturers, so hardware from a previous supplier does not have to be scrapped. One part number covers supply voltages from 110 to 480 Vac nominal at 50/60 Hz. Node firmware is updated over the air rather than by a crew in a truck.

Networks already running on the platform account for more than 219,500 connected endpoints, by the company's count. Dimonoff states that all of its hardware and software is designed, developed, manufactured and supported in North America. The support FAQ names Groupe Vectanor as the parent company and says it joined the Wi-SUN Alliance as a Contributing Member in April 2026.
