after.name: Fonroche Lighting America
after.description: Autonomous off-grid solar streetlights with remote monitoring; 1,000+ municipalities, 43 states (French parent)

paragraphs: Fonroche Lighting America designs and sells off-grid solar lighting for streets and roadways, parking lots, parks, pathways, campuses and other public infrastructure. The range runs from SmartLight solar streetlights to NOWATT solar bollards and solar studs.

Because each system operates independently of the grid, a project can skip underground cabling and utility connections. Pre-wired modular power centers hold the energy storage. The company says a crew can install and activate a lighting system in under an hour. Designs begin with an analysis of ten years of local solar data using the PVsyst software suite and Meteonorm historical irradiation data. Once installed, the lights can be monitored remotely through a wireless network called Fonroche Connect.

The systems are built for municipalities, tribal communities, federal campuses, developers and commercial properties. Case studies describe Augusta, Georgia, which addressed safety and budget problems on Windsor Spring Road by deploying 42 autonomous solar streetlights. In Rowlett, Texas, the city is installing 425 solar-powered SmartLights across a 5.5-mile stretch of three corridors. The American business took its present form when Fonroche Lighting acquired SolarOne Solutions and incorporated Fonroche Lighting America. The site invites visitors to join 1,000+ communities and businesses already using its lighting.

quote.text: Because reliability isn’t optional when you’re off the grid.

paragraphs: Dareesoft sells road hazard detection that rides along in vehicles already using the road network. The offering is packaged as Road Information as a Service, an all-in-one solution for road maintenance. The company describes itself as an integrated road data company.

A device in the vehicle analyzes the road and transmits hazards to a cloud platform instantly. Each detection carries a high quality image with GPS coordinates, road network, timestamps and object size. Detected hazards appear on a road monitoring dashboard for remote inspection. An API suite lets the hazard data flow into systems an agency already runs.

Dareesoft was founded in 2020. Its company timeline lists a contract for the Seoul Metropolitan Government video-based pothole detection project. The same timeline records a project secured with Brazoria County, Texas. Another entry lists a project contract signed with New York City for speed signage. It also lists a Series B raise of KRW 4 billion.

after.description: Connected-vehicle ITS and the Glance smart-city platform: signal monitoring, preemption, school beacons

paragraphs: Applied Information makes traffic technology that turns intersections, school zones and connected vehicles into one real-time system. The customers are cities, which manage their traffic and ITS assets through a web-based application called Glance.

Glance monitors intersection cabinet equipment, reporting AC power, battery back up, cabinet flash, stop time, conflict monitor status, door switches, fan status and vehicle detectors. For emergency vehicles, an in-vehicle unit uses a cellular signal to tell the system a route has started. The system works out the route and talks wirelessly to the traffic cabinet to clear traffic ahead of the vehicle. School beacon flashers and their schedules can be viewed and controlled from anywhere. A connected vehicle product communicates over C-V2X, 4G LTE cellular and 900MHz.

The company states its hardware is designed, assembled and tested in Alpharetta, Georgia, with components meeting domestic content thresholds. A connected school bus system warns drivers approaching an active school safety zone or exceeding the speed limit. A smartphone app, Glance TravelSafely, extends the technology to residents.

quote.text: The drivers know they’ve got a green light in front of them, they know that everyone else has a red light, and they know the traffic is going to move ahead of them.

paragraphs: HAAS Alert sells a collision prevention service that sends real-time digital alerts warning drivers about nearby emergency vehicles and roadway hazards. Its customers are fleets that work at the roadside, including tow trucks, utility vehicles, waste management trucks, school buses and snowplows.

The system is wired to a vehicle's warning light bar or master switch, so alerting begins when crews turn on their lights and stops when they turn them off. Motorists install nothing, because alerts are broadcast directly to the navigation platforms they already use. Fleets can activate the service through three primary methods, depending on their existing setup. The company says drivers get up to 30 seconds of advance warning to slow down and move over.

The company traces its start to 2015, when co-founder and CEO Cory Hohs was almost struck by an ambulance on the road. He co-founded the business with Noah Levens and Jigar Patel. Its timeline notes that the United States Department of Homeland Security awarded $1.1 million toward development for digital alerting. It also states that digital alerting was codified and funded in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

quote.text: Built in America for first responders and roadside workers so everyone gets home safely.

paragraphs: Compass IoT sells connected vehicle data for road networks, taken from the cars themselves rather than roadside equipment or phones. The company says more than 3,000 users globally use its connected vehicle data to understand traffic across their road networks. Its Road Intelligence platform presents that network-wide vehicle data in a browser.

The data comes from cloud-connected vehicles that have an internet connection. Compass says it receives over a billion connected vehicle data points every day from 64 different car manufacturers. Each record can carry location, timestamp, speed, acceleration, make and model, plus road attributes such as the speed limit and pavement type. Coverage runs across virtually every road in Australia.

Published case studies show clients using the tools for road safety, city planning, and infrastructure questions. One covers Sunshine Coast Council measuring how speed cushions retrofitted at a pedestrian crossing changed driver behaviour. Afterwards, average speed in both directions dropped to 22km/h. Another describes the Inner West Council using data-driven evidence to lower speed limits for pedestrian and cyclist safety. Compass IoT UK has received funding from EIT Urban Mobility as part of the third SME Expansion Open Call.

Detection happens on the camera itself, which uploads what it finds to the cloud for review. Staff get notifications carrying the location and images of the issue. The camera picks out potholes, manholes, dumped garbage, transit infrastructure problems and signs. Two other families sit beside it: PULSE for pavement rating, pavement markings and survey imagery, and COMPANION, an app for inspectors and work crews.

Government inspectors are the main users, reporting maintenance and operations issues automatically. An open API and off-the-shelf connectors move the data into systems an agency already runs. The site claims hundreds of governments as customers.

paragraphs: SWARCO supplies road marking systems, traffic technology and industrial glass products to the people who build and operate roads. The group is headquartered in Wattens near Innsbruck, Austria, and runs an international network of plants, offices and partners. Its portfolio reaches across road marking, signage, urban traffic management, parking, highway and tunnel management, public transport and street lighting.

For cycling infrastructure the company offers coloured area markings, using green for general lanes and red to flag spots where the risk is higher. Pictograms are made from preformed thermoplastics so they sit in a rider's line of sight. Choosing a system means weighing location, traffic intensity, cost and environmental compatibility. A separate line covers runways, taxiways and aprons, where markings have to hold up against fuels, deicers, engine oils and hydraulic fluids.

Airfield marking systems have been tested and approved by the German Federal Institute for Material Research and Testing. Airport paints and marking products are made in compliance with FAA and Federal specifications as well as EASA. The company counts 5,300 transportation experts and traces its outlook to founder Manfred Swarovski.

paragraphs: Ecopia AI uses artificial intelligence to convert high-resolution geospatial imagery into accurate, up-to-date vector maps for data-driven decision-making. For municipal and state government the data is offered for transportation networks, public safety and stormwater planning. Off-the-shelf offerings sit alongside customized global feature extraction.

Its 3D Land Cover product delivers planimetric vector layers for buildings, roads, driveways, sidewalks, water bodies, sports fields and overlapping tree canopy, with height attribution for buildings. The company states that features are extracted from high-resolution imagery with greater than 95% geometric accuracy. Partner imagery providers capture fresh imagery every year, which lets the company detect change and deliver annual updates. A separate transportation product covers sidewalks, crosswalks, medians, bike lanes, turning lanes, paint striping and intersections. Those layers carry attributes such as width, material and feature type, distinguishing a left turn lane from a right turn lane.

The transportation data is aimed at AEC firms, MPOs and DOTs. Stated uses include assessing sidewalk width and curb characteristics against ADA regulations. Another stated use is emergency services and dispatch planning, drawing on 3D maps of buildings, roads and driveways. Ecopia says it produces millions of square kilometers of vector data per month. It also announced a self-serve platform for high-precision geospatial data downloads.

paragraphs: GoodVision sells traffic analysis software to transportation professionals, who use it to collect, analyze and act on traffic data taken from video footage or live camera streams. Its main platform, Video Insights, extracts data from videos in place of manual collection and uses AI to analyze traffic and automate model calibration.

A second product works on live feeds rather than uploads, analysing camera streams on the fly and passing traffic data to third-party systems such as traffic management systems and controllers. The incident detection module recognises user-defined traffic events, flags them and reports them to traffic management centre controllers. At intersections and roundabouts it counts volumes and derives parameters such as speed, gaps between vehicles, dwell time and passage time. Finished reports can be edited, regenerated and exported in Excel, CSV or custom formats.

The company describes the same monitoring applied to bridges and tunnels, where the goal is to prevent congestion and catch accidents early. Alongside direct sales, GoodVision runs a partner program and says it is seeking global distribution and service partners.

paragraphs: The business sells a traffic signal priority control platform, marketed as Opticom, to cities that want essential vehicles moving through intersections without delay. It covers two jobs: preemption that clears a path for fire, police and ambulance crews, and signal priority that keeps buses and light rail closer to schedule.

Whichever communication method a city uses, the steps are the same. When a crew activates lights and siren, equipment on the vehicle sends a request ahead to equipped intersections, which then sequence the lights to green on the approach being used. As soon as the vehicle is through, the intersection goes back to its normal cycle. Agencies can run cloud, satellite positioning and infrared deployments side by side rather than replacing everything at once.

The buyers are the people who run those services: fire and police leadership, ambulance directors, transit operations staff and fleet managers. The site dates the technology back close to six decades. Fleets can be connected through integrations with a number of vehicle and telematics vendors.

paragraphs: Blyncsy helps cities and state departments of transportation automate their roadway maintenance and asset inventory activities. Rather than sending crews out to look, it works from crowd-sourced dash camera imagery.

Machine learning algorithms and image processing applied to that imagery detect where and when pavement needs maintenance. Condition assessments run from pot holes to paint striping and crosswalk conditions. Paint lines are rated from 1, the worst, to 5, the best. In construction zones the same imagery detects work zone equipment to put those zones on the map. Those detections can also check whether a maintenance of traffic plan matches reality. A further model detects the presence of debris on and beside the road. The AI also estimates the size of the debris it finds.

Results are delivered directly into OpenGIS or another preferred platform. The company claims savings of up to 90% compared to traditional manual inspections. It puts the cost at $10 per centerline mile against $200 or more for a LiDAR scan. News items on the site include a City of Fort Worth partnership on the first phase of automated asset inventory. Another announces a sustainability partner designation in the Google Cloud Partner Advantage Program.

paragraphs: Acusensus sells automated traffic enforcement systems to the road authorities and police agencies that are trying to cut deaths and injuries on the road network. paragraphs: Aatral builds extended reality training and guidance software for industrial teams, combining VR, AR, AI and digital twins. It sells to defence and aerospace, automotive, manufacturing, steel, energy and infrastructure teams.

The platform is arranged around DAXR, described as its core intelligence layer, with verticals for training, field guidance and review. Named products cover safety training, crane simulation, remote guidance, inspection workflows, content deployment and performance intelligence. The safety product is a VR training library for hazard practice, emergency response, SOP awareness and readiness tracking. Module topics run to work at height, confined space, electrical safety, hot work, welding and chemical safety.

The company states it is headquartered in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India, with work across India and international markets. Its defence section lists a memorandum of understanding with HAL for XR solutions. Safety modules are presented as standardized across multiple plants and teams.

paragraphs: A-Frame Solutions sells ArcSuite AI, a no-code operations platform for federal, state, local and education agencies. Agencies use it to track work, evaluate vendors, compose documents and analyze data in one place, without developers.

Four integrated modules make up the suite, and a customer can use one or all four. ArcTracker holds configurable items, checklists, role-based access, relationships and rollups, and is the record every other module hangs off. ArcInsight is an assistant that answers plain English questions grounded in that tracker data. That assistant is powered by Claude on AWS Bedrock. ArcProcure covers solicitations, evaluations and contract management end to end, while ArcSelect is a multi-evaluator consensus platform for scoring or ranking decisions.

A-Frame Solutions was founded in 2014 by three former federal Contracting Officers. Its first contract was with the NOAA acquisition and grants office. The platform is available on GSA MAS Schedule 47QRAA18D003H. State agencies, counties, cities and special districts can buy it through the Purchasing Solutions Alliance cooperative with no competitive solicitation required. FedRAMP authorization is listed as in process. An IRS contract and an Authority to Operate brought ArcSuite AI into live federal production.

paragraphs: Corveris builds OneReport, which the company calls the AI intake and workflow agent for public safety. It gives a police department a way to take in what residents report, routing submissions from crime reports to intelligence tips.

A resident starts in their own words and the software asks follow-up questions, capturing people, places, property, evidence, legal elements and agency-required facts. The company states that it automatically detects and translates more than 100 languages in real time, so a resident can report in their native language. Report types cover theft, vehicle burglary, shoplifting, vandalism, fraud, forgery, harassment, threats and hit and run, and each department configures which ones to turn on. Anything describing an emergency or a crime in progress is pointed to 911 instead.

Finished records land in a review queue where department personnel correct and approve them before they move into the agency records system. The company lists Versaterm, Axon Records, Tyler Technologies, CentralSquare and Mark43 among the records platforms it pushes reports into. It says the product runs on CJIS-compliant infrastructure hosted on AWS GovCloud, with data encrypted at rest and in transit. Published department stories describe Laredo Police opening a smartphone-friendly reporting path for eligible incidents.

before.name: Elenium Automation
before.description: Touchless self-service check-in and bag drop technology for airports

after.name: Elenium Automation
after.description: Touchless self-service check-in and bag drop technology for airports

paragraphs: Elenium Automation makes self-service check-in kiosks and bag drops for airports and airlines. The company describes bag drops that cut queues and keep passengers moving through the terminal. It pitches the same equipment to airlines as a way of activating their services instantly at any airport.

The product suite is called VYGR, short for Voyager, and covers self-service steps of the passenger journey. Elenium says it is built on computer vision, AI, modern UX, and a cloud backbone. The company reports achieving over 97% first-time read rates and sub-15 second processing speeds on its bag drop. In 2020 it launched HealthGate, described as an automated, touchless fever detection device approved by both the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration and the European Medicines Agency. The company also says it achieved ISO 13485 certification.

Elenium was founded in 2015 by Aaron Hornlimann, Fred Melki, and Heinz Corona. It says it now operates in over 35 airports, serving more than 45 airlines and 250 million passengers annually across Australasia, Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and the UK. For service, the company describes partnering with Unisys to provide global 24 by 7, remote and onsite support coverage.

quote.text: Building a frictionless future

before.location: Paris, France (offices in San Francisco and Singapore)
before.description: LiDAR-based spatial intelligence software turning 3D sensor data into anonymous passenger flow, queue wait time and occupancy analytics for terminals and curbside.

after.name: Outsight SA
after.location: Paris, France (offices in San Francisco and Singapore)
after.description: LiDAR-based spatial intelligence software turning 3D sensor data into anonymous passenger flow, queue wait time and occupancy analytics for terminals and curbside.

paragraphs: Outsight sells software that turns 3D sensor feeds into a running account of how people, vehicles, and robots move through a site. The buyers are operators of large shared spaces such as airports, hospitals, and factories.

Anything entering the scene is given an anonymous identifier and held to centimeter precision until it leaves. No faces or plates are captured, only the geometry of motion. Operators define zones and the measures they care about, such as counting, density, queue length, wait time and throughput, and the analytics engine computes them continuously. Results come back as live 3D playback, custom indicators, alerts, dashboards, and APIs. Before any of that, a multi-vendor simulator tests layouts and sensor mixes and proposes the hardware configuration.

The company says the platform is deployed at scale across five continents. It calls the result a Motional Digital Twin and says these are running in production. Its newsroom announces a strategic partnership with AWS around spatial AI in aviation. The pitch behind all of it is that movement is the next layer of business to be digitized.

quote.text: The bottleneck of Physical AI is not models, it is real-world data

paragraphs: Copenhagen Optimization sells planning software and consulting to airports that are running into capacity limits in their terminals. Its platform, Better Airport, is a cloud-based system for running core operations such as check-in, baggage, security, stand and gate, and immigration.

The company says the platform ties together operations that were once run separately, so data can move between them. Consulting sits alongside the software and draws on operational strategy, analytics, planning and optimization. Individual modules cover forecasting, security and shift planning.

Case studies describe Sydney Airport adopting the suite with two modules and later extending one of them across all terminals. At Manchester Airport, a rostering project cut the security roster count from more than 60 to 10. Heathrow Airport Limited commissioned an assessment of planning maturity across 15 operational areas. The company dates its airport work to 2014.

after.description: Mobile augmented-reality game platform licensed to airports, parks and public agencies to engage visitors with location-triggered educational missions and wayfinding-style content.

paragraphs: Agents of Discovery turns physical spaces such as museums, airports, campuses, libraries, stadiums and entire cities into interactive learning environments by blending AI-driven content generation with place-based augmented reality gameplay. Customers become what the company calls Mission Makers, turning their own stories, spaces and content into augmented reality experiences.

Location-based challenges are placed on site and tied to the customer's own content, or played from anywhere. A site can also deploy a fully customized AI avatar as its on-site guide. Self-guided tours are offered around the clock. Exhibits can be built for aquariums, zoos and museums. Text-to-speech and multiple language options are meant to keep the platform reachable for players with diverse abilities and backgrounds.

Airports are one named setting, where the pitch is turning downtime into interactive adventures built for travelers. Junior Ranger Missions on the platform cover subjects from palaeontology and fossils to International Migratory Bird Day. The chief academic officer works with public and private organizations across the United States, Australia and Canada on visitor experience. The company describes itself as a Harvard-incubated AI and augmented reality company.

paragraphs: Pointr sells indoor mapping and wayfinding software that turns a venue, office or campus into interactive digital maps. Customers put those maps into their own apps, on the web, or on kiosks, using dedicated mobile and web SDKs. One stated use is guiding travelers to their gate with turn-by-turn updates and estimated arrival times.

Maps are generated from CAD files by an AI tool called MapScale. Blue dot positioning indoors runs on Bluetooth Low Energy rather than a satellite signal. The site says accuracy holds without fingerprinting or geomagnetism, so the system needs less ongoing maintenance. Geofences drawn on the map trigger actions when visitors enter or leave a zone.

The company describes itself as the top choice for Fortune 100 companies. Its homepage names product wayfinding work at The Home Depot. It states that its positioning technology is patented, with more than ten years of testing and development behind it. On privacy, the geofencing page says visitor location data is collected anonymously and aligned with GDPR.

paragraphs: Durham School Services runs contracted student transportation for school districts across the country. The company describes itself as part of a network that carries more than a million students every day.

A district that contracts with Durham hands over routing, fleet, staffing and maintenance. Beyond daily routes, the company offers specialized service designed around student-specific needs and IEP requirements. It also covers field trips, athletics and special events. Support can extend to driver recruiting, screening and training. Fleet procurement, maintenance and lifecycle planning can sit with the company as well.

Durham has worked with school districts since 1917. It began as a three-bus operation in California's San Gabriel Valley, with early expertise in transporting students with specialized needs. Local operating teams are backed by the broader Summit School Services network for safety, recruiting, maintenance and technology.

paragraphs: Bytecurve sells operations software for school bus fleets, tying routing and GPS data into driver management, dispatching and payroll. Private student transportation contractors are one audience for it, and school districts are the other.

Real-time integration with routing systems and GPS lets dispatchers reassign drivers on the fly and break routes apart. Time and attendance removes manual calculation of employee guarantees, contracts and overtime, and runs through a mobile app or a garage-based tablet. Drivers check in and out remotely, view schedules and receive messages on their phones. The company says dozens of districts use the system across more than 40,000 buses and 50,000 drivers. Its founders claim over 30 years of combined transportation experience, with a focus on student transportation. One case study states that Rome Public Schools reduced payroll by $30,000 per month.

paragraphs: GreenPower Motor Company builds battery-electric buses and trucks for schools, public transit, delivery work, vanpools, micro-transit and shuttles. It began in 2010 with the goal of making battery-electric buses and trucks affordable, durable and easy to deploy.

Vehicles are built from the ground up to be electric rather than converted from existing diesel platforms. The BEAST school bus comes with air ride suspension, pass-through storage and seating for up to 90 students. The EV Star line is offered in configurations holding up to 19 passengers, with ADA wheelchair provisions or cargo delivery setups.

paragraphs: CP Group designs, manufactures, installs, and services sorting machinery for the waste and recycling industry. It sells turnkey systems for both new material recovery facilities and retrofits of existing ones. A project management team handles third parties, scheduling, shipping, and installation.

Designing a facility begins with collaborative design meetings, cost reviews, and civil and electrical considerations. The equipment itself is engineered and manufactured in the United States. The shop has 115,000 sq. ft. of manufacturing space and 435,600 sq. ft. of storage on 9 acres. At startup and commissioning, the team goes over compliance, operations, and safety with the customer. Support afterward covers spare parts, process upgrades, and troubleshooting.

The company dates its machinery to the invention of the first commercial aluminum can flattener in 1977, and its name to Can Pac. It later acquired Krause Manufacturing, which makes construction and demolition separation equipment, and Advanced MRF, a specialist in intelligent motor controls and data acquisition. It says it owned and operated a material recovery facility for over 25 years, processing half of the city of San Diego's curbside recycling. That adds up to nearly 50 years of hands-on experience by its own account.

paragraphs: Routeware sells digital technology for waste, recycling and heavy-duty fleet operations. The buyers are private haulers and municipal fleets. The software pulls collection, customer and business operations into one place.

Its routing product lets staff densify and edit routes and optimize entire fleets. Routes can be updated and stops reassigned in real time, with automatic sequencing. Dispatch gives a single view of orders, resources, status and inventory. Helper routes are built by drag and drop and resequenced on the spot. The back-office dispatch system is tied to the on-board computers in the truck.

Some customers run several heavy-duty fleets, including snowplows and sweeper trucks. A separate product handles medical waste from end to end. Another is recycling software built around California mandates. The company says it has worked on digital transformation in waste and recycling for over twenty years.

paragraphs: Greyparrot turns the waste passing through materials recovery facilities into data, serving both the teams that sort materials and the brands that design them. Its main product, Analyzer, is a process optimisation tool giving recyclers and waste sorting facilities continuous AI waste analytics across every sorting line.

Camera units above conveyor belts identify materials continuously, generating a real-time stream of composition, throughput and purity data across every monitored line. That data feeds a portal that organises it into four interlinked dashboards. Staff can review composition down to the minute and replay actual line images to identify where and when issues happened. A second product, Sync, connects Analyzer data into operational control systems and business reporting environments.

The practice this displaces, manual sampling, ties up operator hours and covers less than 0.1% of throughput. The company lists 250+ Analyzer units active. The same page states ISO 27001 and Cyber Essentials. One named user is KSI Recycling, described as one of the largest recyclers in the Netherlands, which did not deploy the portal all at once. A press item listed on the homepage reports a $27M Series B raise.

after.name: 3rd Eye
after.description: Camera and telematics systems for refuse fleets used by municipal sanitation departments

paragraphs: 3rd Eye sells modular, subscription-based software that runs on top of its own heavy-duty truck camera systems. Its buyers are waste hauling companies that have to manage collection fleets safely and stay connected to their customers. A truck can carry up to eight cameras for a full view around the vehicle.

Video and telematics data upload to the cloud, where they become safety events that a review team turns into driver coaching material. A maintenance module watches the chassis, body and equipment continuously. It hands mechanics a list of repairs ranked by severity or by how long remains before failure. Other modules take on tax paperwork, recording the data behind IFTA reporting and excise fuel tax recovery.

Contamination detection spots recycling contamination and other non-conforming refuse at the point of collection. Adding the route review module helps haulers plan and report the annual reviews that California State Bill 1383 requires. The company dates itself to 1901 and says it has built its reputation in the solid waste industry since then. It began as the Heil Railjoint Welding Company, founded by Julius P. Heil. before.description: Stormwater program and MS4 compliance software for municipalities

after.name: 2NDNATURE
after.description: Stormwater program and MS4 compliance software for municipalities

paragraphs: 2NDNATURE sells stormwater software built on GIS, aimed at streamlining compliance, asset tracking and reporting. Buyers fall into two camps, those tackling MS4 permit requirements and those advancing corporate water stewardship. Two products carry that work, 2NFORM and Rainsteward, both pitched at streamlining compliance and showing measurable results.

2NFORM is organized around municipal permit programs, covering post-construction, industrial and commercial, and illicit discharge detection and elimination. In Oceanside it was connected to the city's existing Esri-based GIS and met local security and IT standards. For longer-range planning the company built a Stormwater Asset Management Model that serves as a decision-making tool. Fed with the storm sewer system and local costs, it lets a city explore how twenty years of asset management would affect the health of that system. Rainsteward points the other way, at owners trying to cut costs and get more value out of stormwater investments.

The customers shown are city stormwater programs; Oceanside had nine separate systems tracking inspections and compliance tasks before it changed course. Salinas is described as a Phase I MS4 with a population exceeding 150,000. That city worked with 2NDNATURE to develop a comprehensive Asset Improvement Plan. Private owners appear too: a real estate company called Reveler implemented Rainsteward in a series of six steps.

quote.text: Mapping your storm sewer system can feel overwhelming, but strategic approaches can make the effort manageable.

before.name: VODA.ai
before.description: AI pipe-failure prediction for main replacement planning - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

after.name: VODA.ai
after.description: AI pipe-failure prediction for main replacement planning - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: VODA.ai sells decision support software to water utilities. The point is helping engineers decide which pipes to replace, assess, monitor or investigate next.

Projects start from data a utility already keeps, such as GIS records, pipe attributes, historical break records, work orders and service line information. Machine learning then flags pipes with an elevated likelihood of failure, including ones that have never broken. Utilities do not need clean records to begin. Initial model outputs, risk scores and prioritized watch lists are often available within three to six months. The same approach supports lead service line programs, sorting likely galvanized lines and prioritizing field verification before replacement work.

The company is Boston-based and was founded in 2017. It says it has worked in 31 states and eight countries and analyzed more than a million miles of pipe. Executives from 78 water utilities at the Smart Water Summit picked it as best smart water solution. Published case studies include lead compliance work in Rock Hill, South Carolina.

paragraphs: Aquasight sells analytics software for the people who run water and wastewater utilities. The company says the software runs in the cloud and calls for no new hardware.

One product is a digital twin for sewer mains, lift stations and combined sewer overflow facilities. It forecasts flows, compares them with expected patterns, picks out unexplained anomalies and estimates inflow, infiltration and capacity limits. A second product joins mapping and maintenance management data so that asset risk keeps updating. From that it recommends whether to inspect, repair or replace, and supports capital planning and financial forecasting.

The company states that it has partnered with over 120 utilities. It says the tools are shaped for operators, engineers, directors and compliance officers alike. A news item announces the company exhibiting and speaking at Weftec in New Orleans in September 2026.

paragraphs: Aquarius Spectrum sells acoustic leak detection systems that let water utilities find and prevent leaks. The stated aim is cutting non-revenue water and putting resources where they matter. The products are meant to suit water networks of any pipe material and size.

Sensors take a daily audio sample and send it to a cloud server for analysis. Every two coupled sensors are then correlated, and when the same noise turns up in the same location an alert gives the exact position of the leak. The AQS-SYS platform pairs those sensors with algorithms, big data analytics and CAT-M or NB-IoT connectivity. Accelerometers fit externally on hydrants above ground and on pressure and air valves below. A hydrophone covers large transmission lines of 24 inches and above, plus plastic and PVC pipe. Where continuous monitoring is not wanted, mobile products let a utility survey large areas instead.

Alongside the hardware the company sells what it calls Human-as-a-Service, described as ongoing human support, expertise and system updates. AQS states that it is a company of the Aliaxis Group. It reports receiving ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification. Published case studies include the national agency that manages Singapore's water loop.

paragraphs: ASTERRA sells insight into what lies beneath the ground, produced without breaking ground using patented algorithms and artificial intelligence to detect leaks. Water and wastewater utilities use it for leak detection to reduce non-revenue water and for analysis of potable and wastewater systems. The same approach maps excess soil moisture near or under dams, levees, roads, railways and mining operations.

The company images a customer's system with polarimetric synthetic aperture radar to sense and evaluate soil moisture. The same regions are revisited every few days or weeks as needed to monitor vast expanses. Results land in EO Discover, described as the repository for all insights from a customer's ASTERRA projects. There, detections, hotspots and network risk appear in a single view. MasterPlan scores pipe segments that show non-surfacing leaks and analyzes leak clusters over time. EarthWorks uses synthetic aperture radar to detect soil moisture up to 10 feet below the surface.

Field crews log investigation results, leak location and other data using U-Collect or the Esri ArcGIS Field Maps app. Within five minutes that reporting is available in EO Discover. The company ties EarthWorks, MasterPlan and Recover to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. MasterPlan is available in the Advise level of an ASTERRA Recover subscription.

paragraphs: InfoSense sells the equipment, software and services that let a city work out which sewer pipes actually need cleaning before crews are sent out. The centrepiece is a handheld acoustic device that scores blockage conditions in small diameter gravity sewer lines.

A transmitter goes on one open manhole and a receiver on the next. Within a few minutes the display returns a rating from zero to ten showing whether the pipe is clear or obstructed. Nothing touches the flow and nobody has to enter a confined space. The company reports that two people can cover fifty to sixty segments in a day. Readings feed a companion platform that records, organises and maps the results. Data can be pushed out to mapping and spreadsheet tools already in use.

Buyers are public works departments and utilities moving away from cleaning on a fixed calendar toward cleaning based on measured condition. The company states that more than 1,350 utilities have used the tool. One published case study covers a small town serving just under ten thousand people. That town is reported to have cut its cleaning workload by more than half.

paragraphs: Electro Scan sells leak detection and lead pipe location work for water and sewer systems. The company says municipal sewer utilities and sewer contractors use it to pin down the location, measurement and flow of defects inside a pipe before a repair or replacement job.

The method rests on a simple claim: pipe defects that leak water also leak electricity, so a defect shows up whether or not it happens to be leaking during the inspection. A low voltage conductivity probe travels through the pipe at 45 to 60 feet per minute, locating and measuring defects as it goes. Crews can then create summary and detail level reports for a team to review. The flagship probe is built for gravity mains between 6 and 30 inches in diameter, and the company says agencies and contractors use it worldwide.

Electro Scan lists ISO 9001:2015 certification for quality management systems. Its case studies page includes a North American benchmark study comparing closed-circuit television inspection with focused electrode leak location on gravity sewer mains. Other write-ups describe a Florida utility dealing with excessive inflow and infiltration in its gravity collection system.

after.description: Machine learning lead service line inventory and prediction for water utilities - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: BlueConduit sells predictive modeling tools to water systems that need to manage risk and make data-driven decisions about their distribution assets. The customers are municipalities and water utilities.

One product builds community-specific models that pinpoint high-risk lead and galvanized service lines, which lets a utility classify its inventory and prioritize replacements. Another scores every main segment in a network for likelihood and consequence of failure. A third uses statistical models to confirm the absence of lead in a water system. The company says model processes, important features, and performance metrics are always shared with customers. Output is integrated with Esri ArcGIS.

The work started at the University of Michigan, where faculty and student researchers saw a use for data science in removing toxic lead from the water supply. In Flint the company used predictive analytics to identify where to dig for lead service lines. A published case study describes Des Moines Water Works classifying unknown service lines and reducing uncertainty by 75% in six months. BlueConduit cites ongoing relationships with EPA and state regulators. Its stated mission is to empower communities to prioritize health and sustainability through data science.

before.why: The homepage explains the device, the procedure and the software in operational detail, and the case study pages give a customer count and specific reported outcomes.

paragraphs.text: InfoSense sells the equipment, software and services that let a city work out which sewer pipes actually need cleaning before crews are sent out.
paragraphs.quote: We help municipalities take control of their sewer maintenance with equipment, software, and services that turn invisible conditions into actionable assessments.

paragraphs.text: The centrepiece is a handheld acoustic device that scores blockage conditions in small diameter gravity sewer lines.
paragraphs.quote: The SL-RAT is a portable acoustic device engineered to assess blockage conditions in small-diameter gravity sewer lines.

paragraphs.text: A transmitter goes on one open manhole and a receiver on the next.
paragraphs.quote: First, set the SL-RAT transmitter device on the open manhole lid. Place the receiver on the other manhole.

paragraphs.text: Within a few minutes the display returns a rating from zero to ten showing whether the pipe is clear or obstructed.
paragraphs.quote: The display shows whether the sewer pipes are good or blocked, with a score ranging from 0 to 10.

paragraphs.text: Nothing touches the flow and nobody has to enter a confined space.
paragraphs.quote: no flow contact, no confined space entry

paragraphs.text: The company reports that two people can cover fifty to sixty segments in a day.
paragraphs.quote: A two-person team on average can inspect 50-60 segments

paragraphs.text: Readings feed a companion platform that records, organises and maps the results.
paragraphs.quote: SL-DOG is the digital platform that captures, organizes, and visualizes SL-RAT inspection data

paragraphs.text: Data can be pushed out to mapping and spreadsheet tools already in use.
paragraphs.quote: Export data to ArcGIS, Google Earth, or Excel to work in existing systems.

paragraphs.text: Buyers are public works departments and utilities moving away from cleaning on a fixed calendar toward cleaning based on measured condition.
paragraphs.quote: It supports a shift to condition-based maintenance, where cleaning decisions are based on actual system conditions

paragraphs.text: The company states that more than 1,350 utilities have used the tool.
paragraphs.quote: More than 1,350 utilities have used the SL-RAT® to shift from fixed-schedule cleaning to data-driven maintenance.

paragraphs.text: One published case study covers a small town serving just under ten thousand people.
paragraphs.quote: Serves a population of just under 10,000

paragraphs.text: That town is reported to have cut its cleaning workload by more than half.
paragraphs.quote: has reduced cleaning by over 50% and has saved over $180k

quote.text: Turn Hours into Minutes and Dollars into Sense

before.name: Craft Education
before.description: Registered apprenticeship and work-based learning management software for state workforce agencies, community colleges, school districts and employer sponsors - exhibited at NASWA 2025

after.name: Craft Education
after.description: Registered apprenticeship and work-based learning management software for state workforce agencies, community colleges, school districts and employer sponsors - exhibited at NASWA 2025

paragraphs: Craft Education sells software for running registered apprenticeships and work-based learning programs. The platform, called Craft Connect, is built for employers, education partners, and intermediaries. Healthcare and education are the fields it is designed around first, though the company says the platform itself is field-agnostic.

A program administrator configures the program to registered-apprenticeship standards and invites learners, employers, and evaluators. Learners then log on-the-job hours against the work-process schedule from any browser. Mentors and reviewers work a queue rather than an inbox, approving hours, submissions, and competencies or sending them back, with every action time-stamped. Sign-offs roll into competency records, and one data model produces the WIOA, Perkins, RAPIDS, and Workforce Pell exports funders and accreditors accept.

The company describes itself as an essential part of WGU and puts mission before margin. Its stated purpose is to change lives for the better by creating pathways to opportunity. For buyers in IT, security, and procurement, the company states SOC2 compliance, invitation-gated access, and audit-ready records by default. It also cites WCAG 2.2 accessibility with a VPAT available and reporting to USDOL and RAPIDS.

quote.text: Craft Connect is not trying to replace the systems you already run.

paragraphs: Career TEAM works on unemployment and poverty for government agencies, pairing staffed services with software. The software is Career EDGE, and the company says every one of its projects runs on it.

The programs covered include WIOA adult, dislocated worker and youth services. On the software side the listed pieces are case management, business services and training. Work also reaches justice involved people: in 2023 the company was selected for a Missouri pilot serving 19,000 returning citizens from thirteen detention centers.

Career TEAM has been serving job seekers and government organizations since 1996. Chris and Sue Kuselias launched the company that year. By 2022 staff had grown past 300 employees with offices in 15 states. Aaron Kelley became chief executive in 2024. In October 2025 it took over management and operations of the workforce development system in North Central Texas.

after.name: Player's Health
after.description: Risk management, insurance and safety compliance for youth sports

paragraphs: Players Health sells insurance together with the staff and software a sports program needs to keep participants protected. The company dates the work to 2016 and has widened the roster since then to insurance, athlete safety, and employee benefits products and services. On the insurance side it describes athlete-first protection sold to youth sports nationwide.

Policies cover a league or program against unexpected accidents, injuries, or property damage. A separate directors and officers line is offered as legal protection for a board. Alongside the policies sits a suite of athlete safety products meant to protect youth and amateur athletes, fitness club members, and student athletes. Programs that do not know where to begin can ask for a Players Health Safety Score to work out what steps they need. Training is pitched at coaches and organizations building team cultures and keeping their programs positive and safe. A reporting platform carries incidents from the first report through to resolution.

The founder, Tyrre, started the company after a playing career at Winona State and in the Canadian Football League was plagued with injuries. By its own account the company now supports over 40,000 sports organizations, impacting more than 5 million athletes. It states its mission as creating the safest and most accessible environments for athletes to play the sports they love.

before.name: Bchex

after.name: Bchex
after.description: Background screening and volunteer management for schools and youth-serving organizations

paragraphs: Bchex runs background screening for organizations that have to vet the people they hire, and it also sells continuous monitoring along with visitor and volunteer management. The company advertises that 92% of background checks are delivered in under 24 hours.

A customer requests checks in seconds, tracks progress in real time from a single dashboard, and gets a report at the end. Candidates can scan a driver's license so their information populates automatically instead of being typed in. The platform connects to an applicant tracking system to sync and automate the screening process. Bchex puts terms behind the service: no payment if it misses its turnaround time or if the customer is unsatisfied, and a price match against a cheaper quote.

The company counts more than 2,000 school districts, non-profits, and US businesses among its customers. It states that it processes over 500,000 background checks per year. It describes nearly 30 years spent on this one line of work. The site states that Bchex is SOC 2 Type 2 certified for security, confidentiality, and availability. Buyers pay per order, with no long-term contracts or subscription fees.

paragraphs: Athletify makes staff scheduling software for parks and recreation departments, pulling every program and every worker into one schedule that a manager can filter as needed. Staff need only one login even when they hold several positions.

Shifts can be filtered and grouped by program, location, position, or staff member, and the views a department reaches for most often can be saved. Requests to drop a shift, claim a shift, or take time off arrive in a centralized inbox that all admins share. Age limitation tools let a department create and enforce scheduling rules for younger workers, including restrictions that keep them off early morning or late evening shifts. Messaging is built in, with channels for different staff groups such as lifeguards or referees.

The company says it has heard from hundreds of cities about the struggle of managing staff, and it is looking for beta partners to help shape the tool. Pricing is advertised without tiers or per-user fees. The site dates the beta program as running until July 1, 2025.

before.description: Sports facility and program management for municipal and community facilities

after.name: Bond Sports
after.description: Sports facility and program management for municipal and community facilities

paragraphs: Bond Sports sells the software that a sports facility runs its business on. It aims at operators of complex multi-sport venues and ice rinks rather than youth clubs alone.

Scheduling, registration, memberships and payments sit on one data model, so availability, billing and reporting stay in sync when something moves. paragraphs: Cuseum sells an engagement platform built for museums, cultural attractions, nonprofits and membership organizations. Its digital tools are aimed at the visitors, members and donors those organizations already deal with.

The anchor product is a digital membership card that gives members wallet passes, benefits, renewals and updates through Apple Wallet and Google Wallet. Around it sit mobile engagement, audio guides, ticketing, loyalty tools, donor engagement and lifecycle communication. On site, the platform covers digital tickets, guest registration and barcode scanning at the door. For staff, Cuseum lists native CRM connectors along with 700 or more apps reachable through Zapier.

Cuseum says hundreds of institutions worldwide rely on it for membership cards, mobile guides, guest passes, loyalty programs and lifecycle communications. The customers it describes are kinds of organizations rather than named ones: art museums, science centers, aquariums and zoos, botanical gardens, libraries, alumni associations and nonprofit foundations. The footer identifies the company as Cuseum, Inc., in Boston.

quote.text: Cuseum gives organizations the tools to connect with people before, during, and after each visit.

paragraphs: DTN sells forecasting and risk planning for organizations whose operations turn on weather. Refined fuel markets are another line of business, with real-time visibility, pricing and supply chain intelligence.

The products are packaged as vertical hubs tailored to the workflows of a given sector. One is aimed at utilities, where the pitch is outage response and grid reliability. A newer platform turns weather intelligence into safety decisions for live events and sports, universities and schools, public safety and construction teams.

The company states that it is certified for data security and quality. Manuel Zepeda was named chief executive officer. He arrived most recently from Spirent Communications, where he led global sales and services. DTN has also announced work on real-time weather intelligence using NVIDIA Earth-2 on AWS.

after.name: Harmari (LTAS Technologies)

paragraphs: Harmari sells tools that identify and monitor short term rentals so a municipality can collect lodging tax and enforce local rules. A companion product covers long term rentals through website monitoring, rental identification and a rental registry. Another line addresses municipal business licensing and revenue enhancement.

The tools analyze many classifieds at once, which the company presents as faster and more complete than working through them by hand. The short term rental product works with Taxcrawler to find and watch properties for lodging tax collection, licensing and code compliance. Evidence collection standards call for at least two screenshots. The company states a 95% accuracy guarantee for houses and 75% for condos. There is a tax reporting module with under-reporting detection. A registration portal is customized to local laws. Enforcement outreach runs by phone and direct mail.

Buyers include state and municipal revenue agencies with units that look for taxpayers who are not compliant. The company says Taxcrawler has helped revenue departments find and recoup tax revenue. Condominium and homeowner associations are addressed by a separate short term rental finder. Work outside those products can be taken on as custom data collection or web scraping.

paragraphs: IDSS sells a cloud-based CRM for the travel and tourism industry. The company says more than 170 destinations around the world run their organizations on the product, called iDSS Cyclone.

before.name: Xplor Recreation
before.description: Parks and recreation management software; brands NextRec (formerly PerfectMind), Vermont Systems, RecDesk and ePACT - exhibited at AB Show 2026, NRPA 2026

notes.text: Merged brand family. The NRPA 2026 exhibitor row named Xplor Recreation, Vermont Systems, RecDesk, NextRec and ePACT in one booth; its attribution is folded here and the row is dropped. The two rosters disagree and both are the family's own material: xplor.com/industries/xplor-recreation/ lists Vermont Systems, RecDesk, NextRec and CampBrain and omits ePACT, while the NRPA booth lists ePACT and omits CampBrain. CampBrain is not in this dataset and no record was invented for it.

Part of Xplor Recreation. Evidenced, not inferred: the rippling board they share, clubessential-holdings-cjb, carries a posting titled Xplor_Logo_withTag_Color.png, and nextrec.com closes with '(c) Copyright 2026 Xplor Technologies' and links to linkedin.com/company/xplor-technologies.

also_known_as: Xplor Recreation I Vermont Systems - RecDesk - NextRec – ePACT

brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

brands.name: RecDesk
brands.description:
recdesk.com could not be read. Both the apex and www forms answer a plain fetch with an HTTP 202 and a Sucuri interstitial, and a real browser is served a "Robot Challenge Screen" that did not clear on repeated attempts. No attempt was made to defeat it, so nothing below comes from RecDesk's own site. What follows is from Xplor's corporate site, which is the family's own material. Xplor writes: "Founded in 2005, RecDesk provides scalable, easy-to-use software for parks and recreation departments, aquatic centers, schools, community centers, HOAs, and small municipalities. Its integrations with access control, GIS/address databases, and financial systems help teams streamline facility scheduling, program management, and operational workflows - reducing manual effort and system fragmentation." Xplor adds that "Business and community leaders can run more efficient programs, offer better resident experiences, and make data-driven decisions that strengthen their community services."

RecDesk is one of the four brands Xplor lists on its Xplor Recreation page, alongside Vermont Systems, NextRec and CampBrain, and Xplor's "Visit RecDesk" link points to recdesk.com. The distinction Xplor's own wording draws between the siblings is the size and type of buyer: RecDesk is described for "small municipalities", aquatic centers and HOAs, where Vermont Systems is described for "municipal, county, state, and federal military recreation organizations". RecDesk's postings run through the Rippling board shared across this family, clubessential-holdings-cjb, which also carries an asset named Xplor_Logo_withTag_Color.png. Beyond that, this record is deliberately short. Anything further about RecDesk's product, customers or scale would have to be invented, because its site refused to be read.

paragraphs: Bloomerang Volunteer is volunteer management software for nonprofits, covering recruiting, scheduling, engagement, tracking and reporting. It is aimed at organizations of any size, including those with large volunteer bases, recurring shifts and multiple sites or programs.

Scheduling filters volunteers by skills, roles, availability and interests to match them to open shifts. Volunteers use a mobile app to manage schedules, stay informed and check in on site. Background checks run inside the platform against an organization's own safety and compliance standards. Reporting turns volunteer hours into custom reports showing dollars saved through volunteer work. Because donors, volunteers and fundraising sit on one platform, volunteer data can be used to identify donor prospects.

The volunteer product arrived by acquisition, and the company milestone list records that Bloomerang acquired InitLive and launched Bloomerang Volunteer Management. Bloomerang presents itself as a unified giving platform built for purpose. The same page claims over ten years of purpose-built software. Other milestones include acquiring Qgiv to expand the giving platform.

brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

brands.name: RecDesk

recdesk.com could not be read. Both the apex and www forms answer a plain fetch with an HTTP 202 and a Sucuri interstitial, and a real browser is served a "Robot Challenge Screen" that did not clear on repeated attempts. No attempt was made to defeat it, so nothing below comes from RecDesk's own site. What follows is from Xplor's corporate site, which is the family's own material. Xplor writes: "Founded in 2005, RecDesk provides scalable, easy-to-use software for parks and recreation departments, aquatic centers, schools, community centers, HOAs, and small municipalities. Its integrations with access control, GIS/address databases, and financial systems help teams streamline facility scheduling, program management, and operational workflows - reducing manual effort and system fragmentation." Xplor adds that "Business and community leaders can run more efficient programs, offer better resident experiences, and make data-driven decisions that strengthen their community services."

RecDesk is one of the four brands Xplor lists on its Xplor Recreation page, alongside Vermont Systems, NextRec and CampBrain, and Xplor's "Visit RecDesk" link points to recdesk.com. The distinction Xplor's own wording draws between the siblings is the size and type of buyer: RecDesk is described for "small municipalities", aquatic centers and HOAs, where Vermont Systems is described for "municipal, county, state, and federal military recreation organizations". RecDesk's postings run through the Rippling board shared across this family, clubessential-holdings-cjb, which also carries an asset named Xplor_Logo_withTag_Color.png. brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

paragraphs: Tranquility AI makes AI-powered evidence analysis software for criminal investigations. Its flagship product, TimePilot, unifies all data sources into a single interface so investigators can surface details quickly. The company describes its technology as serving the entire justice system, from law enforcement to prosecuting attorneys.

For law enforcement, the company pitches TimePilot to agencies of all sizes as a way to streamline investigation workflows and accelerate case clearance. The company says the software can process months of data in minutes, automate manual evidence review, and build case timelines and summaries. For prosecutors, it says using TimePilot cuts the average time to negotiate a plea from 30 days to 3 days. A corrections version brings together jail calls, contraband phone extractions, drone data and incident reports to surface threats and networks inside and outside a facility.

Founder and CEO Jim Penrose spent 17 years at the NSA, where he became Technical Director for Counterterrorism, and later held executive roles at BlueVoyant and Darktrace. Testimonials on the site come from a District Attorney in Orleans Parish, Louisiana, Sheriff Max Dorsey of Chester County, South Carolina, and Sheriff Ryan Spurling of Mason County, Washington. A detective at the Adams County Sheriffs Office in Colorado says the tool helped lead to an arrest and additional charges in one of that detective's cases.
