paragraphs: Kaiden AI sells AI simulation training software to law enforcement agencies and academies. The product turns an agency's policies and training standards into AI simulations, guided coaching, and evaluations that officers can complete anywhere. Agencies build scenarios, assign practice, and measure officer performance from one platform. The simulations use AI personas meant to cover the full range of people officers encounter in the field.

The company frames the product around the law enforcement training lifecycle. Recruits get more opportunities to practice communication, judgment, articulation, and policy application before the situations evaluated in the FTO program. For serving officers, scenarios cover policy changes, legal updates, emerging threats, and high-risk encounters, with a separate track for interviewing and investigative decision-making. Instructors can assign targeted practice based on documented performance gaps without adding role-player or instructor burden.

Testimonials on the site come from the Baltimore and Atlanta police departments; Lt. Jason Foore of Atlanta says recruits using Kaiden AI felt more confident during practical exercises. A blog post says the Baltimore Police Department has launched a pilot of Kaiden AI at the Baltimore Police Academy for academy and in-service programs. The company reports completing a SOC 2 Type 1 attestation to protect agency and trainee data. A January 2025 post announces a $1M pre-seed round.

before.name: City Detect
before.description: AI cameras on city fleet vehicles detect blight, graffiti, dumping for code enforcement - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: City Detect sells a camera and software service that helps municipalities and counties find and address urban blight before complaints pile up. Cameras ride on a city's existing fleet vehicles and collect images of properties as those vehicles drive their normal routes. The company's PASS AI then detects and maps signs of urban blight and decay from the public right of way.

Roof-mounted data collection units capture street-level imagery during routine city operations. Once the images are processed, each detection is assigned a severity score from 1 to 4 and placed on an interactive map. The conditions it picks up run to illegal dumping, tire accumulations, snipe signs, and graffiti. Staff can export timestamped, image-backed reports in a few clicks.

The company says it was founded in 2021. One published case study describes Cathedral City partnering with City Detect in June 2025. For each municipality the company performs local calibration meant to cut false-positive detections and match local rules.

paragraphs: Bloomerang Volunteer is volunteer management software for nonprofits, covering recruiting, scheduling, engagement, tracking and reporting. It is aimed at organizations of any size, including those with large volunteer bases, recurring shifts and multiple sites or programs.

Scheduling filters volunteers by skills, roles, availability and interests to match them to open shifts. Volunteers use a mobile app to manage schedules, stay informed and check in on site. Background checks run inside the platform against an organization's own safety and compliance standards. Reporting turns volunteer hours into custom reports showing dollars saved through volunteer work. Because donors, volunteers and fundraising sit on one platform, volunteer data can be used to identify donor prospects.

The volunteer product arrived by acquisition, and the company milestone list records that Bloomerang acquired InitLive and launched Bloomerang Volunteer Management. Bloomerang presents itself as a unified giving platform built for purpose. The same page claims over ten years of purpose-built software. Other milestones include acquiring Qgiv to expand the giving platform.

paragraphs: Key Data sells lodging market data and analytics used by vacation rental property managers, destination organizations, investors and enterprise analytics teams. The argument it makes is that its figures come from actual bookings rather than estimates read off public listing calendars.

The dataset joins direct-source short-term rental reservation data with Airbnb and Vrbo listing coverage and hotel performance benchmarks. The company states integrations with more than 80 property management systems and direct-source data from more than 17,000 property managers, covering over 1.15 million vacation rental properties. Reporting covers occupancy, ADR, RevPAR, guest nights, booking pace and length of stay.

Destination organizations use it to understand event performance, find high-value feeder markets, time campaigns and report results to boards, elected officials and stakeholders. The company says more than 300 destination organizations choose it. Enterprise teams can take the same data through APIs, flat files, S3 buckets, Snowflake delivery or custom feeds rather than through a dashboard.

paragraphs: This company sells AI-driven youth sports management software marketed as OTTO SPORT AI. It is shaped around feedback from club directors, coaches, families and athletes.

The platform covers club and league management, tournaments, ticketing and athlete recruitment. Tournament and ticketing tools handle registration, scheduling and communication for events. before.name: Skedda
before.description: Space and facility booking platform used by municipal and campus facilities

paragraphs: Skedda sells booking software for shared workplace space, giving staff self-serve booking of desks, rooms and other resources. The company frames it as one platform to book space and manage operations, backed by data about how the square footage is used.

People browse desks by neighborhood on an interactive floor plan and see where colleagues are sitting. A desk takes three clicks to reserve from a desktop, a phone or Microsoft Teams. Check-in by QR code or automatic Wi-Fi connection frees desks that nobody claims. Administrators set approvals, quotas, priority windows and check-in rules that govern when and where people book. Room bookings sync with Outlook or Google calendar events, and release automatically when the calendar event is declined. Reporting covers desk and room usage, peak hours and booking patterns over time.

The company says it has 8,000 global customers across 28 countries and 3m active users. For campuses it describes cleaning buffers between sessions and approval workflows for spaces in high demand. Customers named on the desk booking page include Toyota Connected EU, PVH Corp, Columbia University, Aon, and Pella Windows & Doors. The site states SOC 2 Type 2 certification with independently audited controls. It also states GDPR compliance, with data processing agreements available.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "© 2026 Pronesis. A MedVanta Company. All rights reserved." Fetched https://mypronesis.com. Live and matches the description 'AI-powered movement assessment platform': the site sells 'AI-driven 3D motion analysis to prevent injuries, optimize performance, and deliver personalized exercise programs for athletes, employers, military, and seniors.' Rule 3 checked carefully because Pronesis is a subsidiary brand ('Pronesis - A MedVanta Company'): mypronesis.com is Pronesis's OWN standalone site, not the parent MedVanta's corporate domain, so this is the correct record and does not risk importing MedVanta's postings. CAVEAT for board fit, flagging rather than rejecting since the description does match: I found NO evidence Pronesis sells to state or local government. Its four stated markets are athletes/trainers/gyms, employers, military, and aging adults/seniors - military is federal, and the rest are commercial or healthcare. No police, fire, public safety or municipal customers appear anywhere on the site. Also note the site has no careers/jobs link of its own, so hiring likely runs through MedVanta - worth checking before the board treats this as a scrapable source.

paragraphs: Players Health sells insurance together with the staff and software a sports program needs to keep participants protected. The company dates the work to 2016 and has widened the roster since then to insurance, athlete safety, and employee benefits products and services. On the insurance side it describes athlete-first protection sold to youth sports nationwide.

Policies cover a league or program against unexpected accidents, injuries, or property damage. A separate directors and officers line is offered as legal protection for a board. Alongside the policies sits a suite of athlete safety products meant to protect youth and amateur athletes, fitness club members, and student athletes. before.name: Baron Weather
before.description: Weather data, alerting and decision tools for government agencies

paragraphs: Baron Weather sells weather data, forecasting and alerting tools to businesses, government agencies and communities. Its catalog holds hundreds of datasets, with information down to the street level. The company argues that free or incomplete sources leave organizations either over-prepared and wasteful or under-prepared and at risk.

Baron blends data from many sources into insights using analytical processes, machine learning, and AI. Many of its products carry built-in alerting and recommended actions to guide a decision. The company also builds weather radar hardware it describes as engineered for durability and sustainability. Its forecast modeling covers atmospheric, hydrological, marine, air quality, and road surface coupled models. Content is prepackaged so it can be shared quickly and understood without expertise.

The company traces its mission to 1989, when an F4 tornado devastated parts of Huntsville, Alabama. Its customer base spans government agencies, emergency managers, small startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Baron lists ISO 9001 quality management among the credentials behind its processes. ISO 14001 environmental management is listed as well.

hiring.note: Account Executive - Mid-Market and (London, United Kin)

paragraphs: ROLLER sells venue management software to attractions businesses, pulling bookings, point of sale, memberships and reporting into a single platform. It is cloud-based and built for growing attractions businesses, meant to stand in for the several tools a venue would otherwise run. The company describes the platform as powering more than 3,000 attractions.

Ticketing is built around flexible bookings and add-on sales for both staff and guests. Operators running more than one site can hold branding consistent across locations and publish changes from a single headquarters account. Plans are tiered, with an entry level covering online and in-venue selling and day-to-day operations. Higher tiers are aimed at established venues wanting more customization and support.

One franchise operator, We Rock the Spectrum, put the platform into more than 120 locations over six months. Another customer, Area 51, is described on the site as an Australian family entertainment center operator running venues across multiple states. The company also publishes a guest survey it says covers 1,500 people.

before.name: EZFacility
before.description: Facility, league and program scheduling for rec centers and parks

paragraphs: EZFacility sells online scheduling, management and membership software for gyms, fitness centers, sports facilities and more. Among the business types it names are gyms and health and fitness centers.

Scheduling centralizes physical resources and consolidates classes, clinics and rentals into a color-coded schedule. League and tournament schedules can handle an even or odd number of teams, single byes, or back-to-back double headers. Referee assignments, printable scorecards and photo ID cards for player verification keep games running on time. Staff can be compensated for sessions, classes or clinics completed and for services sold. Payments run through an integrated PCI-compliant product at what the company calls a competitive rate. A branded mobile app gives clients facility information, schedules, trainer profiles and push notifications.

The company says it was created in 2003. It describes itself as one of the largest providers of management software for the sports and fitness industries. It claims thousands of businesses around the world as customers. The software is hosted on Amazon Web Services with a stated 99.99% uptime.

paragraphs: Brandkit gives an organization one searchable, shareable home for its logos, guidelines, images, video, presentations, stories and press releases. It bundles a brand portal, media center, brand guidelines, digital asset management, a CMS, a knowledge library and file transfer into one system. The buyers it names include national and local government agencies, tourism boards, place brands, economic development agencies, universities and franchises.

Uploaded assets are organized with automatic tagging and metadata generated by AI. Search combines multi-faceted keywords with AI-powered semantic search. Brand guidelines, rights management and licensing information surface alongside the assets themselves. The platform also generates llms.txt and llms.html plain text files so chatbots and language models can read the content. Pricing is based on usage rather than per seat, which the company ties to public sector bodies sharing resources with many end users.

The founder writes that Brandkit began in 1994 to fix the same problem it addresses now. The company says it is still privately held, has never taken outside money, and is profitable. One published case study covers how VisitScotland built a media library across several organisations.

before.name: CommunityPass
before.description: Online registration, membership, and payments for parks & rec departments and community schools

paragraphs: CommunityPass is cloud-based software that powers schools, recreation centers, community organizations, and sports leagues. It comes from Capturepoint, whose founder the company names as Joe Oriente.

The product began in 2002 with a town Sports Council overwhelmed by hundreds of paper registration forms as athletic sign-ups climbed. The answer was a single account on one website through which families reach registration for every participating organization in town. Departments can offer registration for classes, activities, programs, and trips, with options to buy merchandise and tickets. Payments accept multiple forms with recurring billing and plans while maintaining PCI compliance.

Check-in and check-out are contactless and digital, with pick-up timestamps and real-time emergency contact information for authorized parents. Staff can choose from 300+ pre-built reports covering attendance, financial, roster, and statistical data, or build their own. The company says CommunityPass has grown to serve parks and recreation organizations and schools all across the country.

paragraphs: CrowdRiff sells visual content software to travel brands, with the stated aim of giving them content and insights that inspire travelers. The pitch is to plan, produce and measure content in one place, replacing multiple tools with one connected solution.

The platform collects user-generated content from a destination, with curation and rights approval before anything is published. It also sources original short-form video to fuel Instagram Reels, TikToks and YouTube Shorts. Visuals are centralized so a team can search, organize and share content instead of digging through folders and drives.

The site states that more than 900 destinations use CrowdRiff for their visual content. Customer stories cover destination marketing organizations, including one on how Destination Madison plans and produces content. The founders describe starting the company with the vision of a local-first travel ecosystem. It also partners with agencies around the world to help their clients use user-generated content and owned visuals.

before.name: Player's Health
before.description: Risk management, insurance and safety compliance for youth sports

paragraphs: Players Health sells insurance together with the staff and software a sports program needs to keep participants protected. The company dates the work to 2016 and has widened the roster since then to insurance, athlete safety, and employee benefits products and services. On the insurance side it describes athlete-first protection sold to youth sports nationwide.

Policies cover a league or program against unexpected accidents, injuries, or property damage. A separate directors and officers line is offered as legal protection for a board. Alongside the policies sits a suite of athlete safety products meant to protect youth and amateur athletes, fitness club members, and student athletes. Programs that do not know where to begin can ask for a Players Health Safety Score to work out what steps they need. Training is pitched at coaches and organizations building team cultures and keeping their programs positive and safe. A reporting platform carries incidents from the first report through to resolution.

The founder, Tyrre, started the company after a playing career at Winona State and in the Canadian Football League was plagued with injuries. By its own account the company now supports over 40,000 sports organizations, impacting more than 5 million athletes. It states its mission as creating the safest and most accessible environments for athletes to play the sports they love.

paragraphs: Bandwango sells mobile passes that let a destination showcase its local restaurants, breweries and attractions while tracking visitor interactions. The pitch to tourism organizations is an easier way to measure economic impact.

Staff start from one of the pass templates and customize it to their needs and brand. They then add local places to go, discounts and admissions, with Bandwango helping onboard each business added. Passes work via any browser and save to a phone home screen, so passholders do not download extra apps. Arrival at a location is verified by GPS and merchant verified check-in. paragraphs: CampDoc sells camp and youth program software built for registration, health management, and day-to-day operations. The buyers are organizations that run programs for children and students, and the company says it powers more than 1,250 camps, youth programs and school programs. Signups, payments, rosters and family-facing workflows sit in one place.

On the health side, staff collect health forms, manage medications, document incidents, and keep records accessible when they need them. The health forms are digital and use conditional logic. Medication administration runs through an eMAR. Attendance, communication, reporting and daily program operations are kept together in one place. Rosters and health records stay aligned across the system.

For IT and compliance reviewers, the company points to SOC 2 Type II controls, role-based access to PHI, single sign-on for organizations that require it, and multi-factor authentication. It also states that the platform is HIPAA and FERPA compliant. Plans start at $355 per month. Onboarding, training, support and compliance are included in every plan, according to the pricing section. Published customer stories include a municipal parks and recreation department that replaced paper forms and manual tracking.

before.name: Skedda
before.description: Space and facility booking platform used by municipal and campus facilities

paragraphs: Skedda sells booking software for shared workplace space, giving staff self-serve booking of desks, rooms and other resources. The company frames it as one platform to book space and manage operations, backed by data about how the square footage is used.

People browse desks by neighborhood on an interactive floor plan and see where colleagues are sitting. A desk takes three clicks to reserve from a desktop, a phone or Microsoft Teams. Check-in by QR code or automatic Wi-Fi connection frees desks that nobody claims. Administrators set approvals, quotas, priority windows and check-in rules that govern when and where people book. Room bookings sync with Outlook or Google calendar events, and release automatically when the calendar event is declined. Reporting covers desk and room usage, peak hours and booking patterns over time.

The company says it has 8,000 global customers across 28 countries and 3m active users. For campuses it describes cleaning buffers between sessions and approval workflows for spaces in high demand. Customers named on the desk booking page include Toyota Connected EU, PVH Corp, Columbia University, Aon, and Pella Windows & Doors. The site states SOC 2 Type 2 certification with independently audited controls. It also states GDPR compliance, with data processing agreements available.

paragraphs: Campminder makes management software for summer camps of every shape, from day camps to sleepaway programs and from twenty campers to two thousand. It is sold by role, with separate material pitched to camp owners and directors and to registrars and administrators.

Families register from their own devices, and the forms they fill out land in one organized place. Payments are collected and tracked inside the enrollment hub. A transportation planner lets staff drag and drop buses, routes, schedules and shuttles. Messaging tools pull camp data to send specific emails and texts to campers, parents, staff and alumni. An API distributes report data instantly to other departments. A companion app gives parents a photo feed that finds their child using facial recognition.

The company describes itself as a customer-centric business 22 years strong. Both product suites are tiered on the number of enrolled campers in the camp. Onboarding covers website integrations, historic data import and merchant account setup in fewer than three weeks. Camps across North America are described as using the platform to coordinate the logistics of running their programs.

before.name: Baron Weather
before.description: Weather data, alerting and decision tools for government agencies

paragraphs: Baron Weather sells weather data, forecasting and alerting tools to businesses, government agencies and communities. Its catalog holds hundreds of datasets, with information down to the street level. The company argues that free or incomplete sources leave organizations either over-prepared and wasteful or under-prepared and at risk.

Baron blends data from many sources into insights using analytical processes, machine learning, and AI. Many of its products carry built-in alerting and recommended actions to guide a decision. The company also builds weather radar hardware it describes as engineered for durability and sustainability. Its forecast modeling covers atmospheric, hydrological, marine, air quality, and road surface coupled models. Content is prepackaged so it can be shared quickly and understood without expertise.

The company traces its mission to 1989, when an F4 tornado devastated parts of Huntsville, Alabama. Its customer base spans government agencies, emergency managers, small startups, and Fortune 500 companies. Baron lists ISO 9001 quality management among the credentials behind its processes. ISO 14001 environmental management is listed as well.

before.name: Greenzie
before.description: Autonomous mowing software retrofitting commercial mowers, sold via OEMs to grounds and parks crews

paragraphs: Greenzie makes self-driving software meant to improve the safety, productivity and profitability of a landscaping fleet. It partners with OEMs to manufacture Greenzie-equipped, Robotic Ready mowers sold at outdoor power equipment dealers throughout the United States. Buyers shop for those mowers at dealer locations nationwide.

Each Greenzie-equipped mower carries sensors the company says are field tested for obstacle avoidance, smooth driving and clean stripes. Operators can switch between manual and autonomous modes. A crew mows the perimeter once and lets the software finish the job while they move on to other tasks. The software is designed in accordance with ANSI/RIA R15.08-1-2020 safety requirements for industrial robots.

The customers are commercial landscaping crews, and the company frames its work as making jobs easier, faster and safer for large landscapers across the country. Greenzie began in 2018, when co-founder Charles Brian Quinn started calling every landscaper he could reach. The team describes itself as roboticists, software engineers and landscaping professionals. It says it is backed by venture capital firms and investors.

before.name: ROLLER
before.description: Venue management, ticketing and POS for aquatic centers and attractions

hiring.note: Account Executive - Mid-Market and (London, United Kin)

paragraphs: ROLLER sells venue management software to attractions businesses, pulling bookings, point of sale, memberships and reporting into a single platform. It is cloud-based and built for growing attractions businesses, meant to stand in for the several tools a venue would otherwise run. The company describes the platform as powering more than 3,000 attractions.

Ticketing is built around flexible bookings and add-on sales for both staff and guests. Operators running more than one site can hold branding consistent across locations and publish changes from a single headquarters account. Plans are tiered, with an entry level covering online and in-venue selling and day-to-day operations. Higher tiers are aimed at established venues wanting more customization and support.

One franchise operator, We Rock the Spectrum, put the platform into more than 120 locations over six months. Another customer, Area 51, is described on the site as an Australian family entertainment center operator running venues across multiple states. The company also publishes a guest survey it says covers 1,500 people.

quote.text: Purpose-built for growing attractions businesses, ROLLER is a cloud-based solution that replaces multiple tools needed to operate effectively and deliver better guest experiences.

paragraphs: Bond Sports sells the software that a sports facility runs its business on. It aims at operators of complex multi-sport venues and ice rinks rather than youth clubs alone.

Scheduling, registration, memberships and payments sit on one data model, so availability, billing and reporting stay in sync when something moves. Rentals, events and leagues share a single calendar with recurring bookings, conflict checks and invoicing. Point of sale covers terminals, concessions, merchandise and pro shop sales. Failed membership charges and missing cards are flagged and retried automatically.

Named users quoted on the site include the general manager of Chelsea Piers Sky Rink. The company says customers process more than $250M in registrations a year through the platform. Most facilities go live in three to four weeks. Data migration, configuration and staff training are handled by Bond during the switch.

before.name: Galaxy Digital

paragraphs: Galaxy Digital sells volunteer management software under the Get Connected name, built for organizations that recruit, schedule, track and report on volunteers. The organizations described range from food banks and healthcare systems to municipal departments and corporate social impact teams.

The platform puts scheduling, hour tracking, communication and reporting in one place. Volunteers check in through an onsite kiosk or a free mobile app. Liability waivers and e-signatures are collected and stored digitally. The software is sold in tiers, with the largest aimed at organizations running multiple programs or locations under separate volunteer coordinators.

A separate edition called Center serves organizations that sit at the middle of a network of nonprofit partners. That edition adds statewide and citywide volunteerism reporting. The company states its network reaches 405 volunteer centers, more than 60,000 mission-driven organizations and millions of volunteers. It also reports acquiring HandsOn Connect.

before.name: Eventeny
before.description: Event management SaaS: vendor applications, ticketing, maps, and sponsors for festivals and city events

paragraphs: Eventeny sells event management software that makes it easier to manage vendors, volunteers, attendees, sponsors and maps in one place. The platform is used for festivals, conferences, expos, markets, parades and community gatherings.

Organizers build maps from scratch or on Google Maps with a drag-and-drop event mapping tool. Booths are assigned and spaces connected to tickets from that same place. Vendor and artist applications move through flexible workflows with built-in jury tools. Ticketing covers sales, upgrades and guest check-in with QR codes. Volunteer shifts can be scheduled, team leads assigned, and the crew contacted in one place. Sponsor packages can be customized to fit an event's needs.

Eventeny was started by two founders, Aly Hussaini and Nausheen Punjani. The company says its product marketplace hosts over 4,000 small business owners around the country. Its homepage says more than 2,550,000 users in five or more countries are on Eventeny. It reports over 34,000 events hosted on the platform. Case studies include the City of Suwanee, whose small event team was hosting more than 40 events a year with a primarily paper-based system.

before.name: Harmari (LTAS Technologies)
before.description: Short-term rental compliance monitoring and enforcement for municipalities

paragraphs: Harmari sells tools that identify and monitor short term rentals so a municipality can collect lodging tax and enforce local rules. A companion product covers long term rentals through website monitoring, rental identification and a rental registry. Another line addresses municipal business licensing and revenue enhancement.

The tools analyze many classifieds at once, which the company presents as faster and more complete than working through them by hand. The short term rental product works with Taxcrawler to find and watch properties for lodging tax collection, licensing and code compliance. Evidence collection standards call for at least two screenshots. The company states a 95% accuracy guarantee for houses and 75% for condos. There is a tax reporting module with under-reporting detection. A registration portal is customized to local laws. Enforcement outreach runs by phone and direct mail.

Buyers include state and municipal revenue agencies with units that look for taxpayers who are not compliant. The company says Taxcrawler has helped revenue departments find and recoup tax revenue. Condominium and homeowner associations are addressed by a separate short term rental finder. Work outside those products can be taken on as custom data collection or web scraping.

before.name: Bchex
before.description: Background screening and volunteer management for schools and youth-serving organizations

paragraphs: Bchex runs background screening for organizations that have to vet the people they hire, and it also sells continuous monitoring along with visitor and volunteer management. The company advertises that 92% of background checks are delivered in under 24 hours.

A customer requests checks in seconds, tracks progress in real time from a single dashboard, and gets a report at the end. Candidates can scan a driver's license so their information populates automatically instead of being typed in. The platform connects to an applicant tracking system to sync and automate the screening process. Bchex puts terms behind the service: no payment if it misses its turnaround time or if the customer is unsatisfied, and a price match against a cheaper quote.

The company counts more than 2,000 school districts, non-profits, and US businesses among its customers. It states that it processes over 500,000 background checks per year. It describes nearly 30 years spent on this one line of work. The site states that Bchex is SOC 2 Type 2 certified for security, confidentiality, and availability. Buyers pay per order, with no long-term contracts or subscription fees.

paragraphs: Earth Networks sells hyperlocal weather intelligence and real-time lightning detection to organizations that have to make safety decisions outdoors. A core use is warning people who work and play outdoors when lightning is approaching.

The company frames the lightning network as detection rather than prediction. It claims coverage in more than 90 countries. Warnings reach people by email, text message and mobile push notification. Audible outdoor horns carry the same warning across a site. Its Sferic Maps product tracks more than 80 real-time weather conditions on a map. Sferic Connect lets administrators notify staff of dangerous weather on iOS and Android devices, and can stop end users from opting out.

Meteorological staff are on hand around the clock when a customer is unsure what to do. Product pages point at schools as one setting for the alerts. Airports are another. The company also publishes a report on lightning detected across the United States.

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile_research.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

https://careers-granicus.icims.com - the iCIMS board itself was not fetched in this task; the link was read off granicus.com/careers/.
Regional sites granicus.com/uk/, /anz/, /india/, /es/ and the per-product pages under /product/ were not read.

paragraphs: Granicus makes software that governments use to reach residents, understand them, and serve them online. A second line serves destination marketing organizations, with tools meant to attract visitors and win events.

The catalog covers agenda and meeting management, digital services and forms, communications and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records compliance. Video streaming and hosting sits alongside those products. The company has since added Government Experience Agent, which it calls the first AI-powered digital agent built specifically for government requirements, giving residents support around the clock.

Granicus states that it has more than 2,000 employees supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations. Customer stories name the Oklahoma Health Care Authority among the agencies using Granicus. Its own history page traces the business to a merger with GovDelivery, after which the combined company took the Granicus name. It later acquired destination marketing services provider Simpleview.

The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. before.name: HydroPoint Data Systems
before.description: WeatherTRAK smart irrigation and water management for public agencies

paragraphs: HydroPoint sells smart water management covering both indoor and outdoor use. That means round-the-clock water use analytics and leak detection alongside irrigation control. Two irrigation brands sit under the company: WeatherTRAK, for portfolio-wide remote management and visibility, and Baseline, which offers sensors and two-wire technology.

A third product, WaterCompass, provides real-time visibility into indoor water use. The company says its solutions typically deliver payback in as little as 24 to 36 months. It also claims benefits past the water bill, including reduced labor and operational costs and prevention of overwatering.

HydroPoint was founded in 2002 by technology entrepreneurs Chris Spain, Peter Carlson, and Chris Manchuck. In 2016 it expanded by acquiring Baseline Systems. One published case study reports that the City of Boise has seen up to 70% water savings on its Baseline sites compared with previous watering methods. Across its customers, the company reports saving over 27 billion gallons of onsite water and over $213 million in water costs in 2025.

paragraphs: Campspot sells campground management and reservation software to park owners and operators. It also runs a consumer booking site where campers search campgrounds, RV parks, cabins, and glamping stays.

On the operations side the software reaches from the front desk to housekeeping. Dashboards and reports track a park's health metrics. The platform connects to dozens of third-party applications. before.description: AI-embedded youth program management (enrollment, payments, safety) from nonprofit BellXcel

paragraphs: Arly is youth program management software that puts every layer of program operations in one platform. The people who buy it run programs for children, handling enrollment, pricing and payments in the same place.

Families sign up through a customized portal with one log-in, completing forms and uploading documents. Billing and account processing sit alongside, with revenue tracked in real time. Participants are grouped and staff assigned to them for attendance taking and access to health and safety information. Check-in and check-out verifies authorized pick-up contacts in real time. An assistant called Arly Compass is described as part of the platform itself.

Curriculum is sold alongside the software, one set of it created in partnership with Scholastic. A summer package runs five to six weeks of ninety-minute daily instruction in reading, writing and math. Testimonials on the site are attributed to program staff at YMCA organizations, including the YMCA of Central Virginia. Staff onboarding includes self-paced learning and support from the company's customer experience team.

before.name: Better Impact
before.description: Volunteer management software for parks, libraries and government agencies - exhibited at Animal Care Expo 2026

paragraphs: Better Impact sells volunteer management software used by organizations to automate scheduling, track hours and communicate with volunteers. A membership product manages member profiles, automates renewals and supports engagement across the member lifecycle. A client product works alongside the volunteer system to coordinate volunteer and client interactions.

Coordinators get self-scheduling, automated communications, online training modules and one-click reports. The broader promise is streamlined scheduling, less administrative burden and hour tracking in one system. A separate offering called Volunteer Link is built for corporate social responsibility teams that want to engage employees, strengthen community partnerships and measure impact. It gives employees access to over 200,000 volunteer opportunities across the US and Canada. Reports come export-ready for ESG disclosures, board presentations and annual CSR summaries.

The company says more than 85,000 organizations use its software. Its published case studies include a hospice rethinking how it coordinates care. In March 2026 it announced the acquisition of Get Connected by Galaxy Digital, another volunteer management software provider. Leadership is listed as chief executive Houston Goodwin and president Tim Sarazen.

before.name: Camis
before.description: Reservation and park operations systems for state, provincial and federal parks

paragraphs: Camis sells reservation and park management software to government-operated parks, marinas and harbors, work the company says it has done for more than 46 years. Visitors use it to book a camping trip, a day-use pass, a harbor stay or a ticketed event.

Bookings can come in ahead of time, at the gate, or through a call center. Payment runs through the same platform, whether the visitor is online or standing at a park office. A combined on-site and webstore system handles merchandise sales with real-time inventory tracking, and the company describes it as fully PCI and SOC compliant. Field staff get a separate enforcement app called Sidekick, built for the job assignments of wardens and rangers. On the back end, staff work from real-time data and customizable reports.

The company describes its origin as outdoor enthusiasts who saw a better way to connect people to parks. Its own timeline starts with a first park contract at Craigleith Provincial Park. The same timeline records that the business was acquired by Banyan Software. It also claims continued expansion across more than 30 national, provincial and state parks.

before.name: BECS Technology
before.description: BECSys pool chemistry automation controllers with cloud remote monitoring for municipal aquatic centers

paragraphs: BECS Technology builds electronic controllers, starting with water chemistry and filtration controls used on swimming pools, water parks, spas and splash pads. A second line goes into pork and poultry barns, where the company says its products help assure livestock health. A third covers refrigeration, with controls that supermarkets, convenience stores and liquor stores use to hold groceries at temperature.

A water chemistry controller watches the pool continuously and decides when the water needs attention. Operators reach those controllers through an online service the company describes as simple and secure. On the livestock side, the systems track feed inventory across a farm and send real-time data back to feed mills.

The company was incorporated in 1991. Its original ownership group has remained unchanged and has been together for over 30 years. More than 50,000 controllers have been designed and manufactured over that period. All manufacturing is performed onsite at a facility in Saint Louis, Missouri. The BECSys line of water treatment controllers was introduced in 2005. Before that, many products were marketed and distributed under the names of partner organizations.

paragraphs: Cuseum sells an engagement platform built for museums, cultural attractions, nonprofits and membership organizations. Its digital tools are aimed at the visitors, members and donors those organizations already deal with.

The anchor product is a digital membership card that gives members wallet passes, benefits, renewals and updates through Apple Wallet and Google Wallet. Around it sit mobile engagement, audio guides, ticketing, loyalty tools, donor engagement and lifecycle communication. On site, the platform covers digital tickets, guest registration and barcode scanning at the door. For staff, Cuseum lists native CRM connectors along with 700 or more apps reachable through Zapier.

Cuseum says hundreds of institutions worldwide rely on it for membership cards, mobile guides, guest passes, loyalty programs and lifecycle communications. The customers it describes are kinds of organizations rather than named ones: art museums, science centers, aquariums and zoos, botanical gardens, libraries, alumni associations and nonprofit foundations. The footer identifies the company as Cuseum, Inc., in Boston.

paragraphs: CourtReserve makes software for running racquet and paddle sports clubs. The platform covers bookings, payments, memberships, events and a mobile app. It is built for racquet and paddle sports facilities.

Clubs run everything from court reservations to payments in one system. Invoicing and billing are automated to keep the books tidy. Players find their club, search and book from a phone. The player app is available on iOS and Android. The company advertises US-based support.

Case studies present the software as a way to simplify scheduling, grow membership and manage reservable spaces. One of them says the pickleball operator Dill Dinkers adopted CourtReserve as its club management system from day one.

before.name: Baseline Irrigation Solutions
before.description: Two-wire smart irrigation control for municipal parks and schools

paragraphs: Baseline provides engineered irrigation solutions built on proprietary two-wire technology and real-time sensor data. The premise is that a sensor-based control system responds dynamically to real-time data, using algorithms to make better irrigation decisions.

Controller platforms listed on the site include BaseStation 3200S, BaseStation 1000, AG 1000, SubStation and FlowStation. Sensors cover soil moisture, precipitation, flow and pressure. The software carries the names AppManager, BaseManager, BACnet Manager and PipeView Analytics. The device catalog runs from two-wire and conventional-wire devices to control point technology, solar and DC power, and the WaterTec S100.

before.name: Athletify
before.description: Staff scheduling software built for parks and rec departments (flat annual pricing)

paragraphs: Athletify makes staff scheduling software for parks and recreation departments, pulling every program and every worker into one schedule that a manager can filter as needed. Staff need only one login even when they hold several positions.

Shifts can be filtered and grouped by program, location, position, or staff member, and the views a department reaches for most often can be saved. Requests to drop a shift, claim a shift, or take time off arrive in a centralized inbox that all admins share. Age limitation tools let a department create and enforce scheduling rules for younger workers, including restrictions that keep them off early morning or late evening shifts. Messaging is built in, with channels for different staff groups such as lifeguards or referees.

The company says it has heard from hundreds of cities about the struggle of managing staff, and it is looking for beta partners to help shape the tool. Pricing is advertised without tiers or per-user fees. The site dates the beta program as running until July 1, 2025.

before.name: Perry Weather
before.description: Weather safety platform: WBGT heat monitoring, lightning alerts, stations and sirens for parks and athletics

paragraphs: Perry Weather sells a weather safety platform that pairs monitoring hardware at a customer site with automated alerting, so an entire staff works from the same reading of conditions. The buyers it names are schools, cities, golf clubs, and industrial firms.

Stations at the customer location measure heat stress, lightning, precipitation, wind, and air quality, refreshing every five minutes in the mobile app and dashboard. Each organization writes its own thresholds and decides who gets notified when one is crossed. Alerts can go to phones or to an outdoor siren system. Countdown timers mark the moment it is safe to resume play or work. All-clears go out automatically once the threat has passed.

Colin Perry founded the company in 2013. It reports more than 5,000 organizations nationwide as customers. It also counts over 200 million alerts sent, covering hazards from heat stress to lightning. Arthur Ventures led a $15M Series B. The stated markets run across athletics, golf, parks and recreation, energy, and airports.

before.name: InitLive (Bloomerang Volunteer)
before.description: Event volunteer scheduling and check-in for festivals and public events

paragraphs: Bloomerang Volunteer is volunteer management software for nonprofits, covering recruiting, scheduling, engagement, tracking and reporting. It is aimed at organizations of any size, including those with large volunteer bases, recurring shifts and multiple sites or programs.

Scheduling filters volunteers by skills, roles, availability and interests to match them to open shifts. Volunteers use a mobile app to manage schedules, stay informed and check in on site. Background checks run inside the platform against an organization's own safety and compliance standards. Reporting turns volunteer hours into custom reports showing dollars saved through volunteer work. Because donors, volunteers and fundraising sit on one platform, volunteer data can be used to identify donor prospects.

The volunteer product arrived by acquisition, and the company milestone list records that Bloomerang acquired InitLive and launched Bloomerang Volunteer Management. Bloomerang presents itself as a unified giving platform built for purpose. The same page claims over ten years of purpose-built software. Other milestones include acquiring Qgiv to expand the giving platform.

paragraphs: Better Impact sells volunteer management software used by organizations to automate scheduling, track hours and communicate with volunteers. A membership product manages member profiles, automates renewals and supports engagement across the member lifecycle. A client product works alongside the volunteer system to coordinate volunteer and client interactions.

Coordinators get self-scheduling, automated communications, online training modules and one-click reports. The broader promise is streamlined scheduling, less administrative burden and hour tracking in one system. A separate offering called Volunteer Link is built for corporate social responsibility teams that want to engage employees, strengthen community partnerships and measure impact. It gives employees access to over 200,000 volunteer opportunities across the US and Canada. Reports come export-ready for ESG disclosures, board presentations and annual CSR summaries.

The company says more than 85,000 organizations use its software. Its published case studies include a hospice rethinking how it coordinates care. In March 2026 it announced the acquisition of Get Connected by Galaxy Digital, another volunteer management software provider. Leadership is listed as chief executive Houston Goodwin and president Tim Sarazen.

before.ats_note: unwired 2026-09-02: the Paylocity tenant is 'AEM', which is not this company's name - a parent's board or a former name. Queued in Boards we found for a person to rule.

paragraphs: Earth Networks sells hyperlocal weather intelligence and real-time lightning detection to organizations that have to make safety decisions outdoors. A core use is warning people who work and play outdoors when lightning is approaching.

The company frames the lightning network as detection rather than prediction. It claims coverage in more than 90 countries. Warnings reach people by email, text message and mobile push notification. Audible outdoor horns carry the same warning across a site. Its Sferic Maps product tracks more than 80 real-time weather conditions on a map. Sferic Connect lets administrators notify staff of dangerous weather on iOS and Android devices, and can stop end users from opting out.

Meteorological staff are on hand around the clock when a customer is unsure what to do. Product pages point at schools as one setting for the alerts. Airports are another. The company also publishes a report on lightning detected across the United States.

before.name: InitLive (Bloomerang Volunteer)

paragraphs: Bloomerang Volunteer is volunteer management software for nonprofits, covering recruiting, scheduling, engagement, tracking and reporting. It is aimed at organizations of any size, including those with large volunteer bases, recurring shifts and multiple sites or programs.

Scheduling filters volunteers by skills, roles, availability and interests to match them to open shifts. Volunteers use a mobile app to manage schedules, stay informed and check in on site. Background checks run inside the platform against an organization's own safety and compliance standards. Reporting turns volunteer hours into custom reports showing dollars saved through volunteer work. Because donors, volunteers and fundraising sit on one platform, volunteer data can be used to identify donor prospects.

The volunteer product arrived by acquisition, and the company milestone list records that Bloomerang acquired InitLive and launched Bloomerang Volunteer Management. Bloomerang presents itself as a unified giving platform built for purpose. The same page claims over ten years of purpose-built software. Other milestones include acquiring Qgiv to expand the giving platform.

before.name: 24/7 Software
before.description: Incident, event day and operations management for public venues and cities

paragraphs: 24/7 Software sells operations management software that venue teams use to communicate in real time and hold down risk on event day. The buyers run stadiums, arenas, performing arts centers and other event spaces.

Staff build their own workflows, dispatch personnel and keep a detailed history of every incident record. Each record and every change to it is time and date stamped, so a response leaves an audit trail behind it. Field staff work from mobile applications for iOS and Android that let them file incident forms and close issues where they stand. The same platform schedules preventive maintenance through a computerized maintenance management system. Analytics dashboards are offered as a way to take guesswork out of guest experience and operating decisions.

Beyond ticketed sport, the company aims the software at amusement parks, zoos, aquariums, museums and fairs. College athletics departments and university facilities are named too, covering game day and wider campus operations. The company says its customer success group trains staff and supports them through onboarding.

before.name: Camis
before.description: Reservation and park operations systems for state, provincial and federal parks

paragraphs: Camis sells reservation and park management software to government-operated parks, marinas and harbors, work the company says it has done for more than 46 years. Visitors use it to book a camping trip, a day-use pass, a harbor stay or a ticketed event.

Bookings can come in ahead of time, at the gate, or through a call center. Payment runs through the same platform, whether the visitor is online or standing at a park office. A combined on-site and webstore system handles merchandise sales with real-time inventory tracking, and the company describes it as fully PCI and SOC compliant. Field staff get a separate enforcement app called Sidekick, built for the job assignments of wardens and rangers. On the back end, staff work from real-time data and customizable reports.

The company describes its origin as outdoor enthusiasts who saw a better way to connect people to parks. Its own timeline starts with a first park contract at Craigleith Provincial Park. The same timeline records that the business was acquired by Banyan Software. It also claims continued expansion across more than 30 national, provincial and state parks.

before.name: GameChanger
before.description: Youth sports scorekeeping and streaming app - exhibited at NRPA 2026

paragraphs: GameChanger sells a youth sports app that athletes, coaches, and families use to stay connected through live streaming, scorekeeping, team management, and developmental resources. The app is free for coaches on teams where they are listed as staff.

Coaches message the team, schedule events and lineups, and review stats, insights, and game film for practice planning and player development. Families and fans follow along with real-time live streaming in HD, GameStream animations, live game alerts, and play-by-plays. Confirmed family members and players can broadcast games live in all sports by default. Watching live streams of sports such as basketball, volleyball, and soccer is free without limit.

The company was founded in 2009, is headquartered in New York City, and says it covers more than nine million games annually across baseball, softball, basketball, volleyball, soccer, football, lacrosse, hockey, and more. It also puts its reach at close to 10 million games and more than a million teams a year. GameChanger is owned and operated by DICK'S Sporting Goods, described as one of the largest sporting goods retailers in the United States.

brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

paragraphs: nextRec sells cloud based software for running parks and recreation departments, from program registration to facility rentals, with a self service side for residents. Buyers range from small villages to large counties and the government staff in between.

Staff set up single or recurring classes, courses, drop-ins, and programs, with conflict checking built in. The booking side covers indoor and outdoor facilities, parks, fields, campgrounds, meeting spaces, and party venues. Payments, memberships, and product sales run through the same system, online or on-site. Reports can be created, run, and exported in real time.

The same platform is marketed to K-12 schools and to higher education institutions. Associations use it so members can pay and manage their own accounts at any hour. The company says the platform complies with PCI, ISO, and SOC standards. Customers keep ownership of their data, which the site says stays in its country of origin. Support is offered 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

before.name: BondLink
before.description: Municipal bond investor relations and debt issuance platform for issuers - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: BondLink sells a platform to municipal bond issuers, aimed at making their bond sales go better. It gathers printing, distribution, deal pages, analytics and support into one place. The company describes itself as a single source for investor relations and debt management for issuers.

On the investor relations side, an issuer gets a website where investors find the finance team, five years of annual reports, project updates and required disclosure documents. Investors who follow a site are alerted when new documents or events are posted to it. An outreach tool lets an issuer filter investors by what they did on the site and email them from inside the product. A debt profile keeps a current view of every outstanding bond, payment and call date so reports and board presentations start from the same data. Exports are meant to line up with what continuing disclosure filings require on EMMA.

It is pitched at debt professionals working with limited time and resources. The debt management page reports the total amount of debt the platform currently tracks. The company says issuer websites built on it have been viewed more than two million times. A news item on the home page announces being named to the GovTech 100 for an eighth consecutive year.

before.name: GUARDIAN RFID
before.description: RFID wristbands and Command Cloud software for inmate tracking, well-being checks, and compliance - exhibited at Michigan Sheriffs Association 2026, North Carolina Sheriffs' Association 2026

paragraphs: GUARDIAN RFID sells jails a way to track inmates, run guard tours and log activity as it happens. Fixed readers identify inmates by RFID wristband or RFID card to confirm presence and location. The company is the exclusive distributor of the Clincher wristbands those readers use.

Behind the hardware sits Command Cloud, a platform of integrated applications and services for corrections staff. Long-range readers create customizable zones over housing units, out of cell areas and corridors. Officers carry a rugged Android handheld for data collection and evidence gathering. Check frequencies can be configured by location and inmate classification. Electronic medication orders carry administration times, allergies, dosage, frequencies and routes.

The company says over 75,000 corrections staff across the United States rely on it. Facilities need no servers of their own, since the system is cloud based. It integrates with a wide range of jail management systems as well as offender and case management systems. An ongoing System Renewal Fee covers software upgrades for Command Cloud and Mobile Command. That fee is invoiced 12 months after go-live.

paragraphs: Continental Utility Solutions, Inc., known as CUSI, has spent decades building utility management software. The line runs from customer information systems and utility billing applications to mobile meter reading and customer web portals.

Billing comes in two forms: UMS, installed on premise, and UB4, a hosted application. The customer web portal gives residents tools to view usage history and financial activity rather than only a place to pay a bill. Mobile meter reading runs on any phone, tablet, or device with a modern internet browser, reading meters and uploading usage data wirelessly back to the billing software. Service orders can be handled from any modern internet-enabled device.

The company states that its products are PCI and FIPS compliant. Support is available by telephone, email, and online chat from 7:00 AM to 6:00 PM Central, Monday through Friday. CUSI says it implements around 70 clients each year. A free web-based learning platform called CUSI Academy provides access to over 100 learning modules.

paragraphs: ADP sells payroll and HR services to employers looking for solutions that support their people and unlock their teams' potential. The site organizes those offerings by employer size and tells visitors that coverage does not depend on how large the business is.

Alongside payroll sits SmartCompliance, described as a connected operating system that unifies compliance work living outside or beside a customer's HCM system. That work spans Affordable Care Act compliance, wage garnishments, and employment tax. The product is presented as platform agnostic, integrating with most ERP, HR, third-party and payroll systems. A health compliance module handles eligibility along with IRS Forms 1095-C and 1094-C and state employer reporting requirements.

The company claims more than 75 years helping organizations manage payroll, HR, and compliance complexity. It says its experts monitor federal, state, and local requirements across 11,000 jurisdictions. By its own count it has filed and furnished over 99 million Forms 1095-C nationwide.

before.name: Tanium
before.description: Endpoint management and security platform - exhibited at NACo 2026, NASCIO 2026, EDUCAUSE 2026

paragraphs: Tanium sells software that gives IT and security teams continuous visibility across an entire endpoint estate. A single agent covers real-time threat hunting, autonomous detection and response, and deep forensics. Vulnerability monitoring runs continuously with risk scoring based on actual exploitability rather than CVSS alone.

A layer called Atlas sits on top, unifying investigation and remediation with agentic AI over real-time endpoint intelligence. Operators type questions in plain English and Atlas translates them into live endpoint queries. Actions then execute within autonomy limits the operator defines. Native connectors link the platform to ServiceNow, Microsoft and Splunk.

Customer pages describe Best Buy consolidating data into a single pane of glass. Another describes Leeds and York Partnership NHS Foundation Trust keeping thousands of endpoints patched and up to date. That page says the platform gives full visibility into all 3,000 PCs and servers. The homepage says the company was named a Leader and positioned furthest in Completeness of Vision in a 2026 Gartner report.

before.name: Aquasight
before.description: AI operations and forecasting software for water and wastewater utilities - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Aquasight sells analytics software for the people who run water and wastewater utilities. The company says the software runs in the cloud and calls for no new hardware.

One product is a digital twin for sewer mains, lift stations and combined sewer overflow facilities. It forecasts flows, compares them with expected patterns, picks out unexplained anomalies and estimates inflow, infiltration and capacity limits. A second product joins mapping and maintenance management data so that asset risk keeps updating. From that it recommends whether to inspect, repair or replace, and supports capital planning and financial forecasting.

The company states that it has partnered with over 120 utilities. It says the tools are shaped for operators, engineers, directors and compliance officers alike. A news item announces the company exhibiting and speaking at Weftec in New Orleans in September 2026.

before.name: Grant Street Group
before.description: Tax collection, auctions and payment processing software for governments - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: Grant Street Group sells software to government entities covering tax calculation, billing, collection and distribution, along with payment processing and online auctions. The company describes those products as secure government cloud solutions for tax collection, e-payment and financial auction services.

TaxSys is the hosted, web-based system for tax calculation, billing, collection and distribution. PaymentExpress brings payment collection, management and reporting together across every channel. On the delinquent side, LienAuction runs tax lien certificate auctions and DeedAuction handles tax-defaulted property sales. Behind the payment side the company points to PCI-DSS Level 1 compliant security infrastructure.

The customers are state and county government offices. One client account describes a tax collector office replacing several legacy vendors with a single integrated Grant Street platform. The firm was founded in 1995. More than 500 full-time professionals now make up the staff. The company says its MuniAuction platform hosted the first online bond auction and that it has since hosted over $13 trillion in auction volume. It also claims the first fully hosted cloud-based tax billing and collection system.

before.name: Gordian
before.description: Construction cost data and job order contracting software - exhibited at NIGP 2026, PWX 2026, NLC City Summit 2026

paragraphs: Gordian sells construction cost data, procurement services and facilities assessments to organizations that budget, build and maintain the capital-intensive assets their communities rely on. Its main lines are Job Order Contracting for construction work and assessments with capital planning for existing assets.

RSMeans Data Online gives estimators more than 92,000 unit line items covering equipment, material and labor prices. Company researchers spend over 30,000 hours a year checking that the listed costs are accurate. Pricing is location-specific for over 970 locations across North America. Job Order Contracting replaces traditional procurement with one competitively-awarded contract used for a variety of projects. On the planning side, four Facility Condition Assessment approaches let an organization match the level of detail, speed and support it needs.

The company states that more than 16,000 organizations worldwide rely on it. Buyers include schools, healthcare facilities and government agencies looking to maximize their resources. Gordian reports completing more than $4B in construction volume in 2024.
