competitors.why: Shift scheduling and workforce management for police, corrections and 911, the direct alternative for the same agency scheduling sergeant
Public safety scheduling and readiness software competing for the same department's shift and personnel scheduling contract

paragraphs: Pace Scheduler sells a cloud-based scheduling system built for organizations that keep 24/7 schedules. Its clients include police departments, sheriff's offices, campus security, fire departments and public transportation agencies. Because that client base varies, the system is modular, so a department's site can be built with only the parts it wants.

The company says it designed the software to be easy to use without dropping the advanced features needed to maintain round-the-clock schedules. A mobile app is included, so staff can view schedules and submit or handle requests from an iOS or Android device as well as from a PC or tablet. In testimonials on the site, departments describe using it to fill shifts, request time off and balance leave banks. One says the shift bidding feature cut a process that used to take a month and a half down to four days.

Those testimonials come from agencies such as Tipp City PD in Ohio, Hudson PD in Colorado, Santa Paula PD in California and the Monroe County Sheriff's Office in Michigan, which says deputies, corrections officers and support staff all use it. Several describe replacing paper or Excel spreadsheets, and one lieutenant says the program replaced over a dozen spreadsheets. The company offers a free online demo to organizations that ask.

before.name: Aurelian
before.description: AI voice agents answering non-emergency calls for 911 centers

paragraphs: Aurelian builds software for the 911 centers known as public safety answering points. One of its two products answers non-emergency calls instantly, so callers are not left on hold. The other sits with call-takers during emergencies and gives real-time, context-aware guidance without taking control.

The automated line resolves routine calls on its own. It detects and escalates emergencies to a person. During live calls, the guidance tool surfaces the relevant SOP checklist for the incident. It also flags missing information before the call ends. The company says the system learns a center's workflows, SOPs, and systems in order to support the full call flow. Aurelian states that humans remain in control of emergencies and decision-making.

The customers page says PSAPs around the country use Aurelian to cut non-emergency workload and return time to their teams. Published stories include Hamilton County 911 automating more than 300 non-emergency calls a day. The about page says the founders, Max and James, were building call automation technology for hair salons before starting the company. That insight led them to pivot to public safety and build for PSAPs.

paragraphs: CentralSquare Technologies sells software to public agencies, from dispatch centers to city halls. On the public safety side, its suite runs from computer aided dispatch and NG911 call handling through to jail management and analytics. On the administration side, the company says public administrators in over 8,000 communities use it for finance, HR, payroll, asset management, permitting and tax collection.

Public Safety Suite Enterprise connects 911, CAD, RMS, Mobile and Jail in a single platform. A version called Public Safety Suite Pro is designed for small and mid-sized agencies that want one vendor rather than several systems. Vertex NG911 Call Handling gives 911 centers a single platform for voice, text, video and caller location. Vertex also carries built-in text translation and transcription for more than 150 languages, which the company says runs in under 10 seconds. The company says it secures cloud data against cyberattacks through a partnership with Amazon Web Services.

The homepage counts more than 8,000 agencies nationwide as customers. Customers named on the site include the California Highway Patrol. Case studies include the Edgar County 911 team, whose partnership with CentralSquare serves a community of 16,000 residents. Morgan County 911 in Alabama is featured for upgrading to Vertex NG911 Call Handling.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "Home | AlmavivA" https://www.almaviva.it 301-redirects to http://www.almaviva.it/it_IT/, which renders the Almaviva S.p.A. group site (page <title> is 'Home | AlmavivA'). It ties to the description directly: 'Trasporti e Logistica' is one of its named industry sectors, the site describes 'competenze esclusive in ambito ferroviario' and 'il trasporto pubblico locale integrato e la logistica intermodale', and it promotes its own 'Moova Mobility Platform' (headline: 'Moova Mobility Platform sbarca in Nord America'), which is Almaviva's transit/ticketing/mobility product. IMPORTANT NEGATIVE CHECK: almaviva.com is a DIFFERENT company entirely - it resolves to 'Atelier Almaviva', a tile workshop ('Fabrication Azulejos, carreaux de Delft, Zellige'). So the .it domain is not merely preferred, it is required; do not let anyone 'fix' this to .com. Caveat for the board: this is the Italian parent group's own site (correct, since the record is named plainly 'Almaviva', not a subsidiary), but its 'Lavora con noi' careers feed is overwhelmingly Italy-based, so US SLED AE roles will be rare to nonexistent.

paragraphs: Vix Technology builds intelligent transportation systems, automated fare collection and transit analytics. Its customers are transit agencies and operators. The company takes a modular approach so that existing partners and technologies can be embedded into a new system.

Operators get operations management tools and detailed performance reporting meant to help optimize services. Riders get live updates through physical displays, audio outputs, websites and mobile apps. Mobile ticketing lets passengers find, buy and use travel accounts, tickets and passes. The analytics side is pitched at spotting gaps in demand or late running services.

The team is over 350 people working from hubs in APAC, Europe and North America. The company says it has helped 200 cities and deployed 500,000 devices. It cites over 35 years in public transit. Vix is part of the ICM Mobility Group, which focuses on private and public transport. It lists BSI ISO certification in quality, health and safety, environment, service management and information security. It also states a commitment to net zero emissions in line with the UK government timeline.

before.name: May Mobility
before.description: Autonomous vehicle technology and driverless shuttle service for transit agencies and cities

paragraphs: May Mobility develops autonomous driving technology and brings it to ride-hail platforms, cities, campuses and businesses. Its operations run from rural Minnesota to Atlanta and the dense streets of Japan.

The cornerstone of the technology is a system the company calls Multi-Policy Decision Making. It is described as a real-time, reinforcement-learning AI algorithm. Vehicles generate training examples relevant to their current environment and learn while driving. The sensor stack and the decision-making platform work together to monitor the road and run simulations of possible situations and hazards.

An autonomous ride-hail preview is live on Lyft. The site notes a first autonomous vehicle fleet deployed with Lyft in Atlanta. It also lists a strategic partnership with Uber to scale autonomous vehicles. An investment from Grab is tied to expansion into Southeast Asia. The chief executive is Edwin Olson.

paragraphs: CSched sells scheduling services and software tools to public transit agencies, private operators, and school boards, whatever their size or mode of transportation. The company is the exclusive authorized reseller of GIRO's HASTUS software in North America.

Its scheduling and operations modules are built on the HASTUS platform. When an agency is short of schedulers, its Rent-a-Scheduler service supplies coverage from the short term to the long term. Training runs from foundational courses to advanced HASTUS workshops. Consulting work covers efficiency audits, labor negotiations, and tender bids. The firm also advises agencies adapting their scheduling practices for the shift to electric buses.

Transit agencies worldwide have relied on CSched since 2008. The site says more than 4,650 buses run every day on schedules developed with its software or services. CSched calls itself the only consulting firm fully dedicated to public transit scheduling. It operates globally with a strong presence in North America, serving agencies, school boards, and private operators. Its experts are described as bringing over 100 years of combined hands-on experience.

before.name: Aesys
before.description: LED and LCD passenger information displays for bus, rail, airports, and VMS traffic signs

paragraphs: Aesys builds passenger information displays for intercity, regional and metropolitan rail. It also makes variable message signs carrying traffic and safety information on highways, in tunnels and in cities. At airports its flight information displays run from the runway to the baggage area. A further line covers industrial displays made to hold up in harsh environments.

Displays carrying road information are built to comply with a European standard for variable message signs. Design and production are handled internally at the Bergamo headquarters. Testing starts early, from the first stages of prototyping. Software staff have written interfaces for standard protocols such as NTCIP, DisplayML, Modbus and TLS.

The company says it has been growing since 1977. It reports over 400 employees dedicated to product excellence. Sales offices sit in Germany, Spain and the United States. Certifications listed include a quality management system under ISO 9001.

before.name: Clever Devices
before.description: Bus ITS: CAD/AVL, real-time passenger info, and fleet health

paragraphs: Clever Devices builds technology for public transportation providers, meant to help them run more efficiently, spend less and deliver the service riders expect. The company says agencies with anywhere from 50 to 5,000 vehicles have chosen it over more than thirty years.

At the center is CAD/AVL software that gives dispatchers real-time information to monitor and manage the fleet. A vehicle health monitoring product is aimed at cutting repair costs and stretching the mean distance between failures. Onboard, automated passenger announcements are synced with LED signage so riders know where they are. Service planning is handled by the MAIOR scheduling suite, a modular set of planning and optimization tools. For agencies that would rather not run servers, CleverCloud takes on the on-premises hosting burden.

The company tells an unusual origin story, beginning in the early 1980s in the basement of a bar on Long Island. It turned to transit in 1990 when the Americans with Disabilities Act passed. The first product automated the stop announcements bus drivers were required to make. Today the company reports over 600 employees across 12 locations in the United States, Canada, Brazil and Italy. It puts more than 30,000 vehicles on its transportation systems technology. The homepage announces that Hitachi Rail has completed its acquisition of the company.

before.name: AngelTrax
before.description: Mobile video surveillance, DVRs, and MotoTrax analytics for transit, school, and municipal fleets

paragraphs: AngelTrax sells mobile video surveillance systems built for transportation safety. The company describes its customers as student transportation, mass transit, fleet, locomotive, and waste operations.

On a school bus, interior, exterior, stop-arm, and windshield views cover students, drivers, and transportation staff. Footage leaves the vehicle two ways, and a cellular link carries live view, active tracking, and instant notifications. Wi-Fi handles automated downloads once vehicles return to range. Video and data can be hosted by AngelTrax at its secure U.S. data center rather than handed to a third party. Its online software covers live view, downloads, vehicle location, health reporting, stop-arm workflows, and driver behavior. Driver behavior events arrive with video meant to support coaching, claims response, and accountability.

The company page dates the business to 2006. It reports 250,000 active systems operating worldwide. It also states $2.5M spent on research and development yearly. The same page describes a SOC 2 Type II-compliant data center for data security.

before.name: Swiftly
before.description: Real-time transit data: arrival predictions and on-time performance

paragraphs: Swiftly sells a cloud platform to public transit agencies for sharing real-time passenger information, running daily operations, and improving service performance. The company puts its customer count above 200 agencies. Those agencies are described as large and small, around the globe.

The platform combines GTFS schedule data with whatever real-time vehicle location feed an agency already has. It then analyzes billions of data points to say where a vehicle was, where it is, and where it will be next. Operations staff use it to make real-time adjustments for on-time performance and headway adherence. Schedulers work from actual run times, vehicle speeds, and dwell times. APIs push the same data out to rider-facing apps, vehicle hardware, and internal tools.

Customer service teams are another audience, answering rider questions from the same information. The site carries comments from transit staff, including an operations technology lead at the MBTA in Boston. Another comes from a transportation planner at MDOT MTA in Baltimore. Jonny Simkin co-founded the company and is its chief executive. Swiftly describes itself as a transit reliability platform meant to keep public transportation a fast and attractive alternative to the private vehicle.

before.name: Citiri
before.description: CitiriOS owner scope management and operational readiness (ORAT) for transit, airports, and utilities

paragraphs: Citiri sells CitiriOS, a system owners use to define readiness, assign accountability, collect accepted evidence, and govern gate decisions. The company aims it at organizations launching complex infrastructure and services.

The premise is that finishing construction is not the same as being ready to operate. The discipline the company calls Owner Scope Management runs as a chain in which the owner defines what must be true to operate, evidence proves it, and gates authorize it. The output is a Ready Score along with accepted evidence and gate decisions. An agent named Opti surfaces false greens, aging blockers, and the decisions that still need an owner. People, not the software, approve every evidence and gate decision.

The company is direct about the boundary, saying CitiriOS is not a PMIS, commissioning tool, EAM/CMMS, document repository, or BI replacement. Citiri says it is helping the ATL team manage a $13B capital program that includes more than 114 distinct projects. It also describes the SFO team using CitiriOS to keep the Harvey Milk Terminal One project on track. A companion layer, OpsCenter, is listed as generally available, while an ecosystem orchestrator called Struxis is listed as limited access.

before.name: Blaise Transit
before.description: Demand-responsive transit dispatch and booking software for transit agencies

paragraphs: Blaise Transit sells software for running transit without a fixed route or a fixed schedule. It was built to equip municipalities, cities, transit agencies, and transit operators. One platform covers demand-responsive service, paratransit, fixed-route integrations, and private shuttles.

The system comes in three parts. Blaise Engine lets operators set the vehicles, drivers, stops, and payment options that make up a transit system. A passenger app is available on Android, iOS, and as a website, where riders book, pay, and follow live vehicle locations. A driver app supplies turn-by-turn navigation on optimized routes and a passenger manifest at each stop. A separate simulations service recommends which transit models to implement and the parameters for each service.

Blaise was started in 2018 by a small group of transit-loving engineers. The site says more than 70 communities have chosen it to optimize their transit services. It reports working with agencies serving a few hundred rides a month up to a few million. Its optimization models are described as patent pending and customizable.

before.name: Agile Fleet
before.description: FleetCommander motor pool and vehicle sharing for agencies

paragraphs: Agile Fleet sells FleetCommander, a fleet management information system, to organizations that run vehicle fleets. The software automates motor pools, vehicle keys, maintenance, fuel and telematics for more than 300,000 drivers across government, university, utility and commercial fleets.

It is web based, and the motor pool side is aimed at raising utilization while lowering costs. Drivers get access only to vehicles they are licensed or certified to operate. Automated dispatching and around-the-clock kiosks are meant to remove wait times and staff involvement. More than 60 built-in reports flag underused assets for right-sizing. Key control runs on configurable touchscreens with an optional keyboard. Odometer, fuel and return location data are collected automatically at check-in. The maintenance module sends automatic preventive maintenance reminders. Parts are tracked across stockrooms and work orders from one interface.

Work orders capture hours, labor, parts and status. The company says it has partnered with municipalities, universities and commercial fleets. It also states that the platform is built on AWS GovCloud, aligned to NIST 800-53 and listed in the FedRAMP Marketplace.

before.name: EasyMile
before.description: Autonomous shuttles and driverless technology deployed with transit agencies

paragraphs: EasyMile makes autonomous driving software for vehicles working at airports, logistics sites and industrial sites around the world. The company supplies the autonomous driving intelligence, a CE-marked stack handling perception, path planning and safety. The vehicles it powers are distributed by TractEasy.

One of them is a heavy-duty autonomous tow tractor built for airports, factories and logistics hubs. It is described as running around the clock with a single operator overseeing an entire fleet. The other is a cargo dolly for air cargo and ground handling operations. It carries up to 7 metric tonnes while navigating around personnel and ground equipment. The software is meant to be modular enough to power other kinds of heavy-duty vehicles as well.

EasyMile says it was founded in 2014 between Singapore and Toulouse. Its timeline starts with a first passenger fleet on the road in Lausanne, Switzerland. The same timeline names Alstom, Bpifrance and Continental as investors backing the company. It records driving in autonomous mode in more than 300 locations worldwide. The company also claims to be the first autonomous technology provider to obtain ISO 9001:2015 certification.

before.name: Cylus
before.description: CylusOne rail OT cybersecurity: threat detection for signaling, trackside, and onboard networks

paragraphs: Cylus makes cybersecurity software for railways, built to continuously monitor, detect, and protect every layer of rail operational technology. Its product, CylusOne, covers mainline, urban, and freight rail operations.

The system integrates passively into an operator's network and existing monitoring tools. It automatically discovers and classifies all assets in the operational networks. Vulnerabilities are prioritized and scored by analyzing their severity in the rail environment. Detection runs continuously using deep packet inspection and machine learning to identify and classify threats across railway and IT protocols. Coverage reaches trackside and wayside networks, train-to-ground communications, operational control and maintenance centers, and station networks.

The company says the product lets operators prove compliance with frameworks including IEC 62443-3-2, NIST 800-82, and EN TS 50701. It describes CylusOne as the first rail cybersecurity solution certified to IEC 62443-4-2 at Security Level 3. Cylus says it works with technology providers, integrators, and rail experts worldwide. For passenger rail, detection is tuned to separate expected supervision and control traffic in ERTMS environments from anomalous behavior.

paragraphs: Cylus makes cybersecurity software for railways, built to continuously monitor, detect, and protect every layer of rail operational technology. Its product, CylusOne, covers mainline, urban, and freight rail operations.

The system integrates passively into an operator's network and existing monitoring tools. It automatically discovers and classifies all assets in the operational networks. Vulnerabilities are prioritized and scored by analyzing their severity in the rail environment. Detection runs continuously using deep packet inspection and machine learning to identify and classify threats across railway and IT protocols. Coverage reaches trackside and wayside networks, train-to-ground communications, operational control and maintenance centers, and station networks.

The company says the product lets operators prove compliance with frameworks including IEC 62443-3-2, NIST 800-82, and EN TS 50701. It describes CylusOne as the first rail cybersecurity solution certified to IEC 62443-4-2 at Security Level 3. Cylus says it works with technology providers, integrators, and rail experts worldwide. For passenger rail, detection is tuned to separate expected supervision and control traffic in ERTMS environments from anomalous behavior.

quote.text: CylusOne enables teams to investigate and contain threats without disrupting service, integrates with existing SOC processes, and keeps freight rail operations at the center of decision-making.

before.name: Automotus
before.description: Computer vision curb management and automated loading-zone payments

paragraphs: Automotus sells automated curb management systems to cities and airports. The company says it works with cities, airports and fleets to make communities better places to live.

The cameras attach to existing infrastructure such as streetlight poles. Once installed, the system automates data collection, invoicing and enforcement. Commercial drivers pay for curb time without apps or meters, and agencies can optionally apply discounted rates for electric vehicles. Violations are captured as they occur, with the option of notifying enforcement or issuing a citation automatically. Agencies also receive curb and traffic activity data broken down by every type of vehicle.

The company describes data security and individual privacy as priorities set from the start. It states that the technology blurs all faces, de-identifies data and captures only the license plates relevant to payment and enforcement. Its privacy policies are presented as independently audited and validated.

quote.text: CurbSight cameras bring AI to the curb.

before.name: BusPas
before.description: Solar smart bus stops with edge AI plus the ORA platform: signage, lane enforcement, passenger counting

paragraphs: BusPas upgrades, connects and modernizes urban furniture, starting with bus stops. It equips that furniture with sensors and edge computing meant to improve transit, protect user privacy and enhance security. The buyers are municipalities and transit agencies looking to optimize operations and improve services.

The ORA Ecosystem is the platform side, giving public transit agencies, cities and their officials access to data services linked to infrastructure within their municipality. The stops display real-time bus wait times and occupancy, count waiting passengers, and track boarding and alighting to analyze connections and origins and destinations. The system can also send specific requests to control traffic lights for buses and emergency vehicles. SaferSmart Zones is a turnkey bus and transit lane enforcement offering. Solar panels are added to minimize dependence on the grid. The products are described as a modular ecosystem of solar-powered, AI-enabled street infrastructure for transit reliability, safety, enforcement and passenger experience.

The company says it started in 2017. It works through standing contracts, so new legislation or an RFP is not required. A statement on the site is attributed to the mayor of Sainte-Julie, Québec. A headline says its smart stop technology was deployed across the TTC network ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026.

quote.text: Every city needs a digital twin to test the efficacy and impact of programs and make data based decisions.

paragraphs: Enghouse Transportation sells operations software for fare collection and ticketing, transit communications, fleet and transport management, and emergency dispatch. Among the organizations it names as buyers are public transport operators, combined authorities and agencies. Separate pages address emergency services and control rooms covering fire, healthcare and police.

The transit side covers automated fare collection with account-based, open loop and mobile ticketing, plus scheduling, journey planning and passenger information. Dispatch software for police, fire and EMS supports real-time coordination, incident management and control room operations. A contact center and interactive voice response product carries passenger updates on schedules, fares and disruptions across voice and digital channels. That product is described as GDPR compliant and aligned to ISO 27001/2 and Cloud Security Alliance requirements.

The company says its systems are used by organisations across transportation and public safety, with deployments in Europe and North America. It states that it has supported transit agencies, emergency services, and transport operators for over 40 years with software built for day-to-day operations. Enghouse Transportation is a subsidiary of Enghouse Systems Limited, a software and services company traded on the Toronto Stock Exchange under the symbol ENGH. The about page dates its work in transportation to 1984.

before.name: Beep
before.description: Turnkey autonomous shuttle operations for transit agencies, airports, and communities

paragraphs: Beep plans, deploys and manages autonomous shuttles for private and public communities. The services answer demand for alternative modes of transportation within communities, campuses and municipalities. Routes run inside geo-fenced areas at a controlled speed.

Deployments are built around first and last-mile trips, linking retail to residential areas, remote parking to campus amenities, and underserved communities to transit stops and stations. The service portfolio runs from upfront analysis, planning and design through turnkey operation of an autonomous mobility network. Underneath sits AutonomOS, a vehicle-agnostic platform for multi-passenger autonomous mobility services. It plans service modes from fixed route to demand-responsive variants. In-cabin monitoring built on machine learning lets remote supervisors react to a passenger safety or roadway issue.

The platform is built for public transit operators and authorities. The company reports deployments in six states and two dozen deployments overall. The purpose-built shuttles carry ADA-compliant wheelchair ramps and restraints. One announced project, ATL Spoke, is a pilot with Atlanta Beltline that the company says is in service and open to the public.

paragraphs: 2getthere builds automated transit vehicles that carry passengers with no driver on board. The systems are sold for smart cities, airports, campuses and industrial zones, and for urban and rural transit applications.

Because the vehicles run in a lane of their own, the company presents them as a way to move more people without adding to road congestion. One entry in the company timeline reports transporting over 2.7 million passengers to date.

before.name: CalAmp
before.description: Telematics devices and fleet tracking software for public fleets

hiring.note: no jobs parsed from iCIMS portal

paragraphs: CalAmp sells telematics devices and cloud software that organizations use to monitor, track, and protect vehicles, equipment, and cargo. The company describes covering the whole chain, from the user experience down to the platform and the edge devices themselves. Its telematics cloud is pitched at fleet operators, logistics companies, equipment manufacturers, and the systems integrators who build on top of it.

Devices on the vehicle collect location, speed, engine health, driver behavior, and outside sensor readings in real time. The cloud then turns protocols such as CAN bus, J1939, OBD-II, and Modbus into clean, structured output. Customers pull that data through APIs, a cloud connector, or event-driven alerts. A device management layer lets administrators assign roles governing who can view, change, or execute particular management functions. Software can be prototyped, tested, and deployed to devices over the air.

CalAmp says the platform is built for commercial fleets and software providers in construction, trucking, utilities, the public sector, and equipment manufacturing. The company states it has been in business for 40 years, with thousands of customers and more than 275 approved or pending patents. For data handling it cites SOC 2 Type II certification along with GDPR and SB327 compliance.

before.name: Ecolane
before.description: Paratransit and microtransit scheduling software for public transit agencies

paragraphs: Ecolane sells scheduling and dispatch software designed for public transit agencies that operate paratransit, non-emergency medical transportation, and microtransit services. Whichever way a trip is booked, the optimization that follows is autonomous and does not require manual intervention from a human.

The software optimizes service at the individual trip level and updates schedules as conditions change during the service day. That lets agencies account for no-shows, cancellations, delays, and staffing changes without rebuilding schedules manually. Eligibility rules, reporting, and compliance are integrated into daily operations. Managers can capture data for every vehicle, including rides per hour, run utilization, on-time performance, and deadhead. For medical trips, the platform helps agencies locate providers, verify rider eligibility, and schedule trips with vehicles equipped to accommodate rider needs.

Agencies supported by city, county, state, or federal funds are the intended buyers. The company says it is a U.S.-based company with U.S.-based product, engineering, and support teams. It states that its self-service applications are compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 Level AA. It also says it holds three clean Voluntary Product Accessibility Templates. The hosted service is described as providing significant cost savings for transit agencies.

before.name: Gatekeeper Systems
before.description: Intelligent video, AI stop-arm analytics, and cloud safety platforms for transit and school districts

paragraphs: Gatekeeper Systems sells video recording and data systems for transportation, meant to make travel safer for children, passengers, and public safety personnel across several modes. The company says it uses AI, video analytics, thermal cameras, and mobile data collectors to inter-connect public transit assets within intelligent transportation systems.

Its mobile data collectors gather video and audio along with GPS tracking and door open and close events, analyzing the data on the bus itself. Those units are ruggedized and crashworthy, serving as black boxes that hold data for accident investigations. Recorders take analog and IP channels at up to 1080P and 30 frames per second, with independently selectable resolutions. Drive caddies have passed MIL SPEC 810F for shock and vibration, and a thermal system warms the hard drive to its prescribed operating temperature before writing or reading in cold weather.

Fleet software called G4 Vision centralizes system health checks, driver behavior analysis, video management, live streaming, GPS, routing and mapping, and student tracking. An Automated Lane Enforcement product for transit buses is named on the home page. The company describes a Platform-as-a-Service business model. Testimonials on that page are attributed to school district transportation directors.

before.name: WeRide
before.description: Autonomous robobuses and robotaxis deployed with transit authorities and cities

paragraphs: WeRide develops autonomous driving technology ranging from driver assistance up to fully driverless Level 4 systems. Its footprint now spans more than 60 cities across 13 countries.

The portfolio holds five products: robotaxis, robobuses, robovans, robosweepers and a driver-assistance system. Between them they cover passenger mobility, logistics and street sanitation. The robobus is offered for public operations including day transport, bus rapid transit and night shuttle service. Robotaxi public operations are listed in cities including Guangzhou, Abu Dhabi, Zurich, Dubai and Singapore. The driverless stack runs on a computing platform rated at 2,000 TOPS.

The company was established in 2017 and has run an autonomous vehicle fleet for more than 2,500 days. It is listed on Nasdaq and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It states that its products hold autonomous driving permits in eight markets, among them China, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore and France. Named partners include global carmakers, ride-hailing firms and Tier 1 suppliers.

before.name: Connixt
before.description: iMarq mobile asset maintenance and MRO platform for transit, rail, and fleets

paragraphs: Connixt sells iMarq, a mobile-first application built for field crews, technicians and mechanics to digitize and automate data collection, paperwork, processes and workflows. The company aims it at fleets, rail, transit, manufacturing, heavy engineering and facilities.

There are native apps for iOS and Android. They run on phones and tablets, both online and offline. Crews record asset details in the organization's own forms, on their own devices, in real time. An assistant called iBot puts institutional knowledge, troubleshooting guidance and compliance support in front of frontline teams, while reporting lets users reach their data on any device and track asset status.

Public agency case studies include a transportation department whose traffic signal division used the customizable mobile app to digitize work orders and improve transparency. Another covers Metrolink, which automated the train delay reporting its conductors had been doing on paper. The company reports winning two Progressive Railroading Reader's Choice Awards for a second consecutive year. It is run by two co-founders, Satish and Prabhu, described as industry veterans, and the site cites a 4.8 rating on Capterra.

before.name: GIRO
before.description: HASTUS scheduling, run-cutting, and rostering for transit agencies and postal operators

paragraphs: GIRO makes software for the organizations that run public transport and postal delivery services, covering the work from planning through daily operations. Its two product families, HASTUS and GeoRoute, are in use in more than 30 countries.

The company grounds the work in knowledge of the problems those operators face day to day. GIRO states that more than 30% of its resources go to research and development. New ideas and solutions are developed with clients and validated by groups of users around the world.

GIRO was founded in the 1970s through the work of a Université de Montréal student and his professor. That early work paved the way for the creation of both products. The company counts over 40 years of experience in the field. It also notes a ranking among the 300 largest companies in Quebec.

before.description: Mobility and curb/parking technology platform - exhibited at APTA 2026

paragraphs: Arrive sells urban mobility technology to city governments, parking operators and businesses. On the parking side that means demand insight and digital payments for parking and EV charging.

Drivers start, stop, extend and pay for a session from an app. Operators run payment stations and in-car integrations from the same platform. License plate recognition can start and end sessions automatically as cars enter and leave. The company says its EV solutions connect with more than 400 charge point operators. For city planners, dashboards report parking use, traffic trends and mobility patterns to guide planning.

Arrive describes itself as a coming together of Flowbird Group, EasyPark Group, Parkopedia and others. The about page dates the story back to 1955. That timeline opens with Cale installing its first parking meters. Within the group, Flowbird is described as delivering mobility solutions in over 6,000 cities across 80 countries. EasyPark is described as present in over 4,000 cities across more than 20 countries.

before.name: Netradyne
before.description: AI dashcam and driver coaching for public fleets

paragraphs: Netradyne sells AI-powered video safety and fleet management technology to organizations that operate vehicle fleets. Its Driver·i platform combines 360-degree AI cameras, real-time in-cab coaching, and positive driver recognition.

The company says it analyzes 100% of driving time, provides real-time alerts, and delivers safety insights meant to improve fleet performance. Instant in-cab alerts let drivers self-correct before incidents occur. Driver performance is summarized in a GreenZone Score the company ties to proving safety impact and retaining drivers. The same platform covers fleet tracking, fuel efficiency, preventative maintenance, and compliance. Driver·i is certified with the FMCSA as an electronic logging device, covering hours-of-service, DVIR, and IFTA requirements on one platform.

Fleets named on the site include Rumpke Waste & Recycling, where severe distracted driving alerts dropped more than 30% over twelve months. The site also reports that Knight-Swift adopted the fleet safety product, bringing in-cab coaching and full drive-time analysis to its trucking fleet. More than 25 billion miles have been analyzed, according to the company. It describes its mission as building intelligence for the physical world.

paragraphs: Fleet Complete sells GPS fleet tracking and telematics to organizations that run vehicles. Customers range from small and mid-sized businesses to large corporations. In October 2024 the business was acquired by Powerfleet. The company says existing customer contracts, services and integrations stay unchanged through the brand change.

paragraphs: Basemap describes itself as an expert in transport software and data for accurate travel analysis. Its main product, TRACC, analyses travel times, optimises transit routes, and identifies accessibility gaps to key destinations. Government departments, city planners, transport operators, and consultants are named as the people who rely on those products.

before.name: IVU Traffic Technologies
before.description: IVU.suite planning, scheduling, dispatch, and ticketing for transit and rail operators

paragraphs: IVU develops integrated IT systems for public transport, and says it has done so for more than fifty years. The customers are bus and rail operators of any size, from five vehicles to fifty and from two routes to two hundred. Its product, IVU.suite, covers planning, dispatch, fleet management, ticketing, passenger information and the settlement of transport contracts.

Timetabling runs from setting up route networks to publishing services and supplying operation control and passenger information systems. Vehicle scheduling is handled by IVU.run, which supports the entire schedule planning process. Duty scheduling merges thousands of duty elements, crewing guidelines and qualifications through optimisation algorithms. For electric fleets the system weighs charging times, ranges, route lengths and depot or opportunity charging. In daily operation it monitors vehicle status, the timetable situation and the current deployment of vehicles and staff. The whole suite is also offered as a hosted service.

The company says more than 500 customers worldwide use the standard products of the suite. Named deployments include the Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority. It reports as IVU Traffic Technologies AG and has published preliminary results for the first half of 2026.

before.name: CivicSmart
before.description: Smart parking meters and occupancy analytics for municipalities

paragraphs: CivicSmart sells cities a curb management system spanning smart hardware at the space, real-time intelligence on every event, enforcement, and the operations software that ties them together. It also aims at universities and campuses. Airports and transit hubs are another target, where rideshare zones, cell lots and passenger loading need managing.

Product lines run from single-space and multi-space meters with integrated sensor options. Curb sensors report real-time occupancy, plate capture, and evidence-grade detection. LaneMaster devices provide automated lane management for loading, pickup-dropoff, rideshare and commercial corridors. Officers write citations on AutoISSUE handhelds. PEMS unifies every meter, sensor, handheld and citation into one dashboard. It publishes open REST endpoints so cities can bring their own BI, GIS and analytics tools.

CivicSmart, Inc. describes itself as a Wisconsin company founded in 2015 around the idea of reimagining the curb. It says it acquired Duncan Parking Technologies from Duncan Solutions in 2015 and renamed it CivicSmart Parking Technologies. The site claims more than 1,500 cities and agencies served. It also claims more than 15 million parking meters shipped. The company says its team holds patents globally for vehicle-detection sensors and parking technologies.

paragraphs: PayByPhone sells a mobile app for paying for parking in a few taps, without coins or hunting for the machine. It is available in over 1,200 cities across North America and Europe, including universities and colleges.

A driver connects a credit or debit card to a PayByPhone account and pays from the phone. Where available, Google Pay or Apple Pay can complete the transaction instead. A session can be extended from the app, with no need to run back to the car to feed the meter.

Ownership sits with Lightyear Capital, a New York-based private equity firm with over US$8 billion in assets under management. The press page also announces a global partnership with SKIDATA covering parking and access control solutions. Jonny Combe is named as President and Chief Executive Officer.

before.name: Hayden AI
before.description: Bus-mounted AI cameras enforcing bus lanes and stops for transit agencies

paragraphs: Hayden AI mounts cameras on transit buses so cities can catch vehicles that block bus lanes and stops. The system pairs vision AI with hardware built for the vehicle and reads the street around it as the bus drives.

Automated bus lane enforcement is the flagship product, meant to clear unauthorized parking and raise bus speeds. The catalog also lists automated bike lane enforcement. Double parking gets its own product, aimed at a habit the company blames for crashes and lost time on transit routes. The platform is described as identifying objects rather than people.

Cities buy it for outcomes on bus routes, and the company frames the payoff as fewer collisions. Leadership comes from artificial intelligence, data science, transportation, and government technology. The company reports six GovTech 100 wins between 2021 and 2026.

before.name: Avail Technologies
before.description: myAvail enterprise transit management ITS and CAD/AVL for mid-size US agencies

paragraphs: Avail Technologies sells enterprise transit management software to public transit agencies. The company states that its target market is transit operators with medium-sized fleets.

The myAvail platform covers vehicle location, dispatching, workforce management, reporting, and rider communications, so a team works from one connected system rather than several tools. A single shared database moves data throughout the organization. Dispatchers see where every bus and driver is, and incidents are tracked as they occur. Business intelligence dashboards report metrics in real time, which the company frames as a way to improve efficiency, justify funding requests, and demonstrate compliance. Features can be added to the platform as an agency's needs grow, and the company says myAvail ships multiple platform updates a year.

Founded in 1999, Avail describes a family-oriented staff working hand-in-hand with transit professionals. It says it has stayed a mid-sized company by design. An announcement on the site names Rick Spangler as president and chief executive as the company continues a transition to full employee ownership.

before.name: Whip Around
before.description: Digital vehicle inspections and maintenance for municipal fleets

paragraphs: Whip Around sells fleet management software that helps operators cut downtime, stay compliant, and replace paper inspections with digital workflows. Coverage runs from vehicles and equipment to supplies and facilities.

Drivers complete customizable digital inspections tied to the fleet's daily compliance. What they find feeds work orders, service schedules and preventative tasks. Compliance workflows are centralized around DOT, state and company requirements. Preventive maintenance schedules can be triggered by mileage or engine hours through connected telematics tools.

The company says it began in 2016, helping freight companies in New Zealand with a paper-based compliance burden. It reports serving thousands of customers with hundreds of thousands of users. Its customer base is described as commercial fleets in all industries, from delivery and distribution to agriculture and construction. Public agencies appear in its case studies, including the Town of New Milford. Another case study covers Poudre Fire Authority.

before.name: Auve Tech
before.description: Autonomous last-mile shuttles sold to cities and public transport operators

paragraphs: Auve Tech develops and manufactures autonomous transportation systems. What it sells is more than the vehicle: the offer covers integration of the vehicles into a given environment and fleet management alongside them. The stated aim is to extend public transport with a weatherproof first and last mile link running from a bus, tram or train stop to the doorstep.

The current shuttle, MiCa, is electronically limited to 25 km/h. The specification lists operating time of up to twenty hours a day. Sensing hardware named on the product page includes lidar, radar, GNSS and an inertial measurement unit. Teleoperation and remote monitoring are offered as options. A later software version added dynamic reaction to objects, detection of overtaking vehicles and side detection.

The company traces its origin to a 2018 project run in cooperation with Tallinn University of Technology. Testing of the earlier Iseauto shuttle on Estonian public streets began in the summer of 2020. One case study describes a scheduled last mile service in Takamatsu, Japan, with the shuttle operated by Boldly. That route ran 2.6 kilometres between a car park and a viewpoint.

before.name: Fybr
before.description: IoT parking sensors and smart city occupancy data for municipalities

paragraphs: Fybr sells parking technology and an operations platform built on privacy by design. It turns anonymous, real-time parking activity into the tools that run an operation and the insights to improve it. The range covers every space, facility, and curb.

The foundation is the FybrPuck, the company's own fourth-generation occupancy sensor, a compact, self-powered, wireless edge device. It covers on-street and off-street spaces, loading zones, no parking zones, ADA spaces, and EV charging stations. Occupancy status feeds real-time guidance through a mobile application, web browsers, and dynamic wayfinding signage. For enforcement, officers can be directed to potential violations rather than running continuous sweeps. Where an ordinance requires vehicle identification, license plate recognition scans vehicles for compliance. Payment is pay-per-use inside the mobile application. A dashboard tracks turnover, session duration, dwell times, rule compliance, peak demand, and utilization trends.

The homepage carries testimonials from municipal staff, one crediting the real-time enforcement app with helping officers identify issues and respond to violations. Another says the sensor technology improved parking enforcement operations in Marysville. A third says that after the parking system was implemented, spots could be found easily through the app.

before.name: AIMS Parking (EDC Corporation)
before.description: Parking citation, permit and enforcement management software for agencies

paragraphs: AIMS is parking management software from EDC Corporation, built to handle citations, permits and field enforcement for whoever runs the parking operation. The company writes that the system is meant to scale whether the buyer runs a city, a university, a hospital campus or an airport.

Citations are entered in real time from the field, with photos, GPS coordinates and notes attached to each one. Permits can be virtual or physical, and the software carries waitlists, renewals and permit prioritization. Fixed and mobile plate recognition cameras push reads, hits and occupancy data back into the system as they happen. A self-service portal gives the public round-the-clock access to payments, permits and appeals.

The site states that more than 300 clients in the United States and Canada use the software. A move onto the platform is described as taking twelve to sixteen weeks. The company describes the system as PCI and SOC 2 compliant. It also says the developers who write the software are the ones who support it.

before.name: Autura
before.description: Towing lifecycle software for city towing programs and impound management (ex-AutoReturn + TSD)

paragraphs: Autura sells software to the people who handle towing on public roads, from the officers and dispatchers who order a tow to the impound teams who store and release the vehicle. The company says it supplies towing management and unclaimed vehicle auction software to public safety agency leaders and towing and recovery business owners.

On the agency side, the product handles tow requests and rotation, and Autura says it gives agencies complete control over their towing program. Impound work is pulled into a single compliant system covering storage lookup, regulated fees, and lien and notification workflows. Lien handling uses state-approved lien search and notification capabilities. A separate marketplace covers how impound facilities sell unclaimed vehicles. Agencies can also see private tows logged in their jurisdiction.

The company took its current shape after a 2024 merger with TRAXERO and other acquisitions. It says many of its team members are former tow operators, impound managers, law enforcement officers, and telecommunicators. Its stated reason for the work is roadside safety.

before.name: Axon Vibe
before.description: Mobility behavior platform powering operator apps: journey detection, BIBO ticketing (built the MTA app)

paragraphs: Axon Vibe sells a smartphone-based, multi-modal mobility platform to public transport operators and authorities. The idea is to match a rider's predicted travel patterns against real-time traffic on roads and rail, then offer more efficient and less polluting travel options.

Patented location tracking predicts what people are going to do next, and psychological communication interventions are used to shift their behaviour. Riders who respond are rewarded with travel fare incentives financed by green governmental funds, plus rewards provided by local merchants. The platform is also sold to enable automatic ticketing, incentivise behaviour change and optimise customer flow management. For cities, understanding why and how people travel in real time is presented as the basis for more accurate planning.

Door-to-door journey detection powers Deutsche Bahn check-in and be-out ticketing, for example in Greater Nuremberg. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority launched its official MTA app in March 2024. Founded in 2014, the company describes a team of more than 100 software engineers, data scientists, location analytics experts, psychologists and communication specialists. Its predecessor Endoxon delivered core technology for Google Maps and was acquired by Google in 2006.

before.name: Littlepay
before.description: Contactless open-loop transit payment infrastructure for 400+ providers in 30+ countries

paragraphs: Littlepay sells payments infrastructure for transit, and public transit providers and vendors of all sizes use it to accept payments in person or online and simplify ticketing for passengers.

Open APIs allow flexible configuration of its capabilities alongside existing AFC and ABT fare collection systems. A single data platform gives operators visibility of passenger behaviour across vehicles, gates, kiosks, mobile apps and web. Risk models optimised across global volumes are meant to minimise losses from fraud and uncollected payments. Advanced PAN and PAR deny lists target card flipping fraud. Multi-operator brokerage services connect operators and agencies in a region under unified customer ticketing.

The company set out in 2016 with a vision to make contactless bank card acceptance faster, cheaper, and less complex for the public transit sector. It now describes working with over 400 transport and mobility providers in over 30 countries, powering payments on local buses, city networks and national public transport systems. One published case study describes Monterey-Salinas Transit deploying a contactless transit fare payment system in May 2021, the first of its kind in California.

quote.text: Why can a retail store set up a payment system in a matter of minutes for a few hundred dollars, while transit agencies take years and spend millions of dollars to do essentially the same thing?

before.name: CurbIQ
before.description: Curb inventory, regulation digitization and curb management for cities

paragraphs: CurbIQ sells curb management software to cities, universities and airports, giving them one place to keep curb regulations and usage data. The problem it addresses is balancing curb access among pedestrians, parking, deliveries, rideshares and vendors.

The platform pulls curb regulation and usage data from multiple sources into a single database. Records are held in curb data standards including CDS, D-TRO and CurbLR. Map overlays show when and where regulations are in effect, and the tool models what a proposed policy change would do. Data sharing runs through APIs so couriers, ride-hailing companies and navigation platforms can see the current rules.

CurbIQ was founded by Peter Richards, formerly chair of the Institute of Transportation Engineers Parking Standing Committee. The team managed the Southern California Association of Governments Curb Space Management Study. The company belongs to the Open Mobility Foundation, a nonprofit that builds open-source tools for cities. CurbIQ itself is a product of the design firm Arcadis.

paragraphs: Emovis sells tolling and mobility technology and operating services to road operators and transport agencies around the world. Its remit covers the tolling chain from roadside systems and revenue collection through enforcement and customer service.

The products bring together vehicle identification and classification, data analytics and back-office software to process large volumes of tolling transactions. An operational back office takes the data captured at the roadside and makes it accurate, enriched and ready for billing. A manual image review service pairs automated processing with human checking to validate vehicle passage records. The gantry-based Identify system reads passing vehicles using video tolling or pay by plate, so no physical barrier is needed.

Buyers are public entities and private companies that need a partner to run tolling operations. The company reports more than 850 experts worldwide and over four decades of experience. It is backed by Abertis Group, which it describes as managing 5000+ miles of motorways with over 17,000 employees. Emovis says it has helped clients in the mobility and transportation industry in more than 10 countries.

A code-free integration tool called Smart Integrate comes as standard. SmartForms builds custom forms, automates processes and captures data in real time at no extra cost. before.name: Genfare
before.description: Fareboxes, validators, TVMs, and Genfare Link cloud fare software for 400+ NA transit agencies (SPX)

paragraphs: Genfare sells fare collection systems to public transit agencies, and describes itself as a partner to transit agencies of every size across the United States and Canada for more than forty years. Its systems cover fixed route service, microtransit, paratransit, ferries, and light rail.

The company is moving its Genfare Link platform to a fully cloud-based software-as-a-service model. Transaction, ridership, and device monitoring data from fareboxes, mobile apps, e-Fare portals, and retail channels are consolidated in one central location. For riders paying with a contactless bank card or phone, existing Fast Fare fareboxes can be upgraded for open payment, or an Open Link validator can be mounted next to the farebox. The Mobile Link application and the e-Fare online ticketing system use open APIs to work with microtransit and shared ride providers.

Genfare Link is built on Amazon Web Services, with APIs linking agency platforms to each other and to riders. Alongside the hardware and software, the company sells packages for training, maintenance and repair, and technical support.

before.name: Gatekeeper Systems
before.description: Intelligent video, AI stop-arm analytics, and cloud safety platforms for transit and school districts

paragraphs: Gatekeeper Systems sells video recording and data systems for transportation, meant to make travel safer for children, passengers, and public safety personnel across several modes. The company says it uses AI, video analytics, thermal cameras, and mobile data collectors to inter-connect public transit assets within intelligent transportation systems.

Its mobile data collectors gather video and audio along with GPS tracking and door open and close events, analyzing the data on the bus itself. Those units are ruggedized and crashworthy, serving as black boxes that hold data for accident investigations. Recorders take analog and IP channels at up to 1080P and 30 frames per second, with independently selectable resolutions. Drive caddies have passed MIL SPEC 810F for shock and vibration, and a thermal system warms the hard drive to its prescribed operating temperature before writing or reading in cold weather.

Fleet software called G4 Vision centralizes system health checks, driver behavior analysis, video management, live streaming, GPS, routing and mapping, and student tracking. An Automated Lane Enforcement product for transit buses is named on the home page. The company describes a Platform-as-a-Service business model. Testimonials on that page are attributed to school district transportation directors.

In one system an agency handles scheduling and dispatch, the rider experience, fleet health, and compliance and reporting. before.name: CITYROVER
before.description: AI dashcams (EDGE/PULSE) for automated pothole and road-defect detection for public works

paragraphs: CITYROVER sells smart cameras and software that governments mount in vehicles already driving their streets, so road problems get spotted without a dedicated inspection trip. The stated aim is taking over inspection work that agencies would otherwise do by hand.

Detection happens on the camera itself, which uploads what it finds to the cloud for review. Staff get notifications carrying the location and images of the issue. The camera picks out potholes, manholes, dumped garbage, transit infrastructure problems and signs. Two other families sit beside it: PULSE for pavement rating, pavement markings and survey imagery, and COMPANION, an app for inspectors and work crews.

Government inspectors are the main users, reporting maintenance and operations issues automatically. An open API and off-the-shelf connectors move the data into systems an agency already runs. The site claims hundreds of governments as customers.

before.name: TransTrack Solutions Group
before.description: Transit performance data warehousing, BI, and automated NTD reporting (Modaxo brand)

paragraphs: TransTrack Systems writes software for public transit agencies that pulls scattered operating data into one place so performance can be watched and reported. The main application collects data from across an agency so teams can follow trends and produce the reports decisions rest on.

Much of the appeal is federal reporting: agency data is applied automatically to the required National Transit Database forms, which the company says turns most of the annual filing from weeks of work into days. A companion analytics product presents the same operating data as dashboards, reports and metrics an agency can adjust. The point of it, in the company's framing, is to replace manual spreadsheets and disconnected systems and keep the numbers behind federal funding accurate.

The firm was formed in 2002 by transit management professionals. More than twenty years on, it describes its business as helping agencies turn operating data into better decisions. Alongside the software it lists consulting work such as transit financial planning and cost analyses. The platform itself was built with transit professionals involved.

paragraphs: AngelTrax sells mobile video surveillance systems built for transportation safety. The company describes its customers as student transportation, mass transit, fleet, locomotive, and waste operations.

On a school bus, interior, exterior, stop-arm, and windshield views cover students, drivers, and transportation staff. Footage leaves the vehicle two ways, and a cellular link carries live view, active tracking, and instant notifications. Wi-Fi handles automated downloads once vehicles return to range. Video and data can be hosted by AngelTrax at its secure U.S. data center rather than handed to a third party. Its online software covers live view, downloads, vehicle location, health reporting, stop-arm workflows, and driver behavior. Driver behavior events arrive with video meant to support coaching, claims response, and accountability.

The company page dates the business to 2006. It reports 250,000 active systems operating worldwide. It also states $2.5M spent on research and development yearly. The same page describes a SOC 2 Type II-compliant data center for data security.

before.name: Blaise Transit
before.description: Demand-responsive transit dispatch and booking software for transit agencies

paragraphs: Blaise Transit sells software for running transit without a fixed route or a fixed schedule. It was built to equip municipalities, cities, transit agencies, and transit operators. One platform covers demand-responsive service, paratransit, fixed-route integrations, and private shuttles.

The system comes in three parts. Blaise Engine lets operators set the vehicles, drivers, stops, and payment options that make up a transit system. A passenger app is available on Android, iOS, and as a website, where riders book, pay, and follow live vehicle locations. A driver app supplies turn-by-turn navigation on optimized routes and a passenger manifest at each stop. A separate simulations service recommends which transit models to implement and the parameters for each service.

Blaise was started in 2018 by a small group of transit-loving engineers. The site says more than 70 communities have chosen it to optimize their transit services. It reports working with agencies serving a few hundred rides a month up to a few million. Its optimization models are described as patent pending and customizable.

The system comes in three parts. Blaise Engine lets operators set the vehicles, drivers, stops, and payment options that make up a transit system. A passenger app is available on Android, iOS, and as a website, where riders book, pay, and follow live vehicle locations. A driver app supplies turn-by-turn navigation on optimized routes and a passenger manifest at each stop. A separate simulations service recommends which transit models to implement and the parameters for each service.

Blaise was started in 2018 by a small group of transit-loving engineers. The site says more than 70 communities have chosen it to optimize their transit services. It reports working with agencies serving a few hundred rides a month up to a few million. Its optimization models are described as patent pending and customizable.

paragraphs: Aesys builds passenger information displays for intercity, regional and metropolitan rail. It also makes variable message signs carrying traffic and safety information on highways, in tunnels and in cities. At airports its flight information displays run from the runway to the baggage area. A further line covers industrial displays made to hold up in harsh environments.

Displays carrying road information are built to comply with a European standard for variable message signs. Design and production are handled internally at the Bergamo headquarters. Testing starts early, from the first stages of prototyping. Software staff have written interfaces for standard protocols such as NTCIP, DisplayML, Modbus and TLS.

The company says it has been growing since 1977. It reports over 400 employees dedicated to product excellence. Sales offices sit in Germany, Spain and the United States. Certifications listed include a quality management system under ISO 9001.

before.name: AngelTrax
before.description: Mobile video surveillance, DVRs, and MotoTrax analytics for transit, school, and municipal fleets - exhibited at CTAA EXPO 2026

paragraphs: AngelTrax sells mobile video surveillance systems built for transportation safety. The company describes its customers as student transportation, mass transit, fleet, locomotive, and waste operations.

On a school bus, interior, exterior, stop-arm, and windshield views cover students, drivers, and transportation staff. Footage leaves the vehicle two ways, and a cellular link carries live view, active tracking, and instant notifications. Wi-Fi handles automated downloads once vehicles return to range. Video and data can be hosted by AngelTrax at its secure U.S. data center rather than handed to a third party. Its online software covers live view, downloads, vehicle location, health reporting, stop-arm workflows, and driver behavior. Driver behavior events arrive with video meant to support coaching, claims response, and accountability.

The company page dates the business to 2006. It reports 250,000 active systems operating worldwide. It also states $2.5M spent on research and development yearly. The same page describes a SOC 2 Type II-compliant data center for data security.

before.name: HopSkipDrive
before.description: Vetted small-vehicle student rides supplementing district bus fleets

paragraphs: HopSkipDrive arranges rides for students who cannot be served by a traditional school bus route. The company calls itself a technology company that solves complex transportation challenges where there is a heightened need for safety, equity, and care.

Rides come through a marketplace connecting kids, older adults, or anyone needing extra support to highly vetted caregivers on wheels. The homepage says rides are licensed, regulated, and ready in six hours. Ride types span McKinney-Vento, foster care, special needs and IEPs, charter schools, general education, after school, and career and technical education. Districts also use RouteWise AI, which optimizes routes for buses and small vehicles.

Denver Public Schools is described on the site as using RouteWise AI to optimize its multimodal transportation system. Cypress-Fairbanks Independent School District decided to outsource its McKinney-Vento and a portion of foster transportation to the company. Counties, government agencies, and nonprofits are also named as groups the company supports. It traces its start to three working moms trying to get their busy kids to and from school and activities.

before.name: Gatekeeper Systems
before.description: Intelligent video, AI stop-arm analytics, and cloud safety platforms for transit and school districts - exhibited at CTAA EXPO 2026

paragraphs: Gatekeeper Systems sells video recording and data systems for transportation, meant to make travel safer for children, passengers, and public safety personnel across several modes. The company says it uses AI, video analytics, thermal cameras, and mobile data collectors to inter-connect public transit assets within intelligent transportation systems.

Its mobile data collectors gather video and audio along with GPS tracking and door open and close events, analyzing the data on the bus itself. Those units are ruggedized and crashworthy, serving as black boxes that hold data for accident investigations. Recorders take analog and IP channels at up to 1080P and 30 frames per second, with independently selectable resolutions. Drive caddies have passed MIL SPEC 810F for shock and vibration, and a thermal system warms the hard drive to its prescribed operating temperature before writing or reading in cold weather.

Fleet software called G4 Vision centralizes system health checks, driver behavior analysis, video management, live streaming, GPS, routing and mapping, and student tracking. An Automated Lane Enforcement product for transit buses is named on the home page. The company describes a Platform-as-a-Service business model. Testimonials on that page are attributed to school district transportation directors.

before.name: First Student
before.description: Contracted school bus transportation services for K-12 districts

paragraphs: First Student moves students to and from school, with a stated mission of the safest, most reliable and most efficient ride. School districts are its partners, in communities big and small.

The company reports more than 48,000 vehicles, including electric buses. It lists over 530 locations across two countries. By its own count, those buses carry 4.8 million student journeys a day. A technology platform called HALO oversees the transportation journey. One piece of it, First View, is a vehicle tracker app for parents and caregivers. Buses can also be rented for events and field trips through a charter quote.

The company says it has provided a safe and reliable experience for nearly half a century. In one award citation it was recognized in a transportation category for HALO's safety tools, predictive maintenance and real-time visibility. A mascot named Safety Dog teaches students about safe school bus behavior. The mascot travels a coast-to-coast, back-to-school tour. Its leadership team spans transportation management, technology and electrification.

paragraphs: 247Security sells video recording systems for vehicle fleets, and school bus video is the product it puts at the front of its site. Its school bus offering pairs on-vehicle cameras with cloud fleet management software. Public transit and motor coach operators are a second market listed on the site.

Video comes off the vehicle wirelessly over cellular or wi-fi rather than by pulling hard drives, and is retrieved from cloud servers. Staff can watch a bus live over a cellular link while recording continues uninterrupted. The lineup also includes a compact sensor that detects smoking and vaping devices on board. The company says its storage device carries a lifetime warranty and keeps recorded video encrypted.

Products are designed, assembled and packaged in Canada and the United States. Installation is handled by the company's own teams, which it says work on more than 3000 buses a year. Feature decisions draw on transportation directors, shop leaders and mechanics, according to the about page. Support is pitched around reaching a person on the phone rather than a call centre.

paragraphs: Motive sells fleet software and hardware as one integrated suite built around AI. The buyers are commercial fleets, which the company describes as ranging from five or ten vehicles up to companies running thousands of them.

On the safety side, cameras and AI flag more than twenty kinds of event on the road. High-confidence events go straight to managers, while a safety team reviews the low-confidence ones to remove false positives. Vehicle tracking uses real-time GPS with traffic updates and weather overlays for route planning. Compliance work such as electronic logs, driver qualification, IFTA and CSA sits in the same platform. Equipment monitoring shows what share of the time an asset is in use and how long it sits dormant. Telematics from various equipment manufacturers is centralized in a single platform.

The company points to operations running from waste services to construction. It says it was named number one in fleet management across every segment. It also cites top rankings for equipment monitoring in G2 asset tracking reports for summer 2026. Its fleet card is issued by Sutton Bank under a license from Mastercard International.

before.name: Routeware
before.description: Routing, in-cab fleet tech, and resident apps for waste operations

paragraphs: Routeware sells digital technology for waste, recycling and heavy-duty fleet operations. The buyers are private haulers and municipal fleets. The software pulls collection, customer and business operations into one place.

Its routing product lets staff densify and edit routes and optimize entire fleets. Routes can be updated and stops reassigned in real time, with automatic sequencing. Dispatch gives a single view of orders, resources, status and inventory. Helper routes are built by drag and drop and resequenced on the spot. The back-office dispatch system is tied to the on-board computers in the truck.

The company describes the setup as hardware-light and cloud-based. It lists integrations with AWS, Esri, Geotab and Samsara. Some customers run several heavy-duty fleets, including snowplows and sweeper trucks. A separate product handles medical waste from end to end. Another is recycling software built around California mandates. The company says it has worked on digital transformation in waste and recycling for over twenty years.

Its routing product lets staff densify and edit routes and optimize entire fleets. Routes can be updated and stops reassigned in real time, with automatic sequencing. Dispatch gives a single view of orders, resources, status and inventory. Helper routes are built by drag and drop and resequenced on the spot. The back-office dispatch system is tied to the on-board computers in the truck.

The company describes the setup as hardware-light and cloud-based. It lists integrations with AWS, Esri, Geotab and Samsara. Some customers run several heavy-duty fleets, including snowplows and sweeper trucks. A separate product handles medical waste from end to end. Another is recycling software built around California mandates. The company says it has worked on digital transformation in waste and recycling for over twenty years.

quote.text: With the help of Routeware, costly complexity gives way to powerful simplicity.

before.name: AMP
before.description: AI robotic sorting systems for recycling facilities (MRFs)

paragraphs: AMP designs, builds, and operates facilities that sort single-stream recycling and municipal solid waste using artificial intelligence. The buyers are waste companies and municipalities, offered sortation services and automation at scale.

The facility product, AMP ONE, is a fully automated sorting plant. It takes in single stream material, municipal solid waste, plant residue and mixed plastics and turns them into bales. Dozens of jet sorters and cameras characterize the stream continuously as it passes. Each finished bale is tagged with a bar code linked to the composition and purity of the material inside it.

For municipal solid waste, AMP states that it operates the facility itself and charges a per-ton processing rate with guaranteed diversion. The company puts typical diversion above 60 percent. It says custom plants can be operational in less than a year. Recovery of target materials is put at more than 90 percent.

quote.text: AMP ONE recovers 90%+ of target materials without touching a human hand.
