before.name: HAAS Alert
before.description: Safety Cloud digital alerting for DOT, fire and public works fleets

paragraphs: HAAS Alert sells a collision prevention service that sends real-time digital alerts warning drivers about nearby emergency vehicles and roadway hazards. Its customers are fleets that work at the roadside, including tow trucks, utility vehicles, waste management trucks, school buses and snowplows.

The system is wired to a vehicle's warning light bar or master switch, so alerting begins when crews turn on their lights and stops when they turn them off. Motorists install nothing, because alerts are broadcast directly to the navigation platforms they already use. Fleets can activate the service through three primary methods, depending on their existing setup. The company says drivers get up to 30 seconds of advance warning to slow down and move over.

The company traces its start to 2015, when co-founder and CEO Cory Hohs was almost struck by an ambulance on the road. He co-founded the business with Noah Levens and Jigar Patel. Its timeline notes that the United States Department of Homeland Security awarded $1.1 million toward development for digital alerting. It also states that digital alerting was codified and funded in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

before.name: PSTrax
before.description: Cloud checklist and compliance management: vehicle checks, SCBA, PPE, and narcotics for 1,400+ agencies

paragraphs: PSTrax sells digital inventory and asset management software built for first responders. The system tracks inspections of vehicles, stations, equipment, supplies, controlled substances and blood products.

Rather than handing over a toolkit, the company builds and implements each system for the department and to that department's specs. Systems are meant to be ready to roll out in a matter of weeks. Ongoing support for changes is unlimited and comes at no extra cost. A one-year money back guarantee is offered to customers.

PSTrax, short for Public Safety Tracking Systems, was founded by Scott Bergeron and Cliff Long in 2009. It is headquartered in Littleton, Colorado, with 22 full-time employees. The company says it serves more than 1,000 organizations worldwide. That count includes more than 850 Fire-EMS agencies across the United States, Canada and Australia. It is privately held and says it answers to customers rather than to VC firms or shareholders. It reports a 98.5% customer retention rate.

before.name: Tablet Command
before.description: Mobile incident command and response for fire/EMS departments

paragraphs: Tablet Command makes mobile incident command and response software for fire and EMS agencies. Commanders run an incident on a digital command board, dragging and dropping unit assignments.

The software is built on the iPad platform. A commander can tap and drag responding apparatus onto a scene, track progress against critical checklists, and time-stamp every maneuver and benchmark. Maps carry pre-plans and custom layers for hydrants, hospitals, landing zones, flood hazards and fire trails. The app is native and designed to run entirely independent of internet connectivity. It connects to CAD systems and integrates Esri GIS map layers, pre-plans, FireMapper and AVL.

The site reports over 250,000 incidents managed, covering everyday calls and multi-agency coordination. The product is also positioned as a complete replacement for mobile data terminals in the fire service. San Bernardino County Fire is named as using it in every front line response unit. A case study describes Stockton Fire Department turning to it as an MDT replacement and fire ground accountability tool.

before.name: Applied Information
before.description: Connected-vehicle ITS and the Glance smart-city platform: signal monitoring, preemption, school beacons

paragraphs: Applied Information makes traffic technology that turns intersections, school zones and connected vehicles into one real-time system. The customers are cities, which manage their traffic and ITS assets through a web-based application called Glance.

Glance monitors intersection cabinet equipment, reporting AC power, battery back up, cabinet flash, stop time, conflict monitor status, door switches, fan status and vehicle detectors. For emergency vehicles, an in-vehicle unit uses a cellular signal to tell the system a route has started. The system works out the route and talks wirelessly to the traffic cabinet to clear traffic ahead of the vehicle. School beacon flashers and their schedules can be viewed and controlled from anywhere. A connected vehicle product communicates over C-V2X, 4G LTE cellular and 900MHz.

The company states its hardware is designed, assembled and tested in Alpharetta, Georgia, with components meeting domestic content thresholds. A connected school bus system warns drivers approaching an active school safety zone or exceeding the speed limit. A smartphone app, Glance TravelSafely, extends the technology to residents.

quote.text: The drivers know they’ve got a green light in front of them, they know that everyone else has a red light, and they know the traffic is going to move ahead of them.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

paragraphs: First Arriving sells a real-time information platform that connects the critical systems an agency already runs. The site claims 1400+ Fire, EMS, Law Enforcement & Local Government Agencies as users. The same information shows up at the station on the big screen, in the office on a desktop, and on a tablet in the field.

The platform centralizes data from 130+ systems into one operational view. Connected sources include CAD, RMS, staffing, fleet, facilities, GIS, scheduling, training, and alerts. Alerts can be pushed with required acknowledgments so the right people act immediately. Individual user accounts and role-based views mean each member of a team sees what they need.

The law enforcement version is designed for police departments, sheriff's offices, campus safety, and agencies of all sizes. It carries things like daily shift briefings and watch commander notes. A local government version covers council meetings, facility schedules, emergency alerts, and public notices. Lobbies, public counters and reception areas are named as display locations. The company notes that its marketing division is now ResponderMAX.

before.name: CredibleMind
before.description: Behavioral health and wellbeing content, screening, and care-navigation platform deployed by public health departments, health plans, and health systems for their communities - exhibited at NatCon 2026

paragraphs: CredibleMind partners with health plans, health systems, employers, and communities to break down the barriers of stigma, navigation, and cost that keep people from mental health care. Its platform blends evidence-based self-care, early intervention, and screening-based navigation into one integrated experience.

People start with validated assessments, and each customer configures referral rules and custom questions that triage higher-acuity needs to in-network care. The catalog runs to over a dozen assessments and more than 100 content topic centers. Behind those sit more than 10,000 evidence-rated resources that the company describes as grounded in science. The experience is designed for accessibility and available in 38 languages. APIs and EHR integrations tie the platform into clinical workflows.

The company says it works with more than 150 partners and supports over 40 million lives. Its stated partners include public sector agencies and community organizations. Deryk Van Brunt is a co-founder of the company and serves as its chief executive. Marcos Athanasoulis, also a co-founder, serves as chief technology officer.

quote.text: Our team of designers, data scientists, behaviorists, content creators, and clinicians share a passion for lighting the path to better mental health, for everyone.

before.name: CHESS Health
before.description: Digital substance use disorder prevention, intervention, and recovery support platform for treatment providers, state and county health agencies, drug courts, and Medicaid plans - exhibited at NatCon 2026

roles.title: Sales Director, Public Sector & Provider SUD

paragraphs: CHESS Health sells digital health software aimed at the substance use disorder crisis, for providers, health plans, and public sector organizations. Its public sector buyers are described as state health and behavioral health departments, county, tribal and local governments, drug courts, and correctional facilities. On the clinical side the site lists SUD providers, detox facilities, hospitals and emergency departments, clinics, FQHCs, and CCBHCs. Payers listed include managed care organizations, Medicaid plans, and commercial insurance.

Connections, the patient-facing app, offers 24/7 access to peer support, meetings, and recovery tools. Patients can be signed up automatically, with every patient invited to the app through EHR integration. A second product, eIntervention, is described as streamlining referrals and access to support services for substance use and mental health. A third, eRecovery, covers patient communication, progress tracking, and 24/7 peer support.

Published case studies include a county coalition in Hancock County, Ohio expanding its reach through community engagement. In one clinic case study, 83% of new patients using the app were still in treatment against 61% of those not using it.

competitors.why: Shift scheduling and workforce management for police, corrections and 911, the direct alternative for the same agency scheduling sergeant
Public safety scheduling and readiness software competing for the same department's shift and personnel scheduling contract

paragraphs: Pace Scheduler sells a cloud-based scheduling system built for organizations that keep 24/7 schedules. Its clients include police departments, sheriff's offices, campus security, fire departments and public transportation agencies. Because that client base varies, the system is modular, so a department's site can be built with only the parts it wants.

The company says it designed the software to be easy to use without dropping the advanced features needed to maintain round-the-clock schedules. A mobile app is included, so staff can view schedules and submit or handle requests from an iOS or Android device as well as from a PC or tablet. In testimonials on the site, departments describe using it to fill shifts, request time off and balance leave banks. One says the shift bidding feature cut a process that used to take a month and a half down to four days.

Those testimonials come from agencies such as Tipp City PD in Ohio, Hudson PD in Colorado, Santa Paula PD in California and the Monroe County Sheriff's Office in Michigan, which says deputies, corrections officers and support staff all use it. Several describe replacing paper or Excel spreadsheets, and one lieutenant says the program replaced over a dozen spreadsheets. The company offers a free online demo to organizations that ask.

before.name: GovWorx
before.description: Software for first responder agencies - exhibited at IACP 2026

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "AI-Powered Solutions Helping ALL First Responders Do Their Best Work" Fetched https://www.govworx.ai. The site is branded GovWorx and the quoted headline ties it directly to the 'software for first responder agencies' description. The buyer is named precisely — 911 Emergency Communications Centers: 'We deliver AI-powered solutions that help ECCs automate tasks and strengthen, guide, and support first responders.' Named products corroborate the sector rather than a same-name firm elsewhere: the CommsCoach suite (QA and call evaluations, pre-hire testing, training and simulations, real-time call guidance) plus MedAssist for paramedics and BluAssist for law enforcement, with claimed scale of 1.2M+ evaluations monthly across 475+ customers. Own primary domain. No concerns.

paragraphs: GovWorx sells CommsCoach, an AI-powered software platform that emergency communications centers use to hire, train, evaluate and support 9-1-1 telecommunicators. It is aimed at the ECC leaders responsible for improving the performance of 9-1-1 professionals. Its modules follow a telecommunicator from candidate through career, linking HIRE, TRAIN, QA and ASSIST in one system, with PROMOTE added for choosing supervisors.

CommsCoach HIRE measures aptitude, resilience, accuracy and composure through structured testing and AI-supported scoring, with tests run onsite or remotely. QA automatically pulls every eligible call and radio transmission, matches transcripts to CAD event data and scores them against the agency's own policies. During live calls, ASSIST listens, transcribes and prompts the call-taker with the policy-specific questions the situation requires. PROMOTE is an evidence-based assessment that identifies leadership potential in supervisor candidates and pairs each result with a personalized development pathway.

An emergency communications administrator at the O'Fallon Police Department in Missouri is quoted saying call-taking compliance rose from single digits to 96% with ASSIST, APCO guidecards and complete QA. In June 2026 APCO International and GovWorx announced a partnership to bring APCO's communications protocols into CommsCoach ASSIST. In August 2026 GovWorx added NEAL, an adaptive non-emergency call handling tool that escalates to a human telecommunicator whenever judgment is needed.

paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

paragraphs: RapidSOS connects public safety agencies, enterprises and large numbers of consumer and corporate devices so emergency information reaches responders. The company states it partners with over 250 enterprise companies and 23,500 public safety agencies.

The premise is that connected systems can share information with responders even before a 911 call is placed. One police department describes adopting a module built around AI-powered live text translation, transcription and call summarization. In an Atlanta deployment, translation covered over 37 languages by voice and over 200 by text. Another center is described using Harmony AI to handle non-emergency calls.

The homepage says agencies and enterprises on the network safeguard over 99% of the country. Published case studies sort customers into categories such as connected vehicles and telematics. One partner statement on the site is attributed to a VP of Safety at Norfolk Southern. A documented problem it addresses is waiting up to ten minutes for a translator on a 911 call.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

before.name: MCM Technology LLC
before.description: Public safety asset and fleet management software - exhibited at IACP 2026, IAFC FRI 2026

paragraphs: MCM sells software that helps public safety agencies stay ahead of risk, increase safety and maintain compliance by managing assets, certifications, maintenance and inspections in one connected platform. The product is framed as intelligent operational readiness for public safety.

Asset tracking keeps a full lifecycle history from procurement through retirement. Issuance and chain of custody let staff issue serialized assets and consumable inventory in the same transaction. Work orders are created automatically when an inspection fails. Custom templates can be built for any inspection type, including vehicles, weapons, jump bags, respirators, facilities and sites. An open REST API is offered for connecting other systems, and the integrations page claims to be the only platform that integrates directly with major radio manufacturers.

The company cites 300+ public safety agencies nationwide. For fire agencies the aim is to keep apparatus, gear and crew inspection-ready at every station and before the next call comes in. For government and utilities it gives full asset visibility and tracks grant-funded resources. A news post announces Anthony Rotoli as new CEO. Agencies that would rather not administer the system themselves can buy managed services, pitched as maximum impact without the administrative overhead.

Named products for community communication include Versaterm CommunityConnect, Versaterm CommunityReport, Versaterm CallTriage, and Versaterm Public Portal. Versaterm IAPro and Versaterm BlueTeam cover professional standards work, alongside professional standards training. Two further named products are Versaterm Mindbase and Versaterm EIPro.

DroneSense by Versaterm handles drone operations, and Glendale Police uses Versaterm DroneSense flight management software with the SafeSky traffic awareness app. The company says it has worked with agencies for over 47 years. The Sumner County Sheriff's Office won first place in the 2026 Versaterm Innovation Awards for its use of technology and data in its school resource officer division.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "Computer Information Systems, Inc. – Future Technology Today" www.cis.com (HTTP 200) is the site of Computer Information Systems, Inc., tagline 'Future Technology Today', and it hits all three products in the description verbatim: 'The CIS Computer Aided Dispatch (CAD) System is a state-of-the-art program that enables dispatchers to efficiently and effectively manage incidents'; 'The CIS Records Management System (RMS) automates the records management functions of an agency'; and 'Jail Management System (JMS) provides comprehensive inmate management, facilities management, billing, and special programs.' Operating since 1985, serving police departments, sheriffs' offices and 911/fire centers across North America. Disambiguation check, since 'CIS' is a heavily contested acronym: this is NOT the Center for Internet Security (cisecurity.org) and NOT any other CIS - the domain's own pages ('Systems', 'Services', 'About' under cis.com) all carry the 'Computer Information Systems, Inc.' name with public safety content. One ownership note that does not change the verdict: a January 2025 announcement covers CIS partnering with investor Arcadea Group, but CIS retains its own brand and its own domain, so cis.com remains the correct record - do not repoint this at Arcadea.

paragraphs: CentralSquare Technologies sells software to public agencies, from dispatch centers to city halls. On the public safety side, its suite runs from computer aided dispatch and NG911 call handling through to jail management and analytics. On the administration side, the company says public administrators in over 8,000 communities use it for finance, HR, payroll, asset management, permitting and tax collection.

Public Safety Suite Enterprise connects 911, CAD, RMS, Mobile and Jail in a single platform. A version called Public Safety Suite Pro is designed for small and mid-sized agencies that want one vendor rather than several systems. Vertex NG911 Call Handling gives 911 centers a single platform for voice, text, video and caller location. Vertex also carries built-in text translation and transcription for more than 150 languages, which the company says runs in under 10 seconds. The company says it secures cloud data against cyberattacks through a partnership with Amazon Web Services.

The homepage counts more than 8,000 agencies nationwide as customers. Customers named on the site include the California Highway Patrol. Case studies include the Edgar County 911 team, whose partnership with CentralSquare serves a community of 16,000 residents. Morgan County 911 in Alabama is featured for upgrading to Vertex NG911 Call Handling.

before.name: Aurelian
before.description: AI voice agents answering non-emergency calls for 911 centers

paragraphs: Aurelian builds software for the 911 centers known as public safety answering points. One of its two products answers non-emergency calls instantly, so callers are not left on hold. The other sits with call-takers during emergencies and gives real-time, context-aware guidance without taking control.

The automated line resolves routine calls on its own. It detects and escalates emergencies to a person. During live calls, the guidance tool surfaces the relevant SOP checklist for the incident. It also flags missing information before the call ends. The company says the system learns a center's workflows, SOPs, and systems in order to support the full call flow. Aurelian states that humans remain in control of emergencies and decision-making.

The customers page says PSAPs around the country use Aurelian to cut non-emergency workload and return time to their teams. Published stories include Hamilton County 911 automating more than 300 non-emergency calls a day. The about page says the founders, Max and James, were building call automation technology for hair salons before starting the company. That insight led them to pivot to public safety and build for PSAPs.

paragraphs: NiCE sells Evidencentral, a cloud-based digital evidence management platform for public safety and justice agencies. The platform is meant to manage data from the moment an incident happens until a case is closed and prosecuted. For emergency communications centers that means incident recording and reconstruction, voice-to-text transcription, quality assurance and coaching, and PSAP performance reporting.

NiCE Inform automates incident reconstruction, evidence production, quality assurance and real-time performance metrics reporting. NiCE Investigate then brings evidence and associated information to investigators, patrol officers and criminal justice partners, with the stated aim of breaking down information silos. Further along the process, NiCE Justice and NiCE Defense help prosecution, defense and courts manage growing volumes of digital evidence. An Evidencentral Marketplace of technology vendors is designed to make it simpler and faster for emergency communications, law enforcement and criminal justice agencies to bring evidence together.

A customer story on the page comes from British Transport Police, attributed to its Senior Project Management for Digital Policing. The company describes the platform as powered by artificial intelligence and offers demos through the site.

paragraphs: Aesys builds passenger information displays for intercity, regional and metropolitan rail. It also makes variable message signs carrying traffic and safety information on highways, in tunnels and in cities. At airports its flight information displays run from the runway to the baggage area. A further line covers industrial displays made to hold up in harsh environments.

Displays carrying road information are built to comply with a European standard for variable message signs. Design and production are handled internally at the Bergamo headquarters. The company says it has been growing since 1977. It reports over 400 employees dedicated to product excellence. Sales offices sit in Germany, Spain and the United States. Certifications listed include a quality management system under ISO 9001.

before.name: AngelTrax
before.description: Mobile video surveillance, DVRs, and MotoTrax analytics for transit, school, and municipal fleets

paragraphs: AngelTrax sells mobile video surveillance systems built for transportation safety. The company describes its customers as student transportation, mass transit, fleet, locomotive, and waste operations.

On a school bus, interior, exterior, stop-arm, and windshield views cover students, drivers, and transportation staff. Footage leaves the vehicle two ways, and a cellular link carries live view, active tracking, and instant notifications. Wi-Fi handles automated downloads once vehicles return to range. Video and data can be hosted by AngelTrax at its secure U.S. data center rather than handed to a third party. Its online software covers live view, downloads, vehicle location, health reporting, stop-arm workflows, and driver behavior. Driver behavior events arrive with video meant to support coaching, claims response, and accountability.

The company page dates the business to 2006. It reports 250,000 active systems operating worldwide. It also states $2.5M spent on research and development yearly. The same page describes a SOC 2 Type II-compliant data center for data security.

before.name: Blaise Transit
before.description: Demand-responsive transit dispatch and booking software for transit agencies

paragraphs: Blaise Transit sells software for running transit without a fixed route or a fixed schedule. It was built to equip municipalities, cities, transit agencies, and transit operators. One platform covers demand-responsive service, paratransit, fixed-route integrations, and private shuttles.

The system comes in three parts. Blaise Engine lets operators set the vehicles, drivers, stops, and payment options that make up a transit system. A passenger app is available on Android, iOS, and as a website, where riders book, pay, and follow live vehicle locations. A driver app supplies turn-by-turn navigation on optimized routes and a passenger manifest at each stop. A separate simulations service recommends which transit models to implement and the parameters for each service.

Blaise was started in 2018 by a small group of transit-loving engineers. The site says more than 70 communities have chosen it to optimize their transit services. It reports working with agencies serving a few hundred rides a month up to a few million. Its optimization models are described as patent pending and customizable.

before.name: CITYROVER
before.description: AI dashcams (EDGE/PULSE) for automated pothole and road-defect detection for public works

paragraphs: CITYROVER sells smart cameras and software that governments mount in vehicles already driving their streets, so road problems get spotted without a dedicated inspection trip. The stated aim is taking over inspection work that agencies would otherwise do by hand.

Detection happens on the camera itself, which uploads what it finds to the cloud for review. Staff get notifications carrying the location and images of the issue. The camera picks out potholes, manholes, dumped garbage, transit infrastructure problems and signs. Two other families sit beside it: PULSE for pavement rating, pavement markings and survey imagery, and COMPANION, an app for inspectors and work crews.

Government inspectors are the main users, reporting maintenance and operations issues automatically. An open API and off-the-shelf connectors move the data into systems an agency already runs. The site claims hundreds of governments as customers.

before.name: Spare
before.description: AI microtransit and ADA paratransit operations: scheduling, dispatch, rider app, analytics

paragraphs: Spare sells operations software that a public transit agency runs its service on. The modes it covers include paratransit, microtransit and fixed route, along with asset management.

In one system an agency handles scheduling and dispatch, the rider experience, fleet health, and compliance and reporting. Because paratransit trips are often contracted out, the platform pulls trips from different providers into one place. Eligibility applications and rider records are digitized, which the company says speeds up the review process. On the fixed route side, an agency can plan service, publish a GTFS feed, build schedules and run live operations together. A voice assistant answers rider calls for bookings, arrival times and common questions.

The platform is described as built to meet ADA, NTD and grant reporting requirements. It connects through open APIs, GTFS, AVL feeds and single sign-on rather than replacing what a technology team already runs. Spare puts its reach at more than 230 communities. Its fixed route page describes coordinating a large event shuttle for LA Metro.

before.name: TransTrack Solutions Group
before.description: Transit performance data warehousing, BI, and automated NTD reporting (Modaxo brand)

paragraphs: TransTrack Systems writes software for public transit agencies that pulls scattered operating data into one place so performance can be watched and reported. The main application collects data from across an agency so teams can follow trends and produce the reports decisions rest on.

Much of the appeal is federal reporting: agency data is applied automatically to the required National Transit Database forms, which the company says turns most of the annual filing from weeks of work into days. A companion analytics product presents the same operating data as dashboards, reports and metrics an agency can adjust. The point of it, in the company's framing, is to replace manual spreadsheets and disconnected systems and keep the numbers behind federal funding accurate.

The firm was formed in 2002 by transit management professionals. More than twenty years on, it describes its business as helping agencies turn operating data into better decisions. Alongside the software it lists consulting work such as transit financial planning and cost analyses. The platform itself was built with transit professionals involved.

before.name: Gatekeeper Systems
before.description: Intelligent video, AI stop-arm analytics, and cloud safety platforms for transit and school districts

paragraphs: Gatekeeper Systems sells video recording and data systems for transportation, meant to make travel safer for children, passengers, and public safety personnel across several modes. The company says it uses AI, video analytics, thermal cameras, and mobile data collectors to inter-connect public transit assets within intelligent transportation systems.

Its mobile data collectors gather video and audio along with GPS tracking and door open and close events, analyzing the data on the bus itself. Those units are ruggedized and crashworthy, serving as black boxes that hold data for accident investigations. Recorders take analog and IP channels at up to 1080P and 30 frames per second, with independently selectable resolutions. Drive caddies have passed MIL SPEC 810F for shock and vibration, and a thermal system warms the hard drive to its prescribed operating temperature before writing or reading in cold weather.

Fleet software called G4 Vision centralizes system health checks, driver behavior analysis, video management, live streaming, GPS, routing and mapping, and student tracking. before.name: AngelTrax
before.description: Mobile video surveillance, DVRs, and MotoTrax analytics for transit, school, and municipal fleets - exhibited at CTAA EXPO 2026

paragraphs: AngelTrax sells mobile video surveillance systems built for transportation safety. The company describes its customers as student transportation, mass transit, fleet, locomotive, and waste operations.

On a school bus, interior, exterior, stop-arm, and windshield views cover students, drivers, and transportation staff. Footage leaves the vehicle two ways, and a cellular link carries live view, active tracking, and instant notifications. Wi-Fi handles automated downloads once vehicles return to range. Video and data can be hosted by AngelTrax at its secure U.S. data center rather than handed to a third party. Its online software covers live view, downloads, vehicle location, health reporting, stop-arm workflows, and driver behavior. Driver behavior events arrive with video meant to support coaching, claims response, and accountability.

The company page dates the business to 2006. It reports 250,000 active systems operating worldwide. It also states $2.5M spent on research and development yearly. The same page describes a SOC 2 Type II-compliant data center for data security.

paragraphs: Samsara sells a platform to organizations that run vehicles and equipment, pitched on improving safety, lowering costs and changing how operations work. For fleets it covers live GPS tracking, vehicle diagnostics, fuel analytics and compliance reporting. The company presents this as one platform working across every part of an operation rather than separate tools.

Its cameras pair safety detections with video that managers can pull on demand. The company says the system watches for drowsiness, distraction, tailgating and forward collision risk. It states that these are caught in real time and trigger an in-cab alert before a manager is involved. A multicamera option adds up to four auxiliary HD feeds for visibility around the vehicle. A separate site product brings third-party cameras at facilities into a cloud dashboard for onboarding and troubleshooting.

The camera pages list transportation and logistics, field services, construction, public sector and essential services among the industries served. For school districts the company describes arm-mounted cameras that enforce school bus stop-arm compliance during pickups and drop-offs. Among its customer stories is one saying the City of El Paso recovered $1.3M in assets and reduced accidents by 29%. A site camera gateway is listed as compliant with the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019.

before.name: HopSkipDrive
before.description: Vetted small-vehicle student rides supplementing district bus fleets

paragraphs: HopSkipDrive arranges rides for students who cannot be served by a traditional school bus route. The company calls itself a technology company that solves complex transportation challenges where there is a heightened need for safety, equity, and care.

Rides come through a marketplace connecting kids, older adults, or anyone needing extra support to highly vetted caregivers on wheels. The homepage says rides are licensed, regulated, and ready in six hours. Ride types span McKinney-Vento, foster care, special needs and IEPs, charter schools, general education, after school, and career and technical education. Districts also use RouteWise AI, which optimizes routes for buses and small vehicles.

Denver Public Schools is described on the site as using RouteWise AI to optimize its multimodal transportation system. Cypress-Fairbanks Independent School District decided to outsource its McKinney-Vento and a portion of foster transportation to the company. Counties, government agencies, and nonprofits are also named as groups the company supports. It traces its start to three working moms trying to get their busy kids to and from school and activities.

before.name: 247Security
before.description: School bus camera and DVR surveillance systems for districts

paragraphs: 247Security sells video recording systems for vehicle fleets, and school bus video is the product it puts at the front of its site. Its school bus offering pairs on-vehicle cameras with cloud fleet management software. Public transit and motor coach operators are a second market listed on the site.

Video comes off the vehicle wirelessly over cellular or wi-fi rather than by pulling hard drives, and is retrieved from cloud servers. Staff can watch a bus live over a cellular link while recording continues uninterrupted. The lineup also includes a compact sensor that detects smoking and vaping devices on board. The company says its storage device carries a lifetime warranty and keeps recorded video encrypted.

Products are designed, assembled and packaged in Canada and the United States. Installation is handled by the company's own teams, which it says work on more than 3000 buses a year. Feature decisions draw on transportation directors, shop leaders and mechanics, according to the about page. Support is pitched around reaching a person on the phone rather than a call centre.

before.name: Routeware
before.description: Routing, in-cab fleet tech, and resident apps for waste operations

paragraphs: Routeware sells digital technology for waste, recycling and heavy-duty fleet operations. The buyers are private haulers and municipal fleets. The software pulls collection, customer and business operations into one place.

Its routing product lets staff densify and edit routes and optimize entire fleets. Routes can be updated and stops reassigned in real time, with automatic sequencing. Dispatch gives a single view of orders, resources, status and inventory. Helper routes are built by drag and drop and resequenced on the spot. The back-office dispatch system is tied to the on-board computers in the truck.

The company describes the setup as hardware-light and cloud-based. It lists integrations with AWS, Esri, Geotab and Samsara. Some customers run several heavy-duty fleets, including snowplows and sweeper trucks. A separate product handles medical waste from end to end. Another is recycling software built around California mandates. The company says it has worked on digital transformation in waste and recycling for over twenty years.

before.name: AMP
before.description: AI robotic sorting systems for recycling facilities (MRFs)

paragraphs: AMP designs, builds, and operates facilities that sort single-stream recycling and municipal solid waste using artificial intelligence. The buyers are waste companies and municipalities, offered sortation services and automation at scale.

The facility product, AMP ONE, is a fully automated sorting plant. It takes in single stream material, municipal solid waste, plant residue and mixed plastics and turns them into bales. Dozens of jet sorters and cameras characterize the stream continuously as it passes. Each finished bale is tagged with a bar code linked to the composition and purity of the material inside it.

For municipal solid waste, AMP states that it operates the facility itself and charges a per-ton processing rate with guaranteed diversion. The company puts typical diversion above 60 percent. It says custom plants can be operational in less than a year. Recovery of target materials is put at more than 90 percent.

before.name: Highland Electric Fleets
before.description: Electric school bus fleet-as-a-service subscriptions for districts

paragraphs: Highland Electric Fleets sells fleet electrification as a service to school districts, municipalities and fleet operators. The company was founded in 2019.

Customers hand over the whole job, and Highland plans, procures, implements and optimizes the electric fleet on their behalf. A performance guarantee reimburses customers for down time if the fleet is not charged and route-ready. The commercial pitch is that an electric fleet can be operated at or below the cost of running a diesel one. Highland also secures grants and incentives on behalf of the agencies it works with.

The company serves as the Official Electric School Bus Provider of the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games and Team USA. It points to vehicle-to-grid work and to managing some of the largest electric school bus fleets in the country. Maintenance figures cited on the site come from Twin Rivers Unified School District, which operates 58 EV buses. The site also counts the states where it has operational and contracted projects.

before.name: BibliU
before.description: Digital textbook and courseware delivery platform for colleges, universities, and school districts - exhibited at NACUBO 2026

paragraphs: BibliU sells a course materials platform to colleges and universities, automating the workflow behind digital textbooks and courseware. It also runs campus stores, pairing that content with physical and online retail.

The platform comes in three named parts: Learn, Engage and Automate. Faculty choose titles and adaptive courseware from thousands of publishers and open educational resources, so the selection stays with academics. The company says the access model cuts textbook costs by 30 to 50 percent. Students can read on any device, online or off. Staff get reporting that tracks content usage and student engagement. A separate procurement option is built for libraries, with flexible pricing and broad title access.

The site says more than 170 institutions worldwide use the company. Dual credit students are called out as one group served, with the same first-day access to required materials. Dave Sherwood is co-founder and chief executive. He started the company while at Oxford University. A case studies page collects customer stories from across higher education.

quote.text: The future of higher education is about ensuring all students have affordable access to their class content.

before.name: Lightspeed Systems
before.description: Web filtering and student safety monitoring for school districts - exhibited at CoSN 2026

paragraphs: Lightspeed Systems sells a connected platform of K-12 edtech products that give schools visibility and control across safety, security, compliance, device management, and analytics. Its filter covers every digital interaction on and off the network, protecting students from cyber risks and distractions while keeping access and compliance in place.

Filtering is enforced on the device itself, with an on-device SmartAgent and SmartShield DNS filtering covering school-managed, BYOD, and IoT devices. Lightspeed Alert monitors online activity, flags concerning behaviors, and enables intervention before a tragedy occurs. Those alerts are backed by round-the-clock monitoring from the company's own safety specialists. Lightspeed Classroom gives teachers visibility into and control over student activity to minimize distractions and maximize instructional time. Lightspeed StopIt is an anonymous reporting system for safety, misconduct, or compliance concerns. An analytics product shows granular app and device usage down to the grade and student level.

The company states that 28 of the 50 largest US school districts use its software, naming Los Angeles Unified, Houston ISD, Miami-Dade County Public Schools, and Fairfax County Public Schools. It puts the wider count at 31,000 schools around the world. The filter is described as designed for CIPA, FERPA, and NIST-aligned environments, with exportable audit trails and long-term retention.

before.name: Senstar
before.description: Perimeter intrusion detection and fence sensors for airports and utilities

paragraphs: Senstar makes security systems for protecting infrastructure and facilities. The portfolio runs across video management, video analytics, access control and perimeter intrusion detection sensors. Products are designed, manufactured and tested in North America.

Perimeter sensors mount on the fence, sit above ground or lie buried, and are meant to locate intruders before they enter a secure area. The MultiSensor unit packs short-range radar, an image sensor, dual PIR, an accelerometer and a high frequency sensor into one device. An embedded engine weighs the data from each of those sensors to decide whether an event is a threat. On the software side, Senstar Symphony is a modular platform for security management and data intelligence. It works with analog and IP cameras, encoders, DVRs and other video devices from many manufacturers.

The company organizes its work by sector, pointing to electrical utility assets exposed to service interruptions from vandalism, theft and targeted attacks. Water treatment plants, pumping stations and storage tanks are another market it names. It states over 40 years of experience working with correctional institutions. A news item on the site reports quarterly financial results for Senstar Technologies Corporation, listed on NASDAQ.

before.name: PaymentWorks
before.description: Supplier onboarding and payee identity verification preventing payments fraud for gov and higher-ed - exhibited at GFOA 2026

paragraphs: PaymentWorks sells software that organizations use to create and maintain vendor records inside their ERP. The company describes the platform as a front door to the ERP that combines vendor onboarding and maintenance, ACH risk transfer, and check-to-digital payment conversion. It is sold into healthcare, higher education, K-12, state and local government, and enterprise.

Each vendor is vetted through what the company calls a proprietary onboarding system before a payment is approved. That onboarding sits on top of a payee network the site puts at more than 1.5 million authenticated payees. Compliance work is automated alongside it, covering sanctions checks, continuous monitoring, W9 and 1099 information, and audit trails. The site states that ACH payments made through the platform are indemnified, with additional coverage available.

Published case studies include the University of North Texas. Another describes a county that fell victim to a $2.5M scam after a request to change vendor banking details. The company says it offers a payments security warranty for fraudulent payments. Its about page introduces a leadership team including a co-founder whose patent work in data management led to the founding of the company.

before.name: Alertus Technologies
before.description: Emergency mass notification hardware and software for schools and agencies - exhibited at EDUCAUSE 2026

paragraphs: Alertus Technologies sells emergency notification hardware and software that organizations install to warn everyone on a site at once. The company positions itself as a single source for mass emergency notification systems and critical communication needs. Its stated goal is to help colleges and universities, K-12 schools, corporations and government organizations solve unified mass notification problems.

The approach is network based, using an organization's existing IP network to turn VoIP phones into alerting devices. Hardware fills the gaps, including a wall-mounted alerting device meant for places with no existing notification endpoints. Outdoor coverage is handled by high power speaker arrays.

The company traces its origin to 2001, when an F3 tornado ripped through the University of Maryland campus. Alertus was founded the following year. It reports serving more than 2,500 organizations across more than 40 countries. Those customers are described as spanning higher education, K-12, industrial, corporate, healthcare, government and military sectors.

before.name: Prepared
before.description: Assistive AI for 911 centers: transcription, translation, text-to-911, and video

paragraphs: Prepared builds assistive artificial intelligence for 911 centers, aimed at the people who answer emergency calls and send help. The company states that it is now the intelligence layer of Axon 911, an emergency communications platform it describes as covering the full lifecycle of a call.

During a call the software transcribes speech as it happens, captures details automatically, and translates, so staff can watch the caller rather than the keyboard. Incoming audio is translated automatically in more than 40 languages, according to the homepage. The call-taking page claims support for over 200 languages for callers who do not speak English. Call-takers can also request a livestream from the caller to see the scene. A separate voice assistant answers non-emergency lines and converses with callers in English or Spanish.

Buyers are public safety answering points, the centers that take 911 calls. Prepared describes the product as a cloud based platform laid over existing systems, with no rip and replace required. Supervisors get automated quality assurance and keyword triggers for visibility into the operation. Its chief executive, Michael Chime, appears in a recorded discussion with three 911 leaders about non-emergency calls.

quote.text: Assistive intelligence, built for the people on the headset.

before.name: Intrado Life & Safety
before.description: 911 call routing, Viper call handling and NG911 for PSAPs

paragraphs: Intrado sells call handling and management systems for emergency response. It describes itself as the connective tissue that gets the right help to the right location as quickly as possible.

Alongside the call center products, one line keeps employees safe wherever they work while meeting state and federal regulations. Another covers incident management for schools from prevention through response and recovery. For carriers, call routing, location and data products connect subscribers to emergency services and keep providers compliant. Network services are offered to improve call routing and data sharing and to deliver on i3 compliance. ECaTS, the Emergency Call Tracking System, generates descriptive reports from 9-1-1 call data.

The company puts its history in the emergency services industry at 45 years. That history includes acquisitions of Lucent Public Safety, Positron Public Safety Systems, ECaTS, 911 ETC and 911 Enable. Headquarters are in Longmont, Colorado, with a manufacturing site in Montreal, Quebec. The company reports approximately 950 employees worldwide, most of them in the Longmont and Montreal regions.

before.name: Perry Weather
before.description: Weather safety platform: WBGT heat monitoring, lightning alerts, stations and sirens for parks and athletics

paragraphs: Perry Weather sells a weather safety platform that pairs monitoring hardware at a customer site with automated alerting, so an entire staff works from the same reading of conditions. The buyers it names are schools, cities, golf clubs, and industrial firms.

Stations at the customer location measure heat stress, lightning, precipitation, wind, and air quality, refreshing every five minutes in the mobile app and dashboard. Each organization writes its own thresholds and decides who gets notified when one is crossed. Alerts can go to phones or to an outdoor siren system. Countdown timers mark the moment it is safe to resume play or work. All-clears go out automatically once the threat has passed.

Colin Perry founded the company in 2013. It reports more than 5,000 organizations nationwide as customers. It also counts over 200 million alerts sent, covering hazards from heat stress to lightning. Arthur Ventures led a $15M Series B. The stated markets run across athletics, golf, parks and recreation, energy, and airports.

before.name: DailyPay
before.description: Earned wage access platform for employers - exhibited at NACo 2026

paragraphs: DailyPay sells on-demand pay, a way for employees to reach wages they have already earned before the regular payday. The buyer is the employer, and the pitch is a benefit that helps with recruiting, retention, and engagement.

The service sits on top of an employer's existing payroll and is described as requiring little change to payroll processes. It connects to the human capital management, payroll, banking, and benefits applications a company already runs. Employees can reach up to 100% of their available earnings when an unexpected expense lands. Transfers and earned pay appear together in one app.

The company timeline records a launch in the United Kingdom. That same history lists a Series C round of $55 million. It has also launched DailyPay Tips, which gives workers access to their gratuities. The chief executive is described as having most recently served as chief financial officer of Uber.

before.name: HopSkipDrive
before.description: Vetted small-vehicle student rides supplementing district bus fleets - exhibited at NAPT Summit 2026

paragraphs: HopSkipDrive arranges rides for students who cannot be served by a traditional school bus route. The company calls itself a technology company that solves complex transportation challenges where there is a heightened need for safety, equity, and care.

Rides come through a marketplace connecting kids, older adults, or anyone needing extra support to highly vetted caregivers on wheels. The homepage says rides are licensed, regulated, and ready in six hours. Ride types span McKinney-Vento, foster care, special needs and IEPs, charter schools, general education, after school, and career and technical education. Districts also use RouteWise AI, which optimizes routes for buses and small vehicles.

Denver Public Schools is described on the site as using RouteWise AI to optimize its multimodal transportation system. Cypress-Fairbanks Independent School District decided to outsource its McKinney-Vento and a portion of foster transportation to the company. Counties, government agencies, and nonprofits are also named as groups the company supports. It traces its start to three working moms trying to get their busy kids to and from school and activities.

before.name: K16 Solutions
before.description: Scaffold platform for LMS migration, course archiving, and data warehousing across LMS, SIS, and CRM systems at colleges and universities - exhibited at EDUCAUSE 2026

paragraphs: K16 Solutions sells data software to colleges and universities, prying campus information out of the systems that hold it and handing it back in usable shape. Everything runs on one patented platform called Scaffold, spanning data warehousing, live LMS course backup, and student data archiving. A fourth product moves online course content from one learning management system to another.

The warehouse product connects to a campus LMS, SIS, CRM, and ERP through public and private APIs. Data lands in a structure specific to higher education, so a student, a course, and an enrollment get defined once instead of differently in every report. The copy lives in the institution's own governed environment, built on Snowflake and hosted on AWS. Staff can ask in plain language, and the SQL the system writes is shown rather than hidden.

Campus customers named on the site include San Diego State University. The company reports more than 12 million courses archived, and says its founders worked together for over 18 years across multiple higher education institutions. For institutions facing audits, it lists ISO 27001 certification by Schellman, SOC 2 Type II, data masking, and FERPA-aligned handling of student records.

before.name: EnergyHub
before.description: DERMS and virtual power plant programs for utilities including public power

paragraphs: EnergyHub sells utilities software for building virtual power plants, helping them scale VPPs to manage load growth and renewables. The resources involved are customer-side devices such as connected thermostats, solar and storage systems, and electric vehicles.

A single platform holds all of a utility's distributed energy resources. Control runs year-round and across resource types, based on price signals and customer rates. The stated aims are to relieve congestion, protect assets, and defer infrastructure investments. The company also points to a deep partner ecosystem behind the platform.

EnergyHub says it has been delivering load control programs since 2009. One customer story describes work with National Grid on a pay-for-performance residential battery program in Massachusetts. Another describes a thermostat demand response program with Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator to reduce peak summer load. That program enrolled more than 100,000 homes within six months. EnergyHub is an independent subsidiary of Alarm.com, listed on Nasdaq as ALRM. A newsroom item reports its acquisition of Resideo Grid Services.

before.name: Eventeny
before.description: Event management SaaS: vendor applications, ticketing, maps, and sponsors for festivals and city events

paragraphs: Eventeny sells event management software that makes it easier to manage vendors, volunteers, attendees, sponsors and maps in one place. The platform is used for festivals, conferences, expos, markets, parades and community gatherings.

Organizers build maps from scratch or on Google Maps with a drag-and-drop event mapping tool. Booths are assigned and spaces connected to tickets from that same place. Vendor and artist applications move through flexible workflows with built-in jury tools. Ticketing covers sales, upgrades and guest check-in with QR codes. Volunteer shifts can be scheduled, team leads assigned, and the crew contacted in one place. Sponsor packages can be customized to fit an event's needs.

Eventeny was started by two founders, Aly Hussaini and Nausheen Punjani. The company says its product marketplace hosts over 4,000 small business owners around the country. Its homepage says more than 2,550,000 users in five or more countries are on Eventeny. It reports over 34,000 events hosted on the platform. Case studies include the City of Suwanee, whose small event team was hosting more than 40 events a year with a primarily paper-based system.

paragraphs: Accela sells software that government agencies use to run permitting, licensing, and asset management from a single system. Its applications are built for individual government service workflows and can operate together or be deployed only where an agency needs them.

For building departments, intake, plan review, inspections, and permit issuance sit in one workflow rather than in separate disconnected steps. Residents and businesses who encounter Accela through a local agency are directed to that agency rather than to the company.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "AI-Powered Solutions Helping ALL First Responders Do Their Best Work" Fetched https://www.govworx.ai. The site is branded GovWorx and the quoted headline ties it directly to the 'software for first responder agencies' description. The buyer is named precisely — 911 Emergency Communications Centers: 'We deliver AI-powered solutions that help ECCs automate tasks and strengthen, guide, and support first responders.' Named products corroborate the sector rather than a same-name firm elsewhere: the CommsCoach suite (QA and call evaluations, pre-hire testing, training and simulations, real-time call guidance) plus MedAssist for paramedics and BluAssist for law enforcement, with claimed scale of 1.2M+ evaluations monthly across 475+ customers. Own primary domain. No concerns.

paragraphs: GovWorx sells CommsCoach, an AI-powered software platform that emergency communications centers use to hire, train, evaluate and support 9-1-1 telecommunicators. It is aimed at the ECC leaders responsible for improving the performance of 9-1-1 professionals. Its modules follow a telecommunicator from candidate through career, linking HIRE, TRAIN, QA and ASSIST in one system, with PROMOTE added for choosing supervisors.

CommsCoach HIRE measures aptitude, resilience, accuracy and composure through structured testing and AI-supported scoring, with tests run onsite or remotely. QA automatically pulls every eligible call and radio transmission, matches transcripts to CAD event data and scores them against the agency's own policies. During live calls, ASSIST listens, transcribes and prompts the call-taker with the policy-specific questions the situation requires. PROMOTE is an evidence-based assessment that identifies leadership potential in supervisor candidates and pairs each result with a personalized development pathway.

An emergency communications administrator at the O'Fallon Police Department in Missouri is quoted saying call-taking compliance rose from single digits to 96% with ASSIST, APCO guidecards and complete QA. In June 2026 APCO International and GovWorx announced a partnership to bring APCO's communications protocols into CommsCoach ASSIST. In August 2026 GovWorx added NEAL, an adaptive non-emergency call handling tool that escalates to a human telecommunicator whenever judgment is needed.

paragraphs: Niche Technology sells NicheRMS365, a records management system for police agencies, which use it to share information and eliminate siloed systems. The company says the system captures every aspect of policing from the front line to the courtroom. It describes the product as designed for multi-agency use and calls large projects its specialty.

Sworn officers in over 180 agencies worldwide use NicheRMS365. Recent announcements on the site include South Yorkshire Police, which plans to implement NicheRMS365 to modernize crime recording and strengthen data integrity. Durham Constabulary and Warwickshire Police have each selected the system as a platform that centralizes operational data. The Toronto Police Service chose it as its records management system. Orange County, New York won a 2025 Government Experience Award from the Center for Digital Government for its NicheRMS project.

Founded in 1992, Niche Technology is a private Canadian corporation based in Winnipeg, Manitoba, with additional offices in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom. It is wholly owned by its founders, who remain active in day-to-day operations. In the United States, NicheRMS365 is available to federal agencies through the General Services Administration Information Technology Schedule 70. It is also offered through the New York State Umbrella Contract and the Dell National Government Contract.

before.name: Bamboo Health
before.description: Care coordination and PDMP network software (PMP AWARxE, OpenBeds) for states, counties, and health systems (Appriss lineage)

paragraphs: Bamboo Health sells software that joins behavioral and physical health data into a longitudinal patient record and places it inside the systems clinicians already work in. Its audiences include community and behavioral health providers and federally qualified health centers. Accountable care organizations and other provider groups are addressed separately.

Alerts are driven by admission, discharge and transfer feeds, and care navigation can be started from inside an electronic health record. For people with substance use disorder, prescription drug monitoring program data and alerts are used to flag risk and guide patients toward care. Care navigators also review rosters by hand to find high utilizers whose behavioral health needs have gone unmet. Behavioral health referrals and crisis resource availability sit alongside that history in one place.

The company took its present form in 2021, when Appriss Health acquired PatientPing and rebranded. It claims a footprint across 52 states and territories. Encounters on its network are put at 3 billion a year. Published material points to work with the State of Delaware on crisis care and behavioral health coordination.

paragraphs: ImageTrend sells software that fire departments, EMS agencies, and hospitals run their emergency response operations on. Its core product is ePCR software built for how medics actually work, with AI-assisted documentation, configurable workflows, and real-time intelligence for agencies at any scale.

NEMSIS, NERIS, NTDB, and TQIP compliance is built into every workflow, with software filling and validating fields while staff review and confirm before submission. A scheduling product, ImageTrend Slate, addresses the demands of EMS, fire departments, and other critical services. It manages time-off requests, shift trades, and employee availability. Separate pre-plan software digitizes floor plans, hazard locations, water supply points, and utility shutoffs so responders have instant access to tactical data on scene.

The company reports 9,000 agencies, 43 state repositories, and more than a billion records processed. It says its sales engineering team is entirely former fire and EMS. It cites 24/7 US-based support and a 96.5% satisfaction rate, backed by 25 years in the field.

paragraphs: Explorance sells software for collecting and analyzing feedback from students and employees. Blue, the survey platform, automates the collection, analysis, and distribution of insights. MLY applies machine learning models built for higher education, human resources, and learning and development. Metrics That Matter serves corporate universities and learning providers measuring employee learning programs.

In higher education the work is course evaluations tailored to an institution's own processes and IT systems. Blue connects to the systems a campus or employer already runs, such as an LMS, HRIS, SIS, or CRM. Surveys adapt their questions and content to each respondent's profile. The platform is described as meeting WCAG 2.2 (AA) and Section 508 accessibility standards. MLY reads open comments against more than 900 topics on the student experience. paragraphs: Earth Networks sells hyperlocal weather intelligence and real-time lightning detection to organizations that have to make safety decisions outdoors. A core use is warning people who work and play outdoors when lightning is approaching.

The company frames the lightning network as detection rather than prediction. It claims coverage in more than 90 countries. Warnings reach people by email, text message and mobile push notification. Audible outdoor horns carry the same warning across a site. Its Sferic Maps product tracks more than 80 real-time weather conditions on a map. Sferic Connect lets administrators notify staff of dangerous weather on iOS and Android devices, and can stop end users from opting out.

Meteorological staff are on hand around the clock when a customer is unsure what to do. Product pages point at schools as one setting for the alerts. Airports are another. The company also publishes a report on lightning detected across the United States.

before.name: Adtran
before.description: Fiber access and broadband network equipment for municipal and rural providers

roles.title: Global Business Development Manager- Time and Frequency

paragraphs: Adtran builds broadband access equipment and software for service providers that are extending fiber across different technologies and deployment settings. Its access platforms are meant to fit several architectures, from disaggregated designs to integrated systems. The company also sells a pluggable optics module aimed at operators of data centers working under power, cooling, space and latency limits.

Deployments run from small sites carrying a few hundred subscribers up to locations serving more than 100,000. Open APIs and OSS/BSS integration connect the equipment to systems an operator already runs, while the Mosaic software suite supplies visibility from end to end. A shared operational layer correlates signals and alarms across areas that were traditionally kept apart, so a team can see how a fault affects subscriber service before tracing where it began. Fiber monitoring runs while the fiber is in service, looking for degradation before subscribers feel it.

Customer stories on the broadband access page name a rural electric cooperative bringing fiber to parts of Indiana. Another names a municipal power and light utility building a multigigabit fiber-to-the-home network. For buyers who want to talk to someone, the contact page sets out regional office details.

quote.text: Broadband networks must scale to support higher speeds and more subscribers while adapting to different deployment models and existing infrastructure.

before.name: Survalent Technology
before.description: SCADA, ADMS and outage management for municipal utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Survalent sells control room software to utilities, bringing SCADA, outage management and distribution management into one system. The company describes its buyers as electric, water and wastewater, oil and gas, renewable energy and transit utilities around the world. It argues that running a distribution network well is hard without a modern, centralized supervisory control and data acquisition system.

One network model and one database sit under every application, so a change made once carries across the platform. Operators work from real-time equipment status, metering data, alarming and control, with the aim of catching problems before outages start. A utility can start with a limited set of feeders, substations and applications and add more over time. A metering interface pulls readings from the AMI system using the MultiSpeak protocol, and a lightning interface fetches strike data and filters it by the utility's area of interest.

MultiSpeak itself is described as an initiative for rural electric co-ops and municipal utilities. The site says more than 700 utilities worldwide use its SCADA product. It reports 800+ customers around the world and 97.6% customer retention. The company also says it puts 20.3% of revenue into research and development.

paragraphs: DTN sells forecasting and risk planning for organizations whose operations turn on weather. Refined fuel markets are another line of business, with real-time visibility, pricing and supply chain intelligence.

paragraphs: Boston Dynamics builds mobile robots that companies use to automate tedious and hazardous work in manufacturing, logistics and other industries. Its product line covers Spot, Stretch, Atlas and Orbit. Spot is a mobile robot that automates sensing and inspection and captures data wherever it is sent. The company states that over 1,500 Spot robots are in customer hands today.

Spot works on factory floors, construction sites and research labs. As a sensing platform it gives teams insight into routine operations, site health or potentially hazardous situations. In energy and natural resources it performs inspections in energized, radioactive or otherwise hazardous areas. Operators can also use it to remotely investigate, assess and de-escalate tense or hazardous situations, reducing the risk to personnel. With the Spot Arm, operators can handle tasks such as nuclear material handling or suspicious package investigation from a safe distance. Standard payload configurations cover inspection, public safety and innovation, including a Government & Public Safety Kit.

Stretch, the company's warehouse robot, handles cases and unloads trailers. Orbit, its fleet management software, manages autonomous tasks, operates robots remotely and analyzes data within the context of a facility map. Atlas, a humanoid robot, is in early field testing with Hyundai on real-world sequencing tasks. The company has announced a new 323,000 square foot facility in Waltham, Massachusetts.

paragraphs: ZOLL makes medical devices, software and related services for patients with serious cardiopulmonary and respiratory conditions. Its buyers include hospitals and other healthcare organizations, emergency medical services and militaries.

One part of the catalog covers acute cardiac care, from sudden cardiac death protection to heart failure management and care after a heart attack. Another covers diagnostics meant to widen access to sleep apnea testing. There is also ventilation technology for patients from neonates to adults. The Zenix monitor/defibrillator is offered for EMS and hospital use. The history page records the launch of RescueNet, described as an EMS information management system covering patient care, operational efficiency and agency compliance. A subsidiary was later renamed ZOLL Data Systems to better reflect the EMS market.

The company traces its origins to Dr. Paul Zoll, a physician who co-founded it in 1980. The history page lists the co-founders as Dr. Zoll, Leigh Stein and Thomas Claflin. Its policy for interactions with health care professionals is based on the Advanced Medical Technology Association Code of Ethics. The company also certifies a compliance program satisfying the requirements of the California Health and Safety Code. Under the Sunshine Act it tracks payments and other transfers of value and reports them annually.

paragraphs: Transoft Solutions makes software for the people who plan, design and operate transportation systems. Its work spans aviation, civil infrastructure, transportation and operational professionals. On the aviation side that means specialized software to plan, analyze and optimize airport and airspace operations.

The company started in 1991, when co-founder Milton Carrasco developed a vehicle tracking program called AutoTURN. One executive is credited with merging AeroTURN and PathPlanner into AviPLAN.

The company reports more than 100,000 customers in over 150 countries. Clients are described as government agencies at the federal, state, county and municipal levels, along with major international airports and engineering and architectural design firms. Headquarters are in British Columbia, Canada, with further offices in the United States, Australia, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Belgium, Germany, France, Sweden, Spain, India and China.

before.name: Propel
before.description: SNAP and EBT benefits mobile app for recipients, plus Propel for States tooling for state benefits agencies - exhibited at APHSA 2026

paragraphs: Propel makes a mobile app for people who receive government benefits on an EBT card, pitched on its own site as the simplest way to check a balance and save money. The app itself costs nothing to use.

With the cardholder's permission, Propel connects to their state benefits portal. It then gathers the EBT balance and transaction history, makes that easier to read, and displays it in the app. That spares people from calling a 1-800 number or logging in to a state website. Balance checking works in 49 states, the District of Columbia, and several U.S. territories. Iowa is the exception. The app also carries card security features such as suspicious activity monitoring and out of state transaction blocking.

The company says it was founded to make government benefits better at the speed and scale recipients deserve. The company points to more than a million 5-star reviews of the app. Money comes from advertising. Most of the promotions are free or discounted services available only to EBT cardholders. paragraphs: KPA sells compliance help to automotive businesses, combining Vera Suite software, consulting, and training across EHS, HR, and FTC regulations. The buyers named throughout the site are dealerships, collision centers, and auto care facilities.

The approach brings together compliance technology, 150 local consultants, and a training library. Vera Suite is offered as one login covering every compliance area, replacing patchwork systems and manual tracking. On the safety side, the tools handle trackable issue management, QR code access to facility-specific Safety Data Sheets, and environmental testing. Consultants add quarterly onsite visits. A separate line handles cybersecurity and data privacy, simplifying compliance for MFA, DSARs, cookie banners, and more. A third covers advertising, sales and finance and insurance work, with an advertising archive, mystery shopping of website leads, and deal jacket analysis.

The company traces its consulting work back to 1986. It states that clients completed over 3 million courses in the past year. Customers span franchise auto groups, RV dealerships, and truck, motorsports, motorcycle, or marine dealerships.

before.description: Language learning platform in 70+ languages licensed by public libraries, school districts, universities and government agencies - exhibited at PLA 2026

paragraphs: Mango Languages sells language courses covering more than 70 languages and dialects, plus English for speakers of more than 20 others. Individuals subscribe, and the company also offers custom arrangements for organizations of any size.

Rather than separating vocabulary, grammar and listening into their own exercises, every lesson works all of them at once inside a real conversation. Each lesson asks the learner to say the phrase out loud before moving on, then plays the recording back against a native speaker. The courses are taught through thousands of authentic native-speaker recordings rather than synthetic voice.

Many public libraries and schools give their patrons full access at no cost, with nothing more than a library card. The school version is pitched as getting students speaking from day one while giving a district the reporting it needs. Mango launched in August 2007, paid for by a web development company two brothers had built in Detroit. It is still led by the four people who started it.
