brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile_research.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

before.name: Limble
before.description: Cloud CMMS for municipal facilities, water plants and public works

paragraphs: Limble sells a computerized maintenance management system for the teams that keep equipment and facilities running. The pitch is simpler work orders, assets that keep running and more productivity across every site. The company says it is rated number one by more than 50,000 maintenance professionals.

A work order can start from a dashboard, an asset record or a vendor, with details and photos added from a phone. Anyone in the organization can submit a request by scanning a QR code or visiting a URL, with no account required. Preventive maintenance is scheduled automatically on time, usage or condition. Parts inventory triggers push and email alerts when stock runs low. The mobile app keeps working without a signal and syncs once the device reconnects. Listed integrations include SAP S/4HANA, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central and QuickBooks Online.

Public sector users shown include a city water treatment plant in Lompoc. The company says a team at the City of Albuquerque was confidently using the mobile app after one day of training. It reports a 4.8 out of 5 rating on G2 and Capterra from well over 1,400 combined verified reviews. It also says customers typically see value in about three weeks.

before.name: Unite Us
before.description: Social care coordination network connecting health and social service referrals for govs and payers - exhibited at MESC 2026

hiring.note: Strategic Sales Director - West Co (United States)

paragraphs: Unite Us sells software and data infrastructure for coordinating whole-person care across healthcare, government and community-based organizations. Its named audiences include public health and human services agencies. Managed care and Medicaid plans are also on that list.

The core product is a closed-loop referral system for sending and receiving electronic social care referrals within a network of community partners. Staff can run social needs screenings, after which the platform automatically suggests resources or referrals. A secure chat feature lets users at partner organizations message each other about shared referrals, cases and clients. Integrations let organizations share resources and send referrals without leaving their own system.

Alongside referrals, the company sells predictive analytics meant to predict long-term risks and measure impact. Its Population Insights tool combines social, economic, environmental and health information with modeling to identify at-risk populations. It also automates payments to community-based organizations. The company states that it partnered with Presbyterian Health Plan to create New Mexico's first statewide closed-loop referral system.

before.name: UVeye
before.description: Automated vehicle inspection portals for airports, borders and government

paragraphs: UVeye builds automated inspection systems that scan the full exterior, undercarriage, and tires of a vehicle in seconds. Dealerships use the scans to document pre-existing damage and avoid unnecessary claims. Seaports and logistics hubs use touchless inspections to speed vehicle handoffs and settle disputes. Bus and truck operators run standardized inspections to improve compliance.

A scan combines high-resolution imaging, sensors, and patented AI to surface problems the eye cannot catch. Findings run from tire wear and misalignment to leaks, rust, and underbody damage. Output arrives as images and measurements of dents, scratches, and undercarriage issues. Automatic notifications flag critical issues that need immediate attention.

Brothers Amir and Ohad Hever founded UVeye in 2016. The first application was undercarriage security screening, which grew into a platform that scans whole vehicles. Systems are now deployed across hundreds of dealerships, fleets, rental agencies, and manufacturing lines worldwide. The company names Amazon, General Motors, Volvo, and CarMax among the companies using it. It reports over $380 million raised.

before.description: AI defect detection and coding for sewer inspection video - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: SewerAI sells a platform for sewer inspection work, aimed at utilities, contractors and engineers. It covers the work from inspection through rehabilitation.

Its AutoCode product reviews every frame of CCTV footage, identifies NASSCO observations and assigns PACP, LACP or MACP codes automatically. The company says this runs on the CCTV equipment a crew already owns. PIONEER, the record-keeping side, brings inspection records, asset histories, maintenance logs and compliance documentation into one platform. It also builds capital plans, letting users lasso-select segments on a map and apply budget constraints and cost guidance.

The site says the platform is used by more than 2,000 cities nationwide. The company describes 400 years of combined experience pulling cable, running cameras and managing programs. Its detection draws on more than 425,000 NASSCO surveys and 40,000 manhole assessments. SewerAI states that it is SOC 2 Type II certified.

before.name: BusPatrol
before.description: School bus stop-arm cameras with violator-funded safety programs

paragraphs: BusPatrol runs school bus stop-arm enforcement programs alongside school districts, municipalities, and law enforcement agencies. The company says communities can enforce the law around stopped buses at no upfront cost.

Cameras on the bus detect illegal passings and capture video evidence of them. Agencies review the results through dashboards, monthly reports, and compliance tools. The program also runs public awareness and public service campaigns meant to change how drivers behave.

BusPatrol states that it partners with school districts in 26 states. It says communities using the program see measurable reductions in dangerous driving around stopped school buses. The company traces its origin to a child killed while getting off his school bus in Ontario, Canada. Its staff, by its own description, includes technologists, retired police officers, and teachers.

hiring.note: Sr. Manager, FP&A & Sales Operatio only

paragraphs: Technosylva sells wildfire and extreme weather risk software to electric utilities and fire agencies. The point of it is turning complicated weather data into something a planning or response team can act on.

For planning, the company combines large numbers of validated fire simulations with historical weather and a customer's own asset data. Its models estimate what an ignition would mean in acres burned, buildings destroyed and people affected. For operations, simulations run nightly to produce the wildfire risk metrics crews plan around. Utilities use the output to target power shutoffs instead of cutting service broadly. Feeds from computer-aided dispatch and IRWIN bring in incidents from federal and state agencies. Flooding, high wind, extreme temperature and winter storms sit in the same view as fire.
The homepage points readers toward Xcel Energy, CAL FIRE and CORE. Bryan Spear is named as chief executive. The company has also announced modeling of urban conflagration in the built environment.

before.name: Hidden Level
before.description: Passive airspace monitoring sensors for airports and government agencies

paragraphs: Hidden Level sells radio-frequency sensing hardware and data services to government, defense and commercial security teams. The sensing is passive, which the company says leaves the equipment undetected and hard to jam.

The Breaker sensor is built for fixed sites and is meant to coexist with infrastructure and telecom equipment already there. The Surge mounts to land and water vehicles and is made to withstand harsh conditions. Customers who would rather not run hardware can buy data from a global sensor network the company owns, operates and maintains. That service pinpoints drone operator location and lets users define zones so alerts arrive only for activity in chosen areas. Data reaches other systems through an open API secured with FIPS 140-2 compliant cryptography, or through a web interface.

Stated uses include protecting airspace around stadiums, airports and buildings, and preventing contraband drone deliveries to correctional facilities. The hardware page cites FCC compliance along with TRL9 and MIL-STD-810 testing. The company says its sensors analyze the physical characteristics of signals without decoding private information. Researchers can reach the collected captures through APIs for training and benchmarking work.

CampBrain is not in this dataset and no record was invented for it.

also_known_as: Xplor Recreation I Vermont Systems - RecDesk - NextRec – ePACT

brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. Day-to-day work happens in Prism, which monitors and manages VMs, storage and networks across on-premises clusters and public clouds from a single console. before.name: Outsight SA
before.location: Paris, France (offices in San Francisco and Singapore)
before.description: LiDAR-based spatial intelligence software turning 3D sensor data into anonymous passenger flow, queue wait time and occupancy analytics for terminals and curbside.

paragraphs: Outsight sells software that turns 3D sensor feeds into a running account of how people, vehicles, and robots move through a site. The buyers are operators of large shared spaces such as airports, hospitals, and factories.

Anything entering the scene is given an anonymous identifier and held to centimeter precision until it leaves. No faces or plates are captured, only the geometry of motion. Operators define zones and the measures they care about, such as counting, density, queue length, wait time and throughput, and the analytics engine computes them continuously. Results come back as live 3D playback, custom indicators, alerts, dashboards, and APIs. Before any of that, a multi-vendor simulator tests layouts and sensor mixes and proposes the hardware configuration.

The company says the platform is deployed at scale across five continents. It calls the result a Motional Digital Twin and says these are running in production. Its newsroom announces a strategic partnership with AWS around spatial AI in aviation. The pitch behind all of it is that movement is the next layer of business to be digitized.

before.name: Geotab

paragraphs: Geotab sells fleet management technology that commercial vehicle operators use to track vehicles and run their operations from one system. The company describes what it offers as an open platform for safe, sustainable and cost-effective mobility powered by AI and data intelligence. Video safety is part of the same package, with dash cameras feeding into the MyGeotab software.

The GO tracking device plugs into a vehicle's onboard diagnostics port. Once driving begins it records location, speed, engine idling and distance. Dash cam footage and alert data upload to the cloud so managers can review video later. An analytics layer standardizes data from every vehicle source and enriches it with context such as road conditions, driver history and maintenance records. Developers can extend the platform with sample code and custom add-in pages.

Police and first responders are among the industries the site lists. Geotab reports more than six million connected vehicles. It also claims 26 years of fleet expertise. The company states that the platform is backed by ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certifications and that its AI aligns with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Support is described as staffed around the clock by experts who are in-market rather than offshored.

paragraphs: Everbridge sells a platform for managing physical and digital threats from end to end. Some of it protects traveling and remote employees. Other parts are built to inform and protect citizens at scale.

The method is to identify threats, work out who and what is affected, coordinate the response, communicate, and learn from every incident. Detection draws on risk intelligence, geospatial analysis, operational data and verified external and internal sources. Messages go out across multiple channels, with more than one delivery method per contact. A separate product centralizes business continuity planning, risk assessment, dependency mapping and testing. The main platform is available in three packages aimed at different kinds of organization.

The company states it has more than 6,500 global customers. Mass notifications are put at 6 billion a year. A customer story describes Fairfax County delivering multilingual safety alerts to over a million people. It cites a Forrester study putting average return on investment for the platform at 358 percent.

roles.title: Senior Account Manager, Strategic Events Accounts

paragraphs: Pointr sells indoor mapping and wayfinding software that turns a venue, office or campus into interactive digital maps. Customers put those maps into their own apps, on the web, or on kiosks, using dedicated mobile and web SDKs. One stated use is guiding travelers to their gate with turn-by-turn updates and estimated arrival times.

Maps are generated from CAD files by an AI tool called MapScale. Blue dot positioning indoors runs on Bluetooth Low Energy rather than a satellite signal. The site says accuracy holds without fingerprinting or geomagnetism, so the system needs less ongoing maintenance. Geofences drawn on the map trigger actions when visitors enter or leave a zone.

The company describes itself as the top choice for Fortune 100 companies. Its homepage names product wayfinding work at The Home Depot. It states that its positioning technology is patented, with more than ten years of testing and development behind it. On privacy, the geofencing page says visitor location data is collected anonymously and aligned with GDPR.

paragraphs: Auror sells a retail crime intelligence platform to retailers and law enforcement agencies, built to bring crime intelligence together across a network of both. Retailers capture events in the platform, connect the dots between stores and cases, and identify potential threats.

Auror Core comprises five modules: Intel for incident reporting, Connect the Dots for AI-assisted person of interest matching with human verification, Investigate for case management, Insights for analytics and Audit for compliance workflows. Reported incidents build into in-depth profiles of the people and vehicles affecting an organization. Investigators then use that intel to build, collaborate on and resolve cases. A Risk Detection add-on extends this to prevention, with automatic alerts when known vehicles of interest enter a location. For law enforcement, the Retail Crime Hub, designed by Auror and Axon, moves packaged evidence from retailers straight into Axon Evidence for intake.

Auror puts its network at more than 85,000 stores and more than 3,500 law enforcement agencies, with a decade of accumulated intelligence across them. Auror says Cosentino's Food Stores achieved a 346% return on investment and a reduction of more than 90% in reporting time with the platform. The company has set itself the goal of reducing retail crime by 50% over the next five years.

before.name: Aurelian
before.description: AI voice agents answering non-emergency calls for 911 centers - exhibited at APCO 2026

paragraphs: Aurelian builds software for the 911 centers known as public safety answering points. One of its two products answers non-emergency calls instantly, so callers are not left on hold. The other sits with call-takers during emergencies and gives real-time, context-aware guidance without taking control.

The automated line resolves routine calls on its own. It detects and escalates emergencies to a person. During live calls, the guidance tool surfaces the relevant SOP checklist for the incident. It also flags missing information before the call ends. The company says the system learns a center's workflows, SOPs, and systems in order to support the full call flow. Aurelian states that humans remain in control of emergencies and decision-making.

The customers page says PSAPs around the country use Aurelian to cut non-emergency workload and return time to their teams. Published stories include Hamilton County 911 automating more than 300 non-emergency calls a day. The about page says the founders, Max and James, were building call automation technology for hair salons before starting the company. That insight led them to pivot to public safety and build for PSAPs.

paragraphs: DroneShield sells counter-drone technology, which it calls counter-UAS, to military, government, law enforcement and critical infrastructure operators around the world. The company describes a portfolio that spans RF intelligence, AI, sensor fusion and software. The stated aim is to help customers detect, understand and defeat increasingly complex drone threats. Engineering, manufacturing and support are spread across Australia, the United States and Europe.

One current product, RfRecon, runs on an AI engine called RfAI-3 and detects, classifies and geolocates AIS/ADS-B signals, unencrypted Remote ID beacons and other RF activity across the spectrum. It interoperates with ATAK-CIV, SAPIENT and third-party command-and-control platforms. Deploying several units across distributed sites yields what the company calls network-scale intelligence.
DroneShield was founded in 2014 with a single focus on countering the threat posed by drones. The company began in Virginia in the United States. DroneShield Limited is publicly listed on the ASX.

before.name: Emburse
before.description: Expense management and payment software - exhibited at NIGP 2026, NACUBO 2026

paragraphs: Emburse sells travel and expense management software to finance teams. The platform covers expense, travel, accounts payable, cards, invoices and ACH payments, with localization for more than 100 countries.

Receipts are read by optical character recognition, whether the paper original or a digital copy. Spend is sorted automatically across dozens of categories, with VAT reconciliation and multiple currencies handled along the way. Policies are written once and enforced across the organization rather than checked afterward. A compliance layer examines receipts before and after submission, applying policy consistently and flagging risk early. For travel, the company sits alongside a customer's existing travel management company rather than replacing it, rebooking air and hotel when prices fall under rules the customer sets. It also connects to ERP, finance and accounting systems.

The company states that it serves over 20,000 organizations in 200 countries and territories. Those customers are described as large enterprises, smaller businesses, public sector agencies and nonprofits. Marne Martin is the chief executive. In July 2026 the company announced that it had been named to CNBC's list of the world's top fintech companies for that year.

before.name: GovWell
before.description: AI permitting and licensing platform: 24/7 resident assistant, AI code-compliance review - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026, Maryland Municipal League 2026
before.source: ICMA 2025; NACo 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026; Maryland Municipal League 2026

paragraphs: GovWell sells software that city and county governments use to run permitting, licensing, planning, and code enforcement work. Residents and businesses use the same system to reach services, pay, and get answers outside office hours.

Permits, plan review, and inspections are handled together in one place for staff. Licensing runs online too, with applicants filing, paying, and renewing while staff keep records and approvals on their side. Code enforcement officers track cases, schedule inspections, and follow issues to closure. The company argues that AI can do real work in these processes, reviewing applications against local code, answering resident questions, flagging violations in plans, and routing inspections.

GovWell says it was founded by the son of a general contractor who watched his father struggle to get permits quickly. Its case for existing is that local governments cannot hire software engineers at competitive salaries. Deployment strategists and configuration tooling are meant to shorten implementations against older systems.

paragraphs: Civica makes software that public bodies use to deliver critical services to citizens around the world. It says over 6,000 public bodies use that software to help provide critical services to over 100 million citizens.

Its solutions span local and central government, health and community care, housing and social care, libraries and education, and regulatory and compliance services. The company describes integrated cloud platforms that automate workflows, support data-driven decision-making and reduce operational costs. Named products include Spydus, a library management system. Civica also sells master data management for state and local government. It says it is an approved supplier on major government frameworks.

Civica was established in 2001 and describes itself as one of the UK's largest software companies. Its team has grown to 5,500 colleagues, one-third of whom have worked in the sectors it serves. Acquisitions are part of the strategy, with more than 37 completed in the last 10 years. The company reports delivery in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, India, North America and Europe. Customer stories on its site include delivering a single citizen view for the State of Alaska.

paragraphs: YuJa sells a portfolio of cloud platforms aimed at clients in regulated sectors. The line covers a cloud-hosted video service for storing, managing and streaming media. It also covers online proctoring, described as an automated, AI and live service with full learning management system integration.

Accessibility is handled two ways: a product built for the learning management system, and a compliance product for automated web governance across an organization's websites. For public sector buyers, the company offers to remediate document libraries for local and state governments. The rest of the portfolio adds lecture and screen capture, a real-time classroom polling and quizzing tool, and a note-taking tool designed for student accommodation. Customer service is included with every deployment license.

Published case studies describe deployments at public universities and community colleges, among them a university serving more than twelve thousand students. One community college adopted both the video platform and the accessibility platform together. Staff at another college describe integration with their learning management system through single sign-on and LTI. They also point to captioning that can be translated into other languages as the change that mattered most.

paragraphs: Robin Radar Systems makes 360 degree, 3D radar systems that detect, track and classify small flying objects such as birds, bats and drones. It sells them to aviation, defence, security and ecology teams that want a full view of their airspace. Its two main products are IRIS, a 3D drone radar in a 29 kg package, and MAX, a 3D bird detection radar.

IRIS uses micro-doppler classification and deep neural network technology to distinguish blades and rotating parts. It combines 360 degree views, 60 degree elevation and a 5 km instrumented range. A software-only update, Long-Range Mode, lets operators switch between 5 km and 12 km instrumented ranges in minutes. MAX pairs with two software interfaces, Bird Viewer for live airspace and Report Viewer for historical analysis. Airports, airfields and wind farms use the bird and bat radars to react to hazards as they emerge.

The name comes from a 1980 project by the Dutch research institute TNO to prevent bird strikes on Royal Netherlands Air Force planes. Siete Hamminga, now CEO, spun the technology out of TNO in 2010 to found the company. It reports more than 300 radars deployed worldwide and a staff of 150 or more people. In 2024 its shareholders reached an acquisition agreement with the Dutch investment company Parcom. Scarecrow, a maker of bird dispersal and data logging systems based on bio-acoustic technology, is a Robin company.

paragraphs: Starbridge sells an AI sales intelligence platform to companies whose customers are public-sector buyers. The target user is anyone selling into state and local government, K-12 districts, or higher education.

The platform collects buying signals from public sources such as district and university websites, board and trustee minutes, budget reports, grants, news, job postings, and FOIA requests. A signal, in the company's definition, is an early sign that a district, university, or agency is planning to spend. It claims to scan more than 320,000 public sector entities daily, surfacing budgets, board discussions, and leadership changes. Those signals and enriched accounts push into Salesforce and HubSpot. The platform also centralizes thousands of state, local, education, and university bid portals.

The buyers are go-to-market teams, and the company puts the number at more than 400 selling to government agencies, K-12, and higher education. On data quality, Starbridge cites a recent test of 14,000 emails with a 98% accuracy rate. New accounts are assigned a customer success manager who builds a tailored target list and syncs it into the CRM in the first week.

before.name: Authorium
before.description: Document-driven workflow for government procurement, budget and HR processes

paragraphs: Authorium sells government agencies a platform meant to connect the flow of public funds across the administrative functions that carry it. The company builds only for government and describes itself as a public benefit company. State and local governments are named as buyers.

On the procurement side, bids are submitted, vendors scored, and evaluation workbooks kept inside the application. Contracts are tracked from request, to award, to obligation management, to renewal. Workflows, templates, rules, and role-based access are meant to be configured without an ongoing technical service contract. A legislative module imports bills and amendments, then tracks them and distributes them to departments and teams for analysis. A smaller product, Authorium Direct, covers direct and non-competitive purchasing in a single, low-cost portal. It is built on AWS GovCloud.

The company says 60% of its staff worked in government themselves. It reports having completed a SBIR phase II with the U.S. Air Force. Implementation is handled by an in-house team. Authorium says it has been named to the GovTech 100 for a third consecutive year.

before.name: Gridware
before.description: Pole-mounted sensors + AI (Gridscope) detecting grid faults, vegetation strikes, and wildfire-risk events

paragraphs: Gridware sells hazard detection to electric utilities, which are expected to maintain near-perfect uptime but typically learn of hazards such as fallen limbs or damaged power lines only after they cause outages or disasters. Its platform gives constant visibility into real-time electrical, physical, and environmental conditions by capturing information directly at the pole.

The company names the problem it targets Hazard Awareness Delay, which it says leads to expensive outages and public safety risks. It calls its own category Active Grid Response, defined by immediate detection, precise localization, detailed identification, and monitoring during outages. The stated payoff for utilities is that crews can get to the right location, with the right gear, armed with the right information.

Gridware says it partners with investor-owned utilities, customer-owned utilities, electric cooperatives, municipal utilities, and public utility districts. It puts its accumulated deployment experience at more than 90 million field hours. Its case studies describe a Puget Sound Energy pilot that the company says improved the utility's ability to identify outages and prioritize repairs during severe weather.

paragraphs: The Weather Company sells weather data, forecasting, and insights to consumers and businesses alike. The industries it names are advertising, aviation, media, and government.

Much of the business runs through a weather data API that customers fold into their own applications, business processes, or custom models. For aviation the pitch is converting complex meteorological data into decision-ready flight and ground insights. The stated aim there is fewer costly delays, better fuel use, and safer crews and passengers from preflight to touchdown. A separate government and defense line is aimed at mission risk from command centers to the tactical edge.

The company traces its work back nearly five decades, combining human meteorological expertise with technology. It also powers a portfolio of three consumer brands used daily around the world. Case studies describe Breeze Airways using its Fusion flight tracking to run more efficiently through major weather events and resume operations faster after disruptions. Another describes NASCAR unifying its weather intelligence with the company to make scheduling and safety calls.

paragraphs: Flock Safety sells license plate readers, video cameras, gunshot detection and response drones to law enforcement agencies, schools, businesses and neighborhoods to help them deter crime, respond to emergencies and investigate safety incidents. Its license plate recognition cameras capture plates and vehicle characteristics such as make, color and body type to generate investigative leads. Responders get an instant alert when a vehicle matches a customer-defined or NCIC hot list. Users include law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, apartment complexes, houses of worship and schools.

Beyond plate readers, Flock sells PTZ video cameras for open areas such as parking lots, intersections and parks, and fixed cameras for buildings and city streets. A gunshot and audio detection product verifies gunfire and links each alert with nearby LPR reads and video. Flock DFR, its drone as first responder system, launches a docked drone to the coordinates of a 911 call, LPR hit or gunshot alert and streams live video to officers before they arrive. Solar-powered mobile trailers cover parking lots, retail centers and construction sites, and an optional Alert Response Service puts trained agents on live alerts.

Flock sells on an annual subscription that covers hardware, software, maintenance and support. The company has reduced its recommended default data retention from 30 days to 7 days, which it says applies to new law enforcement customers. Customers control their data and how it is shared, and every search is logged.

before.name: Frontline Wildfire Defense
before.description: Exterior retardant/foam systems and app-based wildfire defense for homes and HOAs

paragraphs: Frontline Wildfire Defense sells exterior sprinkler systems and companion software that defend homes and businesses against wildfire. The company describes its mission as providing faster, safer and more precise ways to protect homes, families, businesses and communities from wildfire.

The second-generation defense system is tied to fire tracking software and turns on automatically when fire comes within seven miles of a home. Once running, it saturates the property with water and biodegradable firefighting foam to create conditions the company calls too wet to burn. A commercial version is aimed at businesses, campuses and critical infrastructure, meant to cut risk before a fire reaches the property. A companion app carries wildfire alerts, maps, fire danger indexes, emergency contact groups and evacuation checklists.

Homeowners, businesses and new housing developments are the audience, and the company says its system will safeguard 151 homes at a Woodside Homes community. Installation is handled by licensed contractors in each state rather than by the company itself. Financing options, including zero-down wildfire protection, are offered to buyers. The company points to embers as the central danger, saying they cause up to 90% of structure loss during a wildfire.

paragraphs: BRINC sells drone hardware, software and services built exclusively for public safety agencies and supported by one partner. The company was founded in response to the 2017 Las Vegas Shooting. An indoor tactical drone was developed over dozens of callouts with the Las Vegas Metro Police Department SWAT team.

The company's 911 response drone responds to calls 24/7/365 and covers 200 square miles. The site says calls for service can be cleared without dispatching a unit, so drones clear non-priority calls while agencies focus elsewhere. Drones can deliver Narcan, AEDs, EpiPens, cell phones and other equipment anywhere in seconds. For tactical use, a drone can enter dangerous places, generate floor plans mid-flight and de-escalate from a distance with two-way audio.

BRINC products are deployed by over 900 public safety agencies globally to initiate contact without force. The company states its drones are designed, supported and made in the USA and are NDAA, CJIS and SOC2 compliant. It offers help across a program's stages, from policy development and Part 107/COA work to training, staffing, maintenance and upgrades. BRINC opened a Seattle, WA headquarters to scale out engineering and manufacturing.

before.name: Routeware
before.description: Routing, in-cab fleet tech, and resident apps for waste operations - exhibited at SWANA WASTECON 2025

paragraphs: Routeware sells digital technology for waste, recycling and heavy-duty fleet operations. The buyers are private haulers and municipal fleets. The software pulls collection, customer and business operations into one place.

Its routing product lets staff densify and edit routes and optimize entire fleets. Routes can be updated and stops reassigned in real time, with automatic sequencing. Dispatch gives a single view of orders, resources, status and inventory. Helper routes are built by drag and drop and resequenced on the spot. The back-office dispatch system is tied to the on-board computers in the truck.

The company describes the setup as hardware-light and cloud-based. It lists integrations with AWS, Esri, Geotab and Samsara. Some customers run several heavy-duty fleets, including snowplows and sweeper trucks. A separate product handles medical waste from end to end. Another is recycling software built around California mandates. The company says it has worked on digital transformation in waste and recycling for over twenty years.

before.name: Clariti
before.description: Community development permitting and licensing software (founded as BasicGov)

paragraphs: Clariti sells community development software to local governments, pitched at any size and budget. One edition is permitting software for large local governments. A second, Launch, is aimed at small to mid-sized local governments. A third product, CivCheck, uses AI to guide applicants toward a complete and compliant submission and staff through every check.

The software keeps the permit counter online, where applicants apply, pay, and track status. It also tracks code violations from report to resolution, with automatic case assignment and links to local zoning and codes. Staff can build a report, adjust a page layout, or create a new permit type themselves. The large-jurisdiction edition runs on the Salesforce Platform, whose APIs let a government connect its other tools. Launch customers can copy a peer's permitting workflows using a cloning tool. It operates less as a single product line than as a group whose focus is to acquire businesses with growth potential, manage them well and then build them for the future. paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

before.name: Neara
before.description: Physics-based digital twin modeling of grid networks for utilities

paragraphs: Neara sells physics-based digital twin software to electric utilities, which use it to model their networks. The pitch is to unify assets, surroundings and workflows in a single physics-accurate view.

The model is built from a utility's existing LiDAR, imagery, GIS and asset records. Teams then simulate wind, ice, thermal, flood, vegetation, reconductoring and new builds on the real network geometry. Outputs include prioritized hardening plans, regulator-ready reports and field-ready work orders. Solution areas cover resiliency and reliability, wildfire mitigation, asset management, risk and value optimization, and design and construction.

On the asset side, replacement candidates are ranked by measured load rather than by install date. Wildfire work pulls pole loading, asset condition, vegetation, GIS accuracy, weather and consequence into one physics-backed model. Resiliency work prioritizes mitigation by how asset condition, vegetation proximity and environmental conditions interact across the network. Case study quotes on the site are attributed to the chief executive of Essential Energy. Another comes from a general manager of network management at SA Power Networks.

quote.text: Utilities on four continents run their networks on Neara, from ambitious regional co-ops to national grid operators.

before.description: Residence life and student housing management software covering applications, room assignment, billing and community programming for universities and colleges - exhibited at EDUCAUSE 2026

paragraphs: StarRez sells a configurable platform that student housing providers use to run housing and event management operations. The same system handles conference and event work, including group bookings, lodging, and event logistics.

On the housing side it covers room selection, roommate matching, and meal plans. Students complete applications, pick rooms themselves, sign contracts, and meet other residents in one place. Residence life staff manage conduct, community operations, and student employment through a module called Rez360. Operations teams handle inspections, maintenance, and package tracking on mobile friendly tools.

The company says it partners with more than 1,300 higher education teams. It lists certification for SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS Level 1, and Cyber Essentials Plus, and describes itself as HIPAA-Ready and FERPA-Ready. Private student accommodation operators are a second market, with links to online travel agency channels to fill vacant spaces. Support runs around the clock through a service the company calls StarCare Online.

paragraphs: D-Fend Solutions sells counter-drone systems to military, law enforcement and homeland security agencies. Its core product, EnforceAir, detects a rogue drone, takes control of it through a radio-frequency cyber takeover and brings it to a safe landing. The company describes the approach as non-kinetic and AI-enhanced, built for sensitive and challenging environments.

EnforceAir can operate autonomously or under manual control, and it detects, locates and identifies rogue drones in a protected airspace before taking them over. It is sold in several deployment packages, including a Homeland Security & Law Enforcement Bundle and two tactical configurations, EnforceAir PLUS and EnforceAir2. EnforceAir PLUS, launched in August 2025, adds radar and a jammer to the RF-cyber layer. Beyond agencies, the company says the system has been chosen for large-scale events at stadiums, arenas and open-air venues and for VIP protection.

In an August 2026 press release the company says EnforceAir provided counter-drone security across World Cup host cities and was adopted by more than 20 public safety agencies. Chairman and CEO Zohar Halachmi co-founded the company after founding two mobile and enterprise application start-ups. Its U.S. arm, D-Fend Solutions AD, Inc., is located in McLean, Virginia. In June 2026 the company announced an agreement to be acquired by Motorola Solutions. Its newsroom now states that it has officially joined Motorola Solutions.

before.name: Objective Corporation
before.description: Objective Build planning and building consent software for government regulators

paragraphs: Objective Corporation sells software meant to help government shift to being completely digital. It says thousands of public sector organizations use its software for developing policies with impact and accelerating processes. One of its stated aims is to streamline the building assessment and consent process.

Objective Trapeze is electronic plan review software that helps planning and building departments review plans quickly and accurately while checking compliance with ICC codes and amendments. Stamping is digital, and a 100-page application can be stamped in a few mouse clicks, with the software finding white space to place the stamp. Objective Connect is an IRAP assessed external file sharing product that gives control over information shared outside a council. Objective RegWorks centralises, tracks and administers the compliance process, including education and engagement. A separate product keeps disclosure document management production, review, verification and publication in one central system.

The company states that more than 500 local governments in the UK, Australia and New Zealand rely on Objective Trapeze to conduct plan reviews faster. It puts the file sharing product at more than 200 organisations worldwide.

before.name: Acentra Health
before.description: Medicaid enterprise systems, care and utilization management for states - exhibited at Healthcare IT Connect 2026, NAMPI 2026
before.source: competitor sweep; Healthcare IT Connect 2026; NAMPI 2026

paragraphs: Acentra Health builds health technology and clinical services for government healthcare programs. Its Medicaid Enterprise System takes in professional, institutional, and dental claims and encounters, whether they arrive by electronic data interchange or on paper.

An automated adjudication engine sends processed claims on for payment and flags the ones that need further review. The rules behind those decisions can be entered without code, so administrators can reflect policy changes and mandates as they arrive. A separate provider management module handles enrollment through a configurable intake application. Before a provider is enrolled, a credentialing service verifies licensing and looks for sanctions. External Quality Review services sit alongside the software.

The company claims more than 30 years of public sector health experience. Its claims platform, it says, has earned CMS certification back to day one of operations with zero CMS findings. The provider module is described as CMS certified and compliant with National Institute of Standards and Technology requirements. A federal claims product is described as carrying an Authority to Operate in secure federal data centers.

before.name: DEVNET Inc
before.description: Property tax, assessment and county financial software for local government

paragraphs: DEVNET sells property tax and land records software to local government, under an Edge product line covering mass appraisal, assessment administration, billing, collection, permitting, records management and mapping. Its applications are meant to give a comprehensive view of the entire property tax life cycle from appraisal to collection.

The suite also reaches personal property, mobile homes, special assessments, tax calculation, distribution and delinquent tax processing. EdgeMaps provides real-time GIS integration, with configurable web maps powered by the Esri ArcGIS platform living inside DEVNET software. A public portal lets residents and outside agencies reach property and appraisal data and pay tax bills online. The maintenance agreement includes future releases, upgrades, bug fixes, training, support, travel and legislative changes at no additional cost.

DEVNET is privately held and was founded in 1997 to supply integrated software and hardware to local government. It serves over 120 jurisdictions across Illinois, Iowa, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Virginia and Wisconsin. The company says its solution values and collects revenues for over 4.5 million parcels each year. Staff include former county government officials alongside developers. DEVNET is a member of the International Association of Assessing Officers.

before.description: Traffic data collection and smart intersection technology

roles.title: Enterprise Account Executive, Opticom Solutions (Southeastern USA)

paragraphs: Miovision sells traffic data collection tools meant to give planners the accurate, verifiable data their mobility plans depend on. It also sells detection equipment that improves signal performance by responding to real-world road user demand, from bicycles to articulated trucks. Its Opticom line clears the path for emergency fleets without re-timing entire corridors.

Portable devices capture comprehensive multimodal count data including cars, trucks, pedestrians and bikes. A newer optimization product replaces manual five-year retiming cycles with iterative, objective-based optimization that the company says cuts manual effort by up to half. before.name: Acusensus
before.description: AI cameras detecting phone use, seatbelt, and speed violations for road authorities

paragraphs: Acusensus sells automated traffic enforcement systems to the road authorities and police agencies that are trying to cut deaths and injuries on the road network. Its main product, Heads-Up, detects drivers illegally using a mobile phone and captures evidence intended to stand up in a prosecution.

The same camera pass picks up other behaviours, so one deployment can address seatbelt non-compliance and speed measured at a point or averaged over a distance. A companion product sends live alerts to officers working the roadside. Assessment happens at the roadside, and images of drivers who are not offending are discarded almost immediately. Evidence that is kept is encrypted so that only the customer agency can open it.

The company says the government of New South Wales used its technology in a program enforcing against illegal phone use by drivers. Its list of delivered work includes an Arkansas speed enforcement program covering work zones. Acusensus also reports ISO accreditation for occupational health and safety, quality, environmental and information security management systems.

paragraphs: Motive sells fleet software and hardware as one integrated suite built around AI. The buyers are commercial fleets, which the company describes as ranging from five or ten vehicles up to companies running thousands of them.

On the safety side, cameras and AI flag more than twenty kinds of event on the road. High-confidence events go straight to managers, while a safety team reviews the low-confidence ones to remove false positives. Vehicle tracking uses real-time GPS with traffic updates and weather overlays for route planning. Compliance work such as electronic logs, driver qualification, IFTA and CSA sits in the same platform. Equipment monitoring shows what share of the time an asset is in use and how long it sits dormant. Telematics from various equipment manufacturers is centralized in a single platform.

The company points to operations running from waste services to construction. It says it was named number one in fleet management across every segment. It also cites top rankings for equipment monitoring in G2 asset tracking reports for summer 2026. Its fleet card is issued by Sutton Bank under a license from Mastercard International.

before.name: GameChanger
before.description: Youth sports scorekeeping and streaming app - exhibited at NRPA 2026

paragraphs: GameChanger sells a youth sports app that athletes, coaches, and families use to stay connected through live streaming, scorekeeping, team management, and developmental resources. The app is free for coaches on teams where they are listed as staff.

Coaches message the team, schedule events and lineups, and review stats, insights, and game film for practice planning and player development. Families and fans follow along with real-time live streaming in HD, GameStream animations, live game alerts, and play-by-plays. Confirmed family members and players can broadcast games live in all sports by default. Watching live streams of sports such as basketball, volleyball, and soccer is free without limit.

The company was founded in 2009, is headquartered in New York City, and says it covers more than nine million games annually across baseball, softball, basketball, volleyball, soccer, football, lacrosse, hockey, and more. It also puts its reach at close to 10 million games and more than a million teams a year. GameChanger is owned and operated by DICK'S Sporting Goods, described as one of the largest sporting goods retailers in the United States.

before.name: ClassLink
before.description: Single sign-on, rostering and usage analytics for public school districts - exhibited at CoSN 2026, EDUCAUSE 2026

paragraphs: ClassLink sells identity, access and analytics software to school systems that have accumulated more educational technology than they can easily manage. The best known piece is LaunchPad, a single sign-on portal that puts a student or teacher's apps behind one login with multi-factor authentication.

Behind the portal, OneSync handles account creation and management and is pitched at tech teams losing hundreds of hours to that work by hand. Roster Server delivers class rosters and carries 1EdTech certification for interoperability. An add-on called DataGuard masks personally identifiable fields before roster data leaves for a vendor. A separate product, ThreatScan, watches the dark web for district credentials that have already been exposed. Analytics reports digital engagement from the district level down to the individual student.

The company says over 3,000 school systems use its products. It describes itself as the single sign-on platform chosen by over 25 million users. ClassLink states that it connects to more than 6,000 digital learning resources.

before.name: Tantalus Systems
before.description: Smart grid AMI and grid analytics for public power utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Tantalus is a technology company selling grid modernization systems to public power and electric cooperative utilities. It has been delivering data-centric products to that market for more than 35 years.

The products sit on the Tantalus Grid Modernization Platform, a modular architecture meant to move data across devices, systems and vendors. One piece is edge-computing metering infrastructure aimed at resiliency, reliability and lower total cost of ownership. Another handles load management and distributed energy resources sitting behind the meter. A gateway device fits any ANSI meter socket and adds visibility and control behind the meter without replacing the meter itself.

Utilities across North America partner with the company on distribution grid work, with published case studies including one in Bolivar, Tennessee. Tantalus Systems trades on the TSX under the symbol GRID and on OTCQX. It is based in Burnaby, British Columbia. Recent announcements include a debt restructuring and an annual survey of how utilities view grid modernization.

paragraphs: SimpliGov sells a workflow platform for government agencies, built around the applications, approvals and casework that programs run on. Its stated scope is anything that moves through approvals, whatever the department.

Intake starts with online forms that meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards. Program teams lay out the steps on a drag-and-drop stage builder instead of writing custom code. The engine routes applications and decisions by rule, data threshold and the agency organizational structure. Approvals are signed inside the workflow with native e-signature tools. Dashboards track processing times, bottlenecks and audit trails.

Agency examples include New Castle County processing $322.8 million in emergency grants and passing its audit with zero findings. Another describes a California city automating more than 70 workflows and saving 17,000 labor hours a month. The forms page cites a federal accessibility mandate, 28 CFR Part 35, that larger public entities must meet by April 26, 2027. The platform is described as cloud-native and meeting government data privacy, security and accessibility mandates.

paragraphs: Overstory sells vegetation intelligence to electric utilities, from investor-owned utilities to municipalities and cooperatives. The analysis rests on satellite imagery, which in one European project was used to identify 37 species of vegetation.

The company notes that vegetation management is typically a utility's greatest operations budget item. Its pitch is spending less on unnecessary trimming and more on riskier areas. Utilities can see strike trees, declining trees and hazard trees individually or aggregated. Encroachment risk, hazard trees and species identification can be laid over wildfire risk maps to show where trimming matters most. The same data lets a utility verify and document risk reduction from work that contractors completed.

Risk reports are meant to support data-driven conversations with regulators, insurers and executives. Indra den Bakker and Anniek Schouten founded the company in Lisbon in 2018. The company says it has worked with more than 50 investor-owned utilities and cooperatives across the Americas and Europe.

paragraphs: Samsara sells a platform to organizations that run vehicles and equipment, pitched on improving safety, lowering costs and changing how operations work. For fleets it covers live GPS tracking, vehicle diagnostics, fuel analytics and compliance reporting. The company presents this as one platform working across every part of an operation rather than separate tools.

Its cameras pair safety detections with video that managers can pull on demand. The company says the system watches for drowsiness, distraction, tailgating and forward collision risk. It states that these are caught in real time and trigger an in-cab alert before a manager is involved. A multicamera option adds up to four auxiliary HD feeds for visibility around the vehicle. A separate site product brings third-party cameras at facilities into a cloud dashboard for onboarding and troubleshooting.

The camera pages list transportation and logistics, field services, construction, public sector and essential services among the industries served. For school districts the company describes arm-mounted cameras that enforce school bus stop-arm compliance during pickups and drop-offs. Among its customer stories is one saying the City of El Paso recovered $1.3M in assets and reduced accidents by 29%. A site camera gateway is listed as compliant with the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019.

before.name: Recidiviz
before.description: Data and case-management tools for state corrections and supervision agencies

paragraphs: Recidiviz is a non-profit that partners with criminal justice agencies on technology and data. Its customers are state departments of corrections and the staff who run prisons and community supervision.

The Corrections Platform is modular, so an agency can replace its legacy software entirely or plug in modules as it wants them. Underneath, the organization joins disconnected agency databases into one standardized data layer that feeds the tools above it. Those tools surface people who are eligible for programs, reclassification, or release.

Day-to-day users are administrators, case managers, and officers, whom the team says it goes into the field to talk with before designing anything. The organization says it works with 19 state departments of corrections responsible for almost 1 in 2 people in U.S. prisons and on community supervision. It began as a volunteer project at Google. In 2019 it became a standalone non-profit.

before.name: FLASH
before.description: Cloud parking OS and reservations for airports, cities and venues

paragraphs: Flash sells parking technology that connects asset owners, operators and drivers through software, hardware and demand channels. It says the platform is implemented across hotels, airports, municipalities, new construction and higher education.

Drivers reserve through the apps, ticket platforms and vehicle interfaces they already use. Camera-based access lets them enter and exit without stopping at a barrier. Express Pay, powered by Vision AI cameras, delivers automated ticketless parking. Enrollment for that happens once through ParkMobile or ParkWhiz. EV charging sits in the same flow, so drivers locate, reserve and pay for charging alongside parking. A valet product lets customers text to request their car.

Support runs through a network of regional offices and field technicians. One highlighted result points to work completed in 22 days at Denver International Airport.

before.name: ADS Environmental Services (IDEX)
before.description: Sewer flow monitoring and I&I analytics for municipal wastewater utilities - exhibited at WEFTEC 2026

paragraphs: ADS Environmental Services provides flow, level and rainfall monitoring for wastewater, storm and surface water systems. The buyers are municipal owners who need to know what is happening in their collection systems when it rains. The problems addressed include sanitary sewer overflows, sewer cleaning, combined sewer overflows and inflow and infiltration.

Monitors in the sewer feed software for visualizing, analyzing and managing the network. An agency can buy the equipment and run the program with its own staff. At the other end of the range, the company handles everything from placing the equipment to sending the alerts. A newer offering applies machine learning to spot developing blockages early enough to act on them.

Peter Petroff established the company in 1975 after a NASA career as a lunar guidance system engineer. A network of more than 400 monitors in Sydney, Australia in 1990 is described as a milestone in the company history. Product quality management certifications have been held since 1994, including an ISO 9001:2015 certificate issued by CSA Group. Offices sit across North America and Australia, with the corporate office in Huntsville, Alabama, and open roles are posted within IDEX Corporation.

before.name: Forerunner
before.description: Floodplain management software: NFIP/CRS compliance, elevation certificates; $26.3M Series B

paragraphs: Forerunner sells software it calls a geospatial intelligence layer. The platform unifies geospatial data, field operations, and AI-powered workflows in one place. Local government is a core buyer, with compliance work across stormwater, floodplain, and code enforcement programs. The company also markets to energy and infrastructure operators handling inspections across active sites and assets.

At the base sits a map-first view holding every asset, permit parcel, violation, and environmental layer. On top of it run configurable workflows for inspections, permits, violations, and grant tracking. Inspection findings then generate corrective actions, and permit deadlines trigger notifications. The company says adoption brings no rip-and-replace projects and no major workflow disruptions. It claims teams are up and running in weeks.

Published case studies name the Puerto Rico Planning Board, which the company says replaced paper forms and spreadsheets for field inspections and code compliance. Another states that Lee County saves approximately 16 hours of staff time per week. A further case study describes Ponce Inlet centralizing National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System workflows to reclaim 10 or more hours per week.

paragraphs: FMX sells facilities and maintenance management software that organizations use to streamline processes and get more out of their assets. For cities and counties, the pitch is maximizing asset performance, allocating spaces and funding, and streamlining resident service delivery. A school edition promises facility management software that will meet a district where it is at.

Work order management streamlines request submissions and helps staff resolve maintenance issues. Preventive maintenance handles compliance and schedules recurring tasks. Reporting tracks labor hours and costs so investments can be justified. Separate products cover vehicles, keeping a fleet on the road and tracking repairs. The products are cloud-based. A 14-day free trial is offered.

The company says it serves over 400K professionals. Beyond schools it sells into public works, covering public infrastructure, assets, public property, capital projects, and community events. It points to 400+ reviews on Capterra, Software Advice, and G2. Pricing turns on how many users an organization has, or the number of students enrolled for public K-12 schools.

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile_research.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.
